# Sketching and constraints

A sketch lies on a plane: an origin plane, a construction plane or a planar face. Start one with
**Create Sketch** (`sketch.create`) and click a plane, or pick a face first. Right-clicking a
plane, in the view or on its browser row, offers **Create Sketch** on that plane too.
**Finish Sketch** returns to the model.

In scripts, `XY`, `XZ`, `YZ` and their `Top`, `Front`, `Right` aliases name origin planes.
These names are reserved: a construction plane cannot be created with or renamed to one
(case-insensitive). If an older design already has a construction plane with such a name, a
string argument naming it is ambiguous and is rejected; use the other alias (`XY` for `Top`)
for the origin plane, the construction feature's numeric ID to select it, or an explicit
`{origin: [x,y,z], normal: [x,y,z]}` plane. Existing saved references retain their meaning;
opening a design does not reinterpret old sketches.

Curves adapt to the current zoom and display scale. Picking and highlighting use the same
visible boundary, including small circles at Fit and sketches in rotated components.
Profile shading follows those curves while preserving holes. Zooming changes the display
without changing sketch geometry, dimensions, or undo history.
On short windows or enlarged displays, the Sketch Palette's options scroll while its
constraint status and **Finish Sketch** button remain visible.

## Geometry

**Point** is available directly on the default Sketch **CREATE** toolbar. Click it, then
click in the sketch to place a point. Existing toolbar customizations are kept; use
**Reset Toolbar** from the toolbar's context menu to restore the default buttons.

Lines and polylines (L), rectangles (two-point R, three-point, centre), circles (centre C,
two-point, three-point, tangent), arcs (three-point, centre, tangent), polygons, slots, ellipses,
fit-point and control-point splines, conics, points and text. **Construction** (X) turns curves
into reference geometry that doesn't form profiles. Modify tools include trim (T), extend, break,
fillet, chamfer, offset (O), mirror, patterns, move/copy and scale.

The Sketch Palette's **Construction Geometries** option hides construction curves while you
work. A hidden construction curve cannot be picked by a click or by a box. Nothing invisible
is selectable. The option belongs to one sketch and is saved with the design. Centerlines are
a line type of their own and keep showing. Projected geometry that carries the construction
line type, such as the trace of a plane, answers to **Projected Geometries** instead. The
option changes display only. Construction curves were already outside every profile.

Polygon tools show their edge outline while positioning the second point, so the orientation
can be checked before placement. Inscribed and circumscribed polygons retain their support
circle and update the outline when the inline **Sides** value changes.

**Text** is set in the built-in font (Liberation Sans) unless it is given another: `sketch.text` and
`sketch.edit_text` take a `font`, the family or full name of an installed font ("DejaVu Sans") or the path
of a `.ttf` / `.otf` file, and the **Edit Text** dialog has a **Font** field for it. An unknown font is an
error, and the font is kept with the text in the design, so the text stays editable in it. `SOLIDCRAFT_FONT_DIRS`
adds folders to the ones searched for installed fonts. A text's `height`, its `angle` and each coordinate of
its `at` can be expressions of the design's parameters, given as strings (`"height": "plate_height / 10"`,
`"at": ["plate_width / 2", 5]`): the text keeps the expression and follows the parameters when they change, and
saves it with the design. A number takes the place of an expression, and so does moving the text or dragging its
handles (what moves becomes a number; turning a text leaves its height as it was). A string that names no
parameter is the number it comes to. The same two commands refuse a `text` that is not a string, an `at` that is
not two numbers or expressions, a `height` or `angle` that is neither (or a `height` that is not positive) and an
expression that cannot be worked out with a message, instead of drawing the text with a default; left out, they
keep their defaults.

Right-click a letter's filled interior or outline and choose **Edit Text**. You can also
start **Edit Text** first and click the letter. All outlines belonging to that text are
highlighted while the dialog is open. A profile bounded by multiple text sources or other
geometry cannot identify one text: use **Select Other** to choose its outline instead.
Change the text, font, baseline X/Y, height or angle, then confirm with **OK**; **Cancel**
keeps the original text. Position and height use the document's units. The four fields take
expressions: one that names a parameter (`plate_width / 2`) stays an expression, is shown as typed
when the dialog is opened again, and keeps the text following the parameter.

To work on the letters' shapes themselves, right-click the text and choose **Explode Text**
(`sketch.break_link` with the text's `link`). Its outlines stay where they are as ordinary
lines, arcs and curves that can be picked, trimmed, dimensioned and extruded one by one; the
text itself is gone, so it can no longer be edited as text or follow parameters. Undo brings it back.

A text can follow a curve of its sketch (its **Path**). That curve becomes construction: the
letters stand on it and their descenders cross it, so as a normal curve it would cut them into
pieces, and picking the text would pick those pieces. Taking the text off the curve leaves it
construction; **Normal/Construction** turns it back.

Drag a text outline to move all its letters together. Let go to finish in one undo step,
or press **Esc** during the drag to restore the original text. The text stays editable.
For an exact displacement, select an outline and choose **Move/Copy** from its context menu.
Enter **Distance X**, **Distance Y** and an optional **Angle** about the text's baseline;
lengths accept document units or explicit units such as `1 in`. Enable **Create Copy** to
leave the original in place and create a separately editable text. **Cancel** leaves the
design unchanged. Projected geometry remains protected from ordinary dragging.


**Project** (P) and **Intersect** bring model edges into the sketch as linked geometry that
follows later changes. Sketching on a face projects its edges automatically.
A projected edge stays the edge that was picked, wherever a later change moves it; when that
edge no longer exists, the projection keeps its last shape and the sketch says it was lost.
For Project, select visible source curves or points from another sketch, model edges,
faces, vertices or bodies, or axes and planes, then press P. The entire supported selection
is projected in one undo step. A rejected projection keeps the selection for correction;
an empty or mixed selection starts the ordinary picking tool. External sketch selections
retain their source sketch, even when the active sketch uses the same point or curve names.

A sketch on a construction plane built from the model (through a sketch line, through three
points, midway between two faces…) projects, intersects, includes and holds text like a sketch
on any other plane, and its links follow when a parameter moves that plane.

Run from a script or the control channel, every command that adds sketch geometry returns the
ids of what it added (`created: {points, curves, constraints, dimensions}`). Ids are stable and
never reused within a sketch, even after a delete, so a script can dimension or constrain the new
geometry right away.

Extend finds intersections with exact ellipses, rational conics and spline spans. It keeps the
original line or circular support and extends only beyond the selected endpoint; conflicting
constraints or an ambiguous overlap leave the sketch unchanged.

Closed convex chains of tangent lines and circular arcs support inward offsets that consume
a rounded corner. When the offset passes the corner radius, the neighbouring straight
supports meet at a sharp corner. The surviving lines and endpoint IDs stay stable; the
retired arcs return under their original IDs if a later edit restores their radius.
Whole-boundary profile selections follow this transition through save and reopen, so an
extruded lip can remain associative. Existing eligible closed analytic offsets upgrade
without changing their saved geometry or IDs.

This transition requires a closed convex boundary with tangent junctions and a certified
nonempty region. An extinguished arc referenced individually by a constraint or another
offset cannot retire. Creating another offset from an already sharp retired boundary also
requires breaking its association first. Open, nonconvex and mixed free-form chains keep
their existing behavior. Break Offset Association freezes the current boundary, including
private arc centres and construction flags, for independent editing.

Offsets of smooth ellipses, conics and splines follow their source after dimension changes,
dragging and reopening a design. Their stored cubic spline has a whole-span normal-distance
error bound of 0.002 mm. Singular tangents, curvature cusps, possible self-intersections and
excessive subdivisions are refused. Offset these curves individually: mixed chain junctions
currently require separate geometry. `sketch.offset.break` releases an offset for independent
editing, and undo restores its association. Older independently sampled offsets remain independent.
The fit points of such an offset stay hidden, except the two ends of an open one: lines and
arcs snap to them and stay coincident with them as the offset follows its source, so the gap
between a spline and its offset can be closed into a profile.
Smooth open and newly created smooth closed offsets can be offset again, including bounded
refinement after a source edit. New closed outputs use a periodic cubic fit with continuous
tangent and curvature at the seam. Break Offset Association preserves that interpolation,
and its closing point remains joined when dragged. Deleting an output also removes its
unused private fit points; deleting a source with a retained dependent is refused.

For explicit closed fit splines, `sketch.spline.fit_point` accepts `periodic: true` and at
least three distinct cyclic samples. It closes the loop automatically. Existing calls and
older saved closed splines retain natural interpolation; older associative closed offsets
also retain their saved natural fit. A legacy seam without a unique normal still refuses
another offset. Periodic intent is stored on each curve and survives save, reopen and Break.
While drawing a fit spline, click its starting point after three distinct samples to close
it smoothly. Right-click finishes an ordinary natural fit. Offset accepts both ellipse
handles and dense fitted curves; the second click sets the side and distance from the curve.

While drawing in a planar sketch, **Construction** (X) changes the line type without
ending the tool or losing picked points and inline values. The preview and hover feedback
keep construction dashes and centerline dash-dot patterns visible. With curves selected,
Construction changes those curves as before.

Enable **3D Sketch** in the Sketch Palette to draw lines, fit splines and points off the plane.
While placing these points, you can snap to points on other visible sketches. For a bridge
line, start Line and click an endpoint on each source sketch; each endpoint uses its source
plane, even when that plane differs from the active sketch. These snaps capture positions;
they do not create associative links to the source points.
New 3D geometry follows its sketch's component placement, including the selected occurrence
and pending position changes. Click a drawn fit point to show its move triad; its arrows move
along world X, Y and Z. Scripts also supply world coordinates to `sketch.line3d`,
`sketch.spline3d`, `sketch.point3d` and `sketch.move3d`. Activate the desired occurrence before
editing an explicit sketch belonging to a component with multiple placements.

Older drawn or detached 3D wires keep their saved world positions. Included and surface-linked
wires with an explicit component marker keep that meaning after the link is broken. Old files
whose links became lost after an incorrectly scoped cross-component refresh may require a
fresh link once the source is available; their stored point values are preserved on opening.

## Constraints and dimensions

**Horizontal/Vertical** accepts a click on a line or clicks on two distinct sketch points,
including the origin, endpoints and circle centres. For two points, it chooses horizontal
or vertical alignment from their current positions. Esc cancels a pending first point.

The solver is SolidCraft's own (damped Gauss–Newton with degree-of-freedom analysis). Constraints:
coincident, horizontal/vertical, parallel, perpendicular, tangent, equal, concentric, collinear,
midpoint, symmetry, fix, curvature (G2) and polygon. **Sketch Dimension** (D) adds linear,
aligned, horizontal, vertical, point-to-line, line-to-circle, radius, diameter and angle
dimensions. Each is a parameter
(`d1`, `d2`, …), so it can hold an expression.

Press D, click what you want to measure and type the value: as soon as the click settles the
dimension (one line, circle or arc, or the second point or line of a distance or angle), its
value box takes the keyboard with the measured value selected, so typing replaces it. Numbers,
units (`1 in`), expressions (`2*width`) and parameter names all work; letters go into the box,
not to tool shortcuts. While you type, the dimension text follows the cursor, and Enter places
it there (or in its default place if you haven't moved the cursor) as one undo step. Esc
cancels the dimension.

You can still place the text first. Before you type, a click on empty sketch space puts the
text there and keeps the value box focused; a click on another point or line makes the
dimension a distance or angle instead; Tab leaves the picks waiting for a click to place the
text.

Between two points, or on a line, that don't line up with an axis, where you place the
dimension picks what it measures: across from them, the distance between them; above or below
them, the horizontal distance; beside them, the vertical distance.

A line and a circle or arc (click the line, then the circle's edge, or the other way round)
measure from the line to the circle's edge, square to the line: the gap between them, 0 when
the circle touches the line. When the line cuts through the circle, the dimension measures how
far the edge reaches past the line instead. An arc is measured to the circle it lies on. For
the distance to the centre, click the centre point instead of the edge. In scripts:
`{"command": "sketch.dimension", "params": {"entities": ["l1", "c1"], "value": 5}}`.

A dimension the sketch can't take, because the geometry is already fixed by other constraints
and dimensions, is added as a driven (reference) dimension instead: it is shown in
parentheses, measures the sketch, and has no value to edit.

For **Coincident**, pick two points, a point and a curve (in either order), or two
distinct straight lines. Two lines join their closest pair of endpoints; the first
picked line stays in place when the existing constraints allow it. Pick endpoints
explicitly when you want to connect a different pair.

Horizontal/Vertical also applies immediately to one selected line or two distinct selected
points. Shift-click to add the second point before choosing the constraint.

For Parallel, Perpendicular, Equal, Tangent, Concentric and Collinear, select exactly two
sketch curves (Shift-click to add the second) and choose the constraint to apply it immediately.
You can also start the constraint first and then pick its curves. An incomplete or mixed
selection leaves the tool ready for ordinary picking.

Coincident accepts an exact selection of two points or a point and a curve. Midpoint
accepts one point and one line, in either selection order. Symmetry accepts two distinct
points and one symmetry line, regardless of where the line occurs in the selection.
Successful constraints clear the selection; rejected constraints preserve it.

Under-constrained geometry is blue and fully constrained geometry turns dark, and the status
shows the remaining degrees of freedom. A constraint or dimension that would over-constrain the
sketch is refused rather than applied. Drag a point to move it; the solver keeps every
constraint while you drag.

## Profiles

Closed loops become profiles automatically, including regions split by crossing lines and
islands inside outlines. Extrude, revolve, sweep and loft pick profiles.

A feature remembers a picked profile by the curves around it, not by where it was clicked:
`"profiles": [{"curves": ["l1", "l2", "a1", "l3"]}]` (or `[{"curves": ["c1"]}]` for a circle)
picks the region whose outer loop is made of exactly those curves, or the pieces of them that
other curves cut off. It is found again on every recompute, so the feature keeps the same region
when a parameter moves the geometry. Islands inside the region are its holes. When no region, or
more than one (both halves of a circle cut by a line), is bounded by exactly those curves, the
feature reports an error rather than taking another region. Profiles picked by index or by point
(`[{"point": [x, y]}]`) are stored the same way when the feature is made.

## Measurement units

Change the current design through **Document Settings > Units** in the browser.
The units preference applies to new designs. Existing sketch annotations, live drawing
lengths and Measure follow the current design units without resizing geometry.
Inches display at least three decimal places and retain a meaningful fourth digit;
a higher display precision can be selected in Preferences. Bare length values typed
in the dimension tool use the current design units. Explicit units such as `25.4 mm`
remain valid in an inch design. Angular dimensions keep their angular units. Deliberately typed four-place inch literals
retain trailing zeros. Component/canvas distance controls and inspection, parts-library
and flat-pattern measurements follow design units too; parameter expressions and metric
standard names retain their explicit authored units.

Measure shows the currently selected distance (centre, minimum or maximum) and separate X, Y and Z
distances on the canvas. The component dimensions follow the world axes and remain visible
until the Measure dialog closes. To hide these extra lines and labels, turn off
**Preferences > Graphics > Show X/Y/Z distances**. The choice is saved between runs.

### Reviewing mirror, pattern, and offset results

Mirror, rectangular/circular Pattern, and Offset show the active selection step in their
shared tool window. Click an input to change it; click a selected object again or Ctrl/Cmd-click
it to remove it. Each input has its own Clear button. Source inputs show a count, and single
references identify the chosen mirror line, direction, or centre. Box selection also works
while the window is open. Sketch modify tools take geometry from the sketch being edited.

Proposed sketch geometry appears **green** before confirmation. Change the inputs or values to
update the preview, then press **OK**. **Cancel** discards the preview. A circular pattern centre
can be an existing point or a position clicked in empty sketch space.

Sketch patterns keep each instance related to the seed geometry: moving the seed updates the
copies, and a copy cannot deform independently. Circle and ellipse radii follow the seed too.
Choose a circle's centre point to keep a circular pattern centred on that circle. A centre
placed in empty space becomes a sketch point that can be dimensioned or made coincident.
Double-click the pattern badge (at the circular centre or beside the rectangular seed), or
right-click a seed or copy and choose **Edit Sketch Pattern**, to change quantity, spacing,
direction or total angle. Confirmed edits preserve surviving instance ids; Cancel discards
the preview. Pattern settings survive save/reopen and undo/redo. Deleting a seed, copy or
pattern relation breaks that association and leaves the remaining geometry independent.
Patterns saved by older versions remain independent copies; recreate them to add associations.

Offset distances are editable driving dimensions: double-click a dimension or change its model
parameter to resize the offset without moving its source curves. The selected side, distance,
and association survive save/reopen and undo/redo. Symmetric offsets share one driving distance;
Two Sides has an independent distance for each side. Disconnected selected curves or chains are
all offset. Breaking an association retains its current geometry and removes that association's
driver. Older offsets retain their saved fixed distances.

resizes or rotates. Two line midpoints can also be aligned. Hovering and the first pick are
only previews; Esc cancels them without changing the sketch. Accepting the second pick reuses
or creates a sketch point with an ordinary Midpoint constraint, then adds the H/V constraint
in one undo step. Both constraints can be selected and deleted independently; deleting either
keeps the point. After a fillet or chamfer, its Midpoint constraint refers to the original full
side, retained as construction geometry, just like a manually constrained midpoint.

Scripts use the same command, with a midpoint reference in the `points` array:

```json
{"command":"sketch.constraint.horizontal_vertical","params":{"points":[{"midpoint":"l1"},"c1.center"],"mode":"vertical"}}
```

`mode` can be `horizontal` or `vertical`; omitting it chooses from the current positions.

The solver is SolidCraft's own (damped Gauss–Newton with degree-of-freedom analysis). Constraints:
coincident, horizontal/vertical, parallel, perpendicular, tangent, equal, concentric, collinear,
midpoint, symmetry, fix, curvature (G2) and polygon. **Sketch Dimension** (D) adds linear,
aligned, horizontal, vertical, point-to-line, line-to-circle, radius, diameter and angle
dimensions. Each is a parameter
(`d1`, `d2`, …), so it can hold an expression.

Press D, click what you want to measure and type the value: as soon as the click settles the
dimension (one line, circle or arc, or the second point or line of a distance or angle), its
value box takes the keyboard with the measured value selected, so typing replaces it. Numbers,
units (`1 in`), expressions (`2*width`) and parameter names all work; letters go into the box,
not to tool shortcuts. While you type, the dimension text follows the cursor, and Enter places
it there (or in its default place if you haven't moved the cursor) as one undo step. Esc
cancels the dimension.

You can still place the text first. Before you type, a click on empty sketch space puts the
text there and keeps the value box focused; a click on another point or line makes the
dimension a distance or angle instead; Tab leaves the picks waiting for a click to place the
text.

Between two points, or on a line, that don't line up with an axis, where you place the
dimension picks what it measures: across from them, the distance between them; above or below
them, the horizontal distance; beside them, the vertical distance.

A line and a circle or arc (click the line, then the circle's edge, or the other way round)
measure from the line to the circle's edge, square to the line: the gap between them, 0 when
the circle touches the line. When the line cuts through the circle, the dimension measures how
far the edge reaches past the line instead. An arc is measured to the circle it lies on. For
the distance to the centre, click the centre point instead of the edge. In scripts:
`{"command": "sketch.dimension", "params": {"entities": ["l1", "c1"], "value": 5}}`.

A dimension the sketch can't take, because the geometry is already fixed by other constraints
and dimensions, is added as a driven (reference) dimension instead: it is shown in
parentheses, measures the sketch, and has no value to edit.

For **Coincident**, pick two points, a point and a curve (in either order), or two
distinct straight lines. Two lines join their closest pair of endpoints; the first
picked line stays in place when the existing constraints allow it. Pick endpoints
explicitly when you want to connect a different pair.

Horizontal/Vertical also applies immediately to one selected line or two distinct selected
points. Shift-click to add the second point before choosing the constraint.

For Parallel, Perpendicular, Equal, Tangent, Concentric and Collinear, select exactly two
sketch curves (Shift-click to add the second) and choose the constraint to apply it immediately.
You can also start the constraint first and then pick its curves. An incomplete or mixed
selection leaves the tool ready for ordinary picking.

Coincident accepts an exact selection of two points or a point and a curve. Midpoint
accepts one point and one line, in either selection order. Symmetry accepts two distinct
points and one symmetry line, regardless of where the line occurs in the selection.
Successful constraints clear the selection; rejected constraints preserve it.

Under-constrained geometry is blue and fully constrained geometry turns dark, and the status
shows the remaining degrees of freedom. A constraint or dimension that would over-constrain the
sketch is refused rather than applied. Drag a point to move it; the solver keeps every
constraint while you drag.

## Profiles

Closed loops become profiles automatically, including regions split by crossing lines and
islands inside outlines. Extrude, revolve, sweep and loft pick profiles.

A feature remembers a picked profile by the curves around it, not by where it was clicked:
`"profiles": [{"curves": ["l1", "l2", "a1", "l3"]}]` (or `[{"curves": ["c1"]}]` for a circle)
picks the region whose outer loop is made of exactly those curves, or the pieces of them that
other curves cut off. It is found again on every recompute, so the feature keeps the same region
when a parameter moves the geometry. Islands inside the region are its holes. When no region, or
more than one (both halves of a circle cut by a line), is bounded by exactly those curves, the
feature reports an error rather than taking another region. Profiles picked by index or by point
(`[{"point": [x, y]}]`) are stored the same way when the feature is made.

## Measurement units

Change the current design through **Document Settings > Units** in the browser.
The units preference applies to new designs. Existing sketch annotations, live drawing
lengths and Measure follow the current design units without resizing geometry.
Inches display at least three decimal places and retain a meaningful fourth digit;
a higher display precision can be selected in Preferences. Bare length values typed
in the dimension tool use the current design units. Explicit units such as `25.4 mm`
remain valid in an inch design. Angular dimensions keep their angular units. Deliberately typed four-place inch literals
retain trailing zeros. Component/canvas distance controls and inspection, parts-library
and flat-pattern measurements follow design units too; parameter expressions and metric
standard names retain their explicit authored units.

Measure shows the currently selected distance (centre, minimum or maximum) and separate X, Y and Z
distances on the canvas. The component dimensions follow the world axes and remain visible
until the Measure dialog closes. To hide these extra lines and labels, turn off
**Preferences > Graphics > Show X/Y/Z distances**. The choice is saved between runs.

### Reviewing mirror, pattern, and offset results

Mirror, rectangular/circular Pattern, and Offset show the active selection step in their
shared tool window. Click an input to change it; click a selected object again or Ctrl/Cmd-click
it to remove it. Each input has its own Clear button. Source inputs show a count, and single
references identify the chosen mirror line, direction, or centre. Box selection also works
while the window is open. Sketch modify tools take geometry from the sketch being edited.

Proposed sketch geometry appears **green** before confirmation. Change the inputs or values to
update the preview, then press **OK**. **Cancel** discards the preview. A circular pattern centre
can be an existing point or a position clicked in empty sketch space.

Sketch patterns keep each instance related to the seed geometry: moving the seed updates the
copies, and a copy cannot deform independently. Circle and ellipse radii follow the seed too.
Choose a circle's centre point to keep a circular pattern centred on that circle. A centre
placed in empty space becomes a sketch point that can be dimensioned or made coincident.
Double-click the pattern badge (at the circular centre or beside the rectangular seed), or
right-click a seed or copy and choose **Edit Sketch Pattern**, to change quantity, spacing,
direction or total angle. Confirmed edits preserve surviving instance ids; Cancel discards
the preview. Pattern settings survive save/reopen and undo/redo. Deleting a seed, copy or
pattern relation breaks that association and leaves the remaining geometry independent.
Patterns saved by older versions remain independent copies; recreate them to add associations.

Offset distances are editable driving dimensions: double-click a dimension or change its model
parameter to resize the offset without moving its source curves. The selected side, distance,
and association survive save/reopen and undo/redo. Symmetric offsets share one driving distance;
Two Sides has an independent distance for each side. Disconnected selected curves or chains are
all offset. Breaking an association retains its current geometry and removes that association's
driver. Older offsets retain their saved fixed distances.

# A tour of the window

![The SolidCraft window](../generated/sample-plate.png)

- **Title bar.** On Windows and Linux the application bar is the window's title bar. On the left:
  the File menu (New, Open, Save, Save As, Export…), undo and redo, the Home tab (the start page)
  and one tab per open design (each with its own undo history, selection and camera; a dot marks
  unsaved changes). On the right: Report a bug, Help (?), Preferences (which hold the theme) and the
  window's buttons.
- **Toolbar.** The workspace switcher (DESIGN) sits on the left. The tabs (SOLID, SURFACE,
  SHEET METAL, PLASTIC, UTILITIES, and SKETCH while you sketch) hold panels of commands. Click a
  panel's name for all its commands. Drag a command from the dropdown onto a panel's label
  or empty space to append it; the insertion line shows its destination. Drop onto an existing
  button to insert before it. Buttons can also move between panels, and the layout is saved.
- **Browser** (left). The design as a tree: document settings and units, named views, the
  origin, bodies, sketches, construction planes, canvases, joints and components. The eye shows or
  hides an item, a component's radio button makes it the active component, and right-clicking any
  row gives that item's menu. Rows drag into groups and other components.
- **Viewport.** Click to select, Shift or Ctrl to add (Preferences › Selection), drag for a window or crossing box. While sketching, Ctrl/Cmd or Alt/Option suppress auto-snap by default; Shift prefers a midpoint. To
  reach something under something else (two lines drawn on top of each other, coincident points,
  an edge in front of a face, overlapping bodies), hold the left button still for half a second
  (long-press on a touch screen) or right-click › **Select Other…**: a list of everything under
  the cursor opens there, the sketch being edited first. Hovering a row lights it up; clicking it
  selects it (Shift or Ctrl adds), and in a command's dialog it goes to the active selection box.
  Esc or a click elsewhere closes the list. Clicking again on the same spot, with nothing changed
  in between, selects the next thing in that list. The
  wheel zooms at the cursor, the middle button pans and right-drag orbits freely (the mouse
  preset in Preferences switches to SolidWorks, Inventor, Alias, Blender, Tinkercad, OpenSCAD or Touchpad style). On a
  trackpad, pinch zooms and two-finger scroll pans (Navigation › Two-finger scroll pans;
  off: scroll zooms like the wheel); mouse wheels zoom and the thumb wheel pans sideways.
  Shift+middle orbits freely
  in the default and Inventor presets. In every preset, Ctrl+left drag (Cmd on macOS) that starts
  on empty space orbits; a Ctrl+click still adds to the selection. Shift+right-drag snaps to the nearest standard or
  diagonal view; Shift does not request snapping when the preset already requires it to orbit.
  **Mouse gestures** (Preferences › Navigation, off by default) work with the SolidWorks mouse preset
  only (the wheel orbits, Ctrl + wheel pans) and take over the right button, which then no longer
  orbits: hold it and move the pointer 4 pt to open a ring of tools (280 pt inside, 350 pt outside), even
  while a tool is active, and touch a tool's zone to take it. A right-click that does not move still
  opens the usual context menu. Each studio has its own
  tools, and **Customize…** sets how many tools a studio's ring holds and in which place. Zones
  alternate between two tints, three when the number of tools is odd. The optional radial context
  menu is a separate setting, and gestures take the right button from it while they are on.

  With **Touchpad** selected in Preferences › Navigation, hold **Shift** and move the pointer to
  pan, or hold **Alt** (**Option** on macOS) and move it to orbit—no mouse button is needed.
  Vertical two-finger scrolling zooms in this preset, regardless of the saved two-finger pan
  setting; switching presets restores that setting. Release the modifier to stop navigating.
  Shift+click and Shift+left-drag still select. Combined Shift+Alt or Ctrl/Cmd modifiers do not
  start pointer-only navigation.
  The axis view shows the world's X/Y/Z directions in SolidCraft's colors. Click a signed
  axis tip to look along that axis; click the aligned tip again to look from the opposite side.
  Drag the axis view to orbit around the view centre, with Shift for snapping. Top and bottom
  keep the nearest quarter-turn heading. The house, the navigation bar's Home button and a middle-button double-click in the view go
  home, framing what is shown now (Navigation › **Middle double-click** can make it Fit, which
  keeps the orientation, or turn it off).
  Right-click for the marking menu: eight commands around the cursor, plus a
  menu for whatever is under it. Near the window's bottom or right edge a menu opens above or
  to the left of the cursor, so it stays in view.
  Shaded views omit certified smooth joins between spline spans on extruded
  walls. Real creases, cap outlines and authored face splits remain visible.
  Wireframe retains its edge presentation, and hiding a join does not remove its CAD
  identity or change the exported solid. Unsupported or uncertain wall geometry
  keeps its existing edge presentation.
- **Dialogs** dock on the right with a live preview. Most features also show drag handles and a
  value box in the viewport.
- **Timeline** (bottom). Every feature in order. Double-click to edit, drag the marker to roll
  back, and drag features to reorder them.
- **S box.** Press S anywhere for a command search at the cursor. Pin the commands you use most
  to its top.

Preferences (File › Preferences) hold the theme, the units of new designs, the mouse preset, the
visual style and autosave. Graphics › Colour vision gives the colours that carry a meaning (sketch
states, axes, bends, analyses, icons) values for a weak red, green or blue sense: Protan, Deutan or
Tritan. In a mode, the faces Draft and Accessibility Analysis mark as failing are striped too.
Command messages and errors show for a few seconds in the status chip at the bottom left of the view. Click the chip, or choose Help › **Messages…**, for every message of the session: newest first, errors in red, each line selectable, with **Copy all** for a bug report.
Help › Keyboard Shortcuts lists every key, and File › Keyboard
Shortcuts changes them.

### Colour themes

General › **Theme** lists Dark, Light and System (follows the operating system), the built-in
Gruvbox themes (dark and light, each in hard, normal and soft contrast) and any themes you have
imported. A choice applies at once.

A theme is a small JSON file that starts from the Dark or Light palette and changes any of its
colours by name:

```json
{
  "format": "solidcraft-theme/1",
  "name": "My Theme",
  "base": "dark",
  "colors": {
    "panel": "#282828",
    "text": "#ebdbb2",
    "accent": "#83a598",
    "viewport_top": "#32302f",
    "viewport_bottom": "#32302f",
    "triad": ["#fb4934", "#b8bb26", "#83a598"]
  }
}
```

Colours are `#rrggbb`, or `#rrggbbaa` for translucent ones. A few colours, such as the view
triad's X, Y and Z, take a list. Any colour the file leaves out keeps the base palette's value.

- **Import…** adds a theme file and turns it on. Importing a file with the same name again updates
  that theme. A file with an unknown colour name or a malformed colour is refused, and the message
  names every problem.
- **Export…** saves the theme on now as a complete file listing every colour. It is a good starting
  point for your own theme.
- **Remove** deletes the selected imported theme.

Imported themes are kept with your preferences, so they work in the browser app too. Colour
vision modes still apply on top of any theme.

Navigation › **Smooth wheel zoom** is on by default. Turn it off to apply each wheel or
trackpad event immediately, with no smoothing tail. It is independent of **Animate view
changes**, which controls axis views, Look At, Home and Fit. Re-enabling smoothing during
a wheel gesture takes effect after that gesture ends, avoiding leftover zoom being replayed.

Navigation › **Alias** uses Alias's camera keys: Shift+Alt+left drag orbits, Shift+Alt+middle
drag pans and Shift+Alt+right drag zooms (drag down to move away, up to move closer). Without
Shift+Alt, a left drag still selects with a box and drags sketch geometry.

Some Linux desktops take Alt+drag for themselves (moving or resizing windows), so the viewport
never sees it. To free it:

- **KDE Plasma:** System Settings › Window Management › Window Behavior › Window Actions, set
  **Modifier key** to Meta (or None).
- **GNOME:** run `gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.wm.preferences mouse-button-modifier '<Super>'`
  (or set Tweaks › Windows › Window Action Key to Super).

Shift-orbit snapping includes 45-degree edge views and isometric corner views, with a
lightly damped spring transition and a small boundary margin to prevent flicker.

On desktop, Ctrl/Cmd+Plus (or Equals) enlarges the interface, Ctrl/Cmd+Minus reduces it,
and Ctrl/Cmd+0 restores 100%. These shortcuts update the UI scale preference. The UI scale
slider in Preferences applies the new layout when released, so it stays still while dragging.

# Import and export

| Format | Read | Write |
|---|---|---|
| `.solidcraft` (versioned container or JSON design) | yes | yes |
| `.json` (self-contained plain JSON design) | yes | yes |
| STEP (AP203, AP214, AP242) | solids, assemblies, units, names, colours | AP242 with names, colours and the component tree |
| IGES 5.3 | manifold solids, or trimmed surfaces sewn into solids | manifold solids with names and colours |
| FreeCAD `.FCStd`, Rhino `.3dm` | solids, through cadmpeg (desktop app only) | |
| 3MF, STL, OBJ | mesh bodies | yes |
| glTF 2.0 (`.glb`, `.gltf` with its `.bin` files) | mesh bodies in the node tree's components, materials as appearances | |
| 3MF with face tags | as 3MF | each triangle tagged with its B-rep face, exact coordinates |
| URDF | | the assembly as a robot: links with meshes, mass and inertia, joints from the assembly's joints |
| DXF, SVG | into a sketch | sketches and flat patterns as DXF |
| PNG, JPEG | canvases and decals | |

Opening a STEP, IGES, FreeCAD or Rhino file creates a design with the file's bodies as a base feature, and
inserting one adds them to the current design. Later features build on them. Mesh bodies render,
measure, move and export, but solid features need B-rep bodies.

Every imported file (STEP, IGES, 3MF, STL, OBJ or glTF) comes in as a new component named after the
file, so its bodies never mix with yours. A STEP assembly keeps its structure: its parts and
sub-assemblies become nested components, and a part used several times is one component with an
occurrence for each place. The imported assembly is rigid: moving its component moves everything,
and its parts don't move on their own. Right-click the component and choose **Unlock Contents** to
joint the parts one by one. Undo removes a whole import in one step.

A glTF file (`.glb`, or `.gltf` with the `.bin` files it names in the same folder) comes in the
same way: its nodes become nested components, a mesh placed several times is one component with
an occurrence for each place, and the whole import is rigid until you unlock it. glTF is in metres
with Y up, so the import is scaled to millimetres and turned to stand Z up (`up: "z"` keeps the
file's axes). Each material's base colour, metal and roughness become the body's appearance, so
the model looks right in Render; textures, skins and animations are not imported. Scaled or
mirrored nodes are baked into their meshes. Compressed meshes (Draco, meshopt) are refused with a
message: save the file uncompressed first.

A 3MF project saved by a slicer comes in too, also when it keeps its objects in model parts of
their own inside the file (the 3MF Production extension): each object on the build plate becomes
a mesh body, with its parts where the slicer placed them.

**File → Save as mesh…** (also on the Mesh tab under Modify, and in the right-click menu of a
body) saves the selected bodies as STL, 3MF or 3MF with face tags (below). With **Send to slicer** ticked, it writes the file to
a temporary folder and opens it in the chosen slicer instead of asking for a file name. The slicer
list shows the slicers found on the computer with their icons; **Custom…** adds any other program
to the top of the list (kept between runs; hover an entry you added and press Delete to remove it).

Closed mechanical meshes with a constant cross-section can be rebuilt as solids with the
`mesh.convert` command (command palette, scripts and the control channel).

**File → Save as mesh…** with the format **3MF with face tags** (`file.export` or `file.save_mesh` with `format: "3mf-tagged"`) writes an
ordinary 3MF in which every triangle also names the B-rep face it lies on and every coordinate
is the tessellation's own double-precision value. Meshing and analysis tools can use the tags to
keep a model's faces (for loads, boundary conditions or feature edges); other 3MF readers ignore
them. The format is specified in [`docs/formats/3mf-face-tags.md`](https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft/blob/main/docs/formats/3mf-face-tags.md).

**File → Export URDF…** (`file.export` with a `.urdf` path) writes the assembly for robot
simulators and ROS: a link per component placement with its mesh, mass and inertia, and the
assembly's joints, so the parts move in the simulator as they do in SolidCraft. The meshes are
written as STL files next to the `.urdf`. See [`docs/urdf.md`](https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft/blob/main/docs/urdf.md).

Saves are atomic: a crash at any moment leaves either the old file or the new one, and the
replaced version is kept as `<file>.bak`. A save keeps the file's permissions, and a design
opened through a symbolic link (a synced folder linked into a project) is saved into the file the
link points to, so the link stays. Unsaved changes are autosaved to a recovery folder,
and the next launch offers to recover them. Older design files are upgraded on open, and files
from a newer version are refused with a message.

**Save** writes a container by default; files named `.json` keep JSON on subsequent saves.
**Save As** offers a container or plain JSON on
desktop; **Save As JSON** is also available in the File menu on desktop and web. Choose
the `.json` extension for plain JSON. **Export Design as JSON** writes an independent,
self-contained copy without changing the current file. Scripts can explicitly pass
`"format": "json"` to `file.save` or `file.save_as` even with a `.solidcraft` name.
Opening detects the format from the contents, so existing JSON designs keep working.
Containers favor fast reading and saving by default. Scripts can request
`"compression": "compact"` when file size matters more than CPU time.

Containers deduplicate identical STEP, mesh and image payloads. Mesh coordinates retain
their original double precision; this is not a conversion to STL. Geometry still rebuilds
from the timeline when opening. When a saved display preview is available, desktop Open
shows it while checking geometry; editing starts after the complete rebuild. Cancelling
keeps the current design. Previews cannot be edited or measured. Scripts can opt in to a disposable geometry
cache with `cache: true` on warm saves; saving never rebuilds cold geometry just to
create one. Ordinary saves and browser downloads default to `cache: false`. An additional display-mesh cache remains opt-in
with `preview: true`. Unsupported or mismatched caches are ignored. Browser opening
still rebuilds synchronously.
Warm saves with explicit `cache: true` can also include a small PNG thumbnail. It travels with the file, so
Home can show the recent design without reconstructing it when no local picture
is available. Missing or incompatible pictures use the usual thumbnail generation.
The default `cache: false` omits the portable thumbnail too.
The repository's `docs/design-container.md` describes limits and encoding details.

Designs are saved in the newest format this version of SolidCraft knows (`"format": "solidcraft/N"`
in the file). It opens designs of every older format and upgrades them as they open; a design
from a newer version asks you to update instead of being guessed at. Development (nightly) builds
save a format number no release reads yet.

Sketch patterns retain their live direction-line references and placement settings when saved.
Older patterns keep their fixed vector directions and original placement defaults.

Upgrading keeps what a design meant. Designs keep recorded body transfers, explicit 3D curve coordinate
spaces and certified face bindings, alongside semantic configuration styles, associative
free-form offsets and cylindrical emboss selections. Older ownership maps, geometry and
expressions retain their saved meaning. Legacy 3D curves with retained associations receive
their producer's coordinate-space marker without changing any saved points; detached curves
retain world coordinates. A lost cross-component association refreshed by an older build may
need an explicit relink or refresh when its source returns. Loading never guesses a numerical
correction. Association records, coordinate arrays and placements are bounded and checked.

## Design properties

**File → Design Properties…** (also under **Document Settings** in the Browser, and on the
top component's right-click menu) records who made a design and what it is: project, part
number, revision, author, organization, description and licence. **OK** applies the changes as
one undo step. Scripts and agents use the same commands: `document.metadata` reads them,
`document.metadata.set` (`key` and `value`, or `values: {key: value, …}`) and
`document.metadata.remove` (`key` or `keys`) change them. `document.inspect` and the MCP
`inspect_design` tool include them.

Exports carry them where the format has a place for them:

| Format | Written |
|---|---|
| STEP | `author` and `organization` in `FILE_NAME`, `description` in `FILE_DESCRIPTION` (on one line) |
| IGES | `author` and `organization` in the global section |
| 3MF | `project` as `Title`, `author` as `Designer`, `description` as `Description`, `license` as `LicenseTerms` |

The part number and revision have no standard place in these formats and stay in the design.

In the file they are one optional top-level `metadata` object; a design without properties has
none, and is saved exactly as before:

```json
"metadata": {
  "project": "ACME enclosures",
  "part_number": "ACME-1042",
  "revision": "B",
  "author": "Jane Doe",
  "organization": "ACME",
  "description": "Vented case for Raspberry Pi 4",
  "license": "CC-BY-4.0",
  "com.acme.description": { "shop_id": 88123 },
  "org.printfarm": { "slicer_profile": "PETG-0.2", "internal_id": 4 }
}
```

- **SolidCraft's keys are unprefixed** and hold text. Every other unprefixed key is reserved for
  later SolidCraft versions.
- **Other tools keep their data under one reverse-DNS key** of their own (`com.example.tool`:
  two or more dot-separated labels of letters, digits, `-` and `_`), holding an object. A tool
  writes only under its own key and leaves the others alone.
- **SolidCraft keeps every key as it is** through open, edit and save, in both the container
  and plain JSON, and never checks what another tool wrote: a well-known key holding something
  other than text (`"author": 42`) is kept, reads as absent, and never stops the design from
  opening. Typing over it in Design Properties replaces it.
- **Other tools' keys are never exported**; Design Properties lists them read-only.
- **Keep values small**: `document.metadata.set` refuses text over 4 KiB, an object over 64 KiB
  or nested more than 32 levels deep, and more than 256 keys or 256 KiB in all. Binary data
  belongs in a file next to the design.

Design properties are first saved in format 21. Inserting or linking another design doesn't
copy its properties; Save As keeps them. A command script of the design
(`timeline.export_script`) sets them in one step.

## Saving in the web app

In Chrome, Edge and Opera, **Save As** opens your browser's save dialog and writes the
`.solidcraft` file to the folder you choose, and **Open** opens the browser's open dialog.
**Save** then writes back to that same file. The browser remembers the file, so after you
reload the page the first **Save** asks once for permission to write to it, and carries on.
A design you open from your computer saves back to the file you opened.

In Firefox and Safari, which can't write to a folder, **Save** and **Save As** keep designs in
this browser's private storage instead, and the app says so. Clearing the site's data
can remove those designs. Download a copy to keep it outside the browser or move it to
another device.

To get a copy as a download in any browser, choose **File → Download design**. It holds the
current design, including its unsaved changes. In **File → Files in this browser…** (and in
Firefox and Safari, **File → Open**), **Download open design** does the same, and **Download**
beside a stored file gives its last saved contents. Whether a folder chooser appears depends
on your browser's download settings.

Use **Open from computer…** in the same window to open a design from your computer; where the
browser can write to a folder it saves back to that file, otherwise it works on a copy kept
in the browser. Use **Rename** beside a stored file to change its name. Autosave and recovery
stay in the browser's private storage in every browser. Exports such as STEP and STL are
downloaded.

# Plastic parts

The PLASTIC tab has a small enclosure subset:

- **Boss** (`plastic.boss`): screw bosses with a hole, fillets and optional ribs.
- **Lip / Groove** (`plastic.lip`): the mating lip and groove along a shell's opening.
- **Snap Fit** (`plastic.snap_fit`): a cantilever snap hook and its catch.
- **Rest** (`plastic.rest`): a pad for a part to rest on.
- **Plastic Rules** (`plastic.manage_rules`, `plastic.assign_rule`): wall thickness, draft and
  clearance per material, used as the features' defaults.

Rib and web (on the SOLID tab) complete the set. These features are checked against
hand-computed geometry.

# Reference tests

Generated by `cargo xtask oracle`. Each case in [`tests/oracle/`](../tests/oracle/) is a part described by our own `recipe.json`. SolidCraft replays the recipe through its command engine and compares the result with `expected.json`: body count, volume and area (relative tolerance 1e-3 unless the case states another), centre of mass and bounding box (within 1e-3 of the part's size), face count where the geometry fixes it, and, where the case has a `reference.stl`, the sampled symmetric (Hausdorff) distance between the two surfaces and the principal second moments of both triangulations. Every rebuilt part is also exported as STEP, validated and read back.

Where the expected values come from (the **Source** column):

- **analytic**: closed-form geometry worked out by hand (prisms, cylinders, cones, spheres, tori and Pappus' theorems, fillets on straight edges with a constant radius or one varying along the edge, sheet-metal bends as annular sectors). The scripts in [`tools/oracle-analytic/`](../tools/oracle-analytic/) compute them and give the formulas.
- **freecad <version>**: the same recipe built with FreeCAD's public Python scripting API by [`tools/freecad-oracle/`](../tools/freecad-oracle/), an independent kernel run as an external program. FreeCAD is not a dependency of SolidCraft. Where the two kernels legitimately build a different shape (for example the corner patch where fillets meet), only volume and area are compared, within the tolerance the case states.

No expected value comes from a commercial CAD product.

**83 / 83 cases pass**; sources: 62 analytic, 21 freecad. 0 known failure(s) tracked in issues; 0 case(s) without expected values yet.

# Parameters and expressions

Every dimension and feature input is a **model parameter** (`d1`, `d2`, …). **User parameters**
are ones you add yourself, with a unit, an expression and an optional comment. Change them in
**Change Parameters** (`parameters.change`). The timeline rebuilds from the first feature that
uses them.

When creating or editing a sketch dimension, its value editor shows its model parameter
name (`d1`, `d2`, …). Double-click another driving dimension to insert its name at the cursor,
replacing selected text; add arithmetic such as `/ 2` to build a dependent dimension.
Single clicks on dimensions leave the expression unchanged. Press **Enter** to apply the
expression or **Escape** to cancel the edit.
Add and edit user parameters through the existing **Change Parameters** command.

In the SOLID toolbar's CONFIGURE panel, click **Parameters** to open the user and model
parameter editor. The separate **Configurations** button opens the configuration table;
**Configure** remains in the dropdown for configuring columns.

Press **Enter** in the new parameter's name, expression or comment field to add it.
Valid entries return focus to the name field for the next parameter; invalid entries remain
editable. In expression fields, type a parameter or dimension name for autocomplete,
or press **Ctrl+Space** to open suggestions, including in an empty field.
**Up/Down** selects an autocomplete suggestion,
**Enter/Tab** accepts it, and **Escape** dismisses the suggestions. Accepting a suggestion
does not also submit the parameter.

Expressions are unit-aware: `2 * width + 5 mm`, `angle / 2`, `sqrt(area)`, `1 in + 3 mm`, using
`+ - * / ^`, parentheses, `sin cos tan asin acos atan atan2 sqrt abs min max floor ceil round mod
trunc` and unit conversion. A decimal comma works too, outside parentheses: `2,5 mm` is
`2.5 mm` (inside a function's parentheses the comma separates its arguments, so write
`max(2.5, 3)` there). A mixed number is one value, as imperial sizes are written: `2 1/8"` and
`3 7/16 in` are 2.125 in and 3.4375 in (a whole number, a space, then a proper fraction of whole
numbers). A length where an angle is expected (or the other way round) is an
error, not a silent conversion. Cycles are reported with their path (`a → b → a`), renaming a
parameter updates every expression, dimension and feature input that uses it, and a parameter
in use can't be deleted (the error lists its users).

The design's units (Document Settings in the browser: mm, cm, m, in or ft) set how a bare number
typed into a feature is read. In an inch design `2` means 2 in. The Box, Cylinder, Sphere, Torus
and Coil dialogs start with their sizes in the design's units, unit shown (`20 mm`, `20 in`).
Changing the units never moves existing geometry. A size worked out from a bare number keeps
the unit the number was given in: a sphere with a bare diameter of 20 has the radius
`(20 mm) / 2` in a millimetre design. Beside a unit-less expression such as `2 * 5` or a
unit-less parameter, which is read in the design's units, the number stays bare and is read
with it.

Parameters export to and import from CSV or JSON (`parameters.export`, `parameters.import`).
**Configurations** (`config.*`) keep a table of rows, each with its own parameter values and
suppressed features, physical materials and body appearances, switched with `config.activate`.
The table's Library picker selects material or appearance values. Choose **Follow material**
to clear an appearance override. Custom looks retain their colour and opacity across
activation, undo and save/reopen. See
[configuration commands and examples](https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft/blob/main/docs/configurations.md).

# Local scalar libraries

The first local-library slice (#846) reuses the existing appearance and physical
material commands. It is a small consumer of the broader [library proposal](libraries.md),
not the complete resource-pack implementation. It adds no texture mapping, wood grain,
PBR shader, HDRI lighting, online discovery or document-format version.

## Desktop workflow

1. Apply a named colour/opacity look using **Appearance**, or define a physical material
   using the existing material commands. An appearance does not change physical density.
2. In Appearance → **Local library**, choose **Export design library...**. The snapshot
   contains explicit body/face/component appearance overrides and design-local physical
   materials, including their default looks. It does not export imported kernel paint,
   unassigned built-in catalog entries or an unapplied colour-picker draft.
3. Open that library in another design, search its appearance presets, select one and
   choose **Apply library appearance**. The normal body/face/component targets are reused.
   OK after this immediate application does not add a second undo step.
4. Save the design. Its selected scalar definitions are ordinary copied design data;
   the source library can be moved or removed without changing the saved result.

Export does not edit the design, its dirty state or history. An existing file is refused
unless **Replace existing library file** is explicitly selected. Export is a snapshot of
the design definitions, not an automatic merge with entries in an existing catalog.
Editing a copied look/material uses the normal commands and does not edit its source.

The combined render integration uses main's merged #1127 asynchronous picker.
Model edits and tab changes wait for its answer while drawing/resizing continues.
Overwrite consent is captured before opening; export snapshots the design when
`library.export` runs after choosing the destination. Document identity is checked,
and an old library answer cannot replace another Appearance editor. Cancellation
does not read or write a library. The earlier #1114 candidate is no longer a runtime
dependency of the refreshed consumer.

The desktop panel applies appearances. Physical-material import/assignment is available
through `library.apply`; imported definitions also appear in the existing material list.
The browser can export a library through the existing download service. Interactive local
library opening is a desktop feature in this first slice. Browser engine commands can
consume a bounded catalog already supplied through VFS; wasm compilation does not prove
an interactive browser importer or download workflow.

## Commands

All programmatic calls use JSON and never open a file picker:

```json
{"command":"library.export","params":{"path":"my-library.solidcraft-library.json"}}
{"command":"library.inspect","params":{"path":"my-library.solidcraft-library.json"}}
```

Inspection/export returns a `catalog` with qualified entry IDs and exact revisions. Use
the returned values when applying; do not replace an unknown revision with a guessed one:

```json
{"command":"library.apply","params":{
  "path":"my-library.solidcraft-library.json",
  "entry":"user.local/appearance-<returned-id>",
  "revision":"<returned-64-character-revision>",
  "targets":{"bodies":["Body1"]}
}}
```

Appearance targets can be `bodies`, `components` or `faces: [{body, point: [x,y,z]}]`.
Points are world-space millimetres. At most 1,024 total targets are accepted. Missing
objects and invalid targets fail; the importer does not invent a nearby replacement.

A material entry can be copied without targets or assigned to body targets. The optional
`name` explicitly selects a new physical-material name on import. An identical existing
definition is reused; a conflicting definition or built-in name is refused. No density,
look or configuration cell is silently overwritten. Creation and assignment share one
outer undo transaction through the existing material commands. Mass remains the existing
volume × density calculation; a generic illustrative density is not an engineering grade.

`library.export` also accepts `id` (default `user.local`), `name` (default `My library`),
`provenance` and `overwrite` (default false). Only explicit assignments/design-local
definitions are inspected, without evaluating geometry. Duplicate exact definitions are
deduplicated; different values with the same display name remain distinct entries.

## Scalar catalog v1

The independent JSON format marker is `solidcraft-library/1`. It has `id`, `name` and an
`entries` array. Each entry has `id`, `revision`, `provenance` and a typed `definition`:

- `appearance`: `value: {name, color: [r,g,b], opacity}`; sRGB bytes and finite opacity 0–1.
- `material`: `value: {name, density_g_cm3, appearance?}`; finite density above 0 and at most
  1,000 g/cm³, with an optional appearance value of the same scalar shape.

Every object rejects unknown fields. Unsupported kinds (including texture/environment
payloads) and versions fail explicitly, rather than dropping fields or pretending that a
colour preview is a textured material. Catalog IDs are 1–64 ASCII bytes, beginning with a
lowercase letter and continuing with lowercase letters, digits, `.`, `_` or `-`. An entry
ID is `<catalog-id>/<local-id>` with the same local-ID rules; paths and labels are not IDs.

An entry revision is lowercase SHA-256 of compact v1 serde JSON `[provenance, definition]`.
Derived struct field order, omission of absent optional fields, UTF-8 escaping and f64
round-trip number formatting are part of this writer contract; this is not arbitrary JSON
canonicalization. Prefer `library.export` or the Rust `Entry::new`/`content_revision` API
when authoring revisions. A future incompatible writer changes the catalog version. The
default export IDs contain a kind and 16 hex revision characters; collisions are rejected,
never used to overwrite a different definition. Explicitly authored stable local IDs can
retain their identity across revisions. Application requires the selected exact revision.
Changing another entry does not change the selected definition's identity.

Provenance contains a required `license`, optional `author` and optional `source_url`.
It is supplied metadata, not verified permission or a publisher signature. URLs are never
fetched. The default `LicenseRef-User-Provided` does not claim that user data is openly
licensed. No external art/data is bundled in this slice. Catalog provenance/revisions stay
in the catalog: the first consumer copies scalar values into existing `Look`/`UserMaterial`
records, without a persistent catalog-origin/update receipt. Full resource embedding,
design-owned provenance, scopes and explicit update links remain proposed follow-ups.

## Bounds and failure behavior

The reader accepts at most 4 MiB encoded JSON and 1,024 entries. Entry decoding stops at
the count cap with fallible vector growth. Names are trimmed, nonempty and at most 128
UTF-8 bytes; provenance license/author/source URL limits are 128/256/2,048 bytes. Control
characters, invalid identifiers, duplicate identities, bad revisions and nonfinite scalar
values fail. Export inspects at most 100,000 source references, deduplicating into at most
1,024 entries. These are encoded/work limits, not a process-memory or latency guarantee.

Native reads are bounded regular-file reads; browser reads check VFS size before cloning.
Native no-clobber writes reuse atomic new-file publication; explicit replacement is atomic
without reading/backing up an arbitrarily large old target. All library command paths
obey the active MCP/control file scope before reading or publishing, including overwrite. Browser VFS publication is
synchronous and reuses the host's download service. No automatic discovery, asset fetch,
relative-resource resolution, executable recipe or plugin is introduced.

Failed application preserves the document and undo/redo history. The source file is read
and checked before copying; a stale selected revision needs an explicit reload/reselection.
The copied design remains independent after successful assignment, undo/redo and cold
reopening. This library has no dependency on the pending render stack and does not change
the document format. User-visible evidence and actual native/wasm results are recorded in the PR;
geometry/robustness checks remain separate and no reference baseline is weakened.

The opaque PBR consumer makes v1 export fail explicitly when any body, component,
face or material-default appearance contains PBR parameters. Neither overwrite consent
nor an existing output file permits a lossy downgrade; use the richer transport
when available. Scalar catalog imports still select the scalar response explicitly.

# Architecture

SolidCraft is a Cargo workspace in layers. A crate only depends on crates in lower layers, and
`cargo xtask layers` fails the build otherwise.

| Layer | Crates | Role |
|---|---|---|
| L0 | `geom` | vectors, planes, profiles, meshes and their measures |
| L1 | `sketch`, `kernel`, `render` | constraint solver and profiles; the B-rep kernel boundary (truck); view math and the headless scene description |
| L2 | `doc` | parameters, expressions, the feature timeline and its incremental evaluation |
| L3 | `io` | design files, STL/OBJ/STEP/3MF export, STEP and 3MF/STL/OBJ/glTF import features |
| L4 | `engine` | the session and the command registry (everything is a command) |
| L5 | `gpu`, `ui-egui`, `mcp` | compute-shader evaluation of display tessellation plans; the swappable desktop front end; the MCP server (headless or bridged to the app) |
| apps | `solidcraft`, `solidcraft-cli` | desktop app, headless CLI |

The web app, `apps/solidcraft-web`, is the desktop front end compiled to wasm with
[trunk](https://trunkrs.dev). `xtask` holds the repository's own tooling: `cargo xtask ci`,
`layers`, `assets`, `features`, `oracle` and `book`.

A few rules follow from the layering:

- **Only `crates/kernel` touches truck.** Everything above it sees SolidCraft's own types:
  bodies, faces, edges, meshes and measures. See [The kernel boundary](kernel.md).
- **The document knows nothing about commands or the UI.** `crates/doc` holds the parameters,
  the feature timeline and the component tree, and evaluates them into a model.
- **Everything the user can do is a command** in `crates/engine`. See
  [The command engine](commands.md).
- **The front end is swappable.** Nothing below `ui-egui` depends on egui. The CLI and the MCP
  server run the same engine without a window. Headless pictures (`solidcraft-cli snapshot`, MCP
  screenshots, `ui.render`, thumbnails) are drawn on the GPU with the viewport's own pipelines
  (`crates/gpu`, `capture`): the engine describes the scene (`view::scene`) and the host installs
  the renderer (`engine::capture`). The tiers, in order: a hardware GPU, a software adapter (Mesa
  lavapipe or llvmpipe, WARP), and last `crates/render`'s CPU rasterizer, which draws no surface
  analysis, highlights or legends. `SOLIDCRAFT_GPU=auto` walks all three, `hardware` and `software`
  stay on their tier (an error without one), `cpu` forces the rasterizer; every picture's reply
  names its `renderer` (`gpu`, `gpu-software`, `cpu`) and a CPU picture carries a warning.
  `solidcraft-cli gpu` lists the adapters and the tier the policy lands on.

# Control protocol

`solidcraft --control PORT` (or `SOLIDCRAFT_CONTROL_PORT=PORT`) listens on `127.0.0.1:PORT` for
JSON lines. Each request is one line `{"id": …, "method": "…", "params": {…}}`; each reply is one
line `{"id": …, "ok": true, "result": …}` or `{"id": …, "ok": false, "error": "…"}`. Requests are
handled on the UI thread between frames; pointer and keyboard input is injected as real egui
events, one pointer event per frame.

### Token

Every connection must authenticate. At start the app makes a random 256-bit token for this
launch and writes it, as one line of hex, to a file only the user can read:

| System | Token file |
|---|---|
| Linux | `$XDG_DATA_HOME/solidcraft/control/PORT.token` (`~/.local/share/solidcraft/control/PORT.token`) |
| macOS | `~/Library/Application Support/SolidCraft/control/PORT.token` |
| Windows | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\SolidCraft\control\PORT.token` |

On Unix the folder is `0700` and the file `0600`; on Windows the file's inherited permissions are
replaced by a single entry for the user. `SOLIDCRAFT_CONTROL_DIR` moves the folder. The file is
removed when the app exits, and the next launch writes a new token. The token file's path is
printed to stderr at start-up.

The first request on a connection must carry the token as a top-level `"token"` member
(`{"id": 1, "method": "ui.inspect", "params": {}, "token": "…"}`); later requests on the same
connection may leave it out. A first line without the right token is answered with
`{"ok": false, "error": "unauthorized: …"}` and the connection is closed, without running
anything. Tokens are compared in constant time.

`solidcraft-cli mcp --connect 127.0.0.1:PORT` reads the token file for that port by itself
(`--token T` or `SOLIDCRAFT_CONTROL_TOKEN` give one explicitly). For a test harness, or a
sandboxed package whose data folder the client can't see, start the app with
`SOLIDCRAFT_CONTROL_TOKEN` set to at least 32 hex characters (for example
`openssl rand -hex 32`) and the app uses that token instead of making one; the file is still
written. A one-line client in Python:

```python
token = (Path.home() / ".local/share/solidcraft/control/7878.token").read_text().strip()
sock.sendall((json.dumps({"id": 1, "method": "ui.inspect", "params": {}, "token": token}) + "\n").encode())
```

### Limits

The channel is untrusted input. A request line may be at most 16 MiB; a longer one is answered
with `{"ok": false, "error": "request too large"}` and the connection is closed, as are
connections that send eight lines that are not JSON. At most 16 connections are served at once
(further ones get `{"ok": false, "error": "too many connections"}`), at most 64 queued requests
run per frame so a flood cannot starve drawing, and a request that the UI thread has not
answered within 60 seconds (3600 seconds for `engine.batch`) is replied to with
`{"ok": false, "running": true, "error": "timeout: … is still running …"}`. The same 16 MiB line
limit applies to the MCP server.

A timed-out request has not failed: it is still running in the app and will still apply (a long
fillet, say), so don't simply send it again. The connection keeps its reply (#1618). Ask for it
with `control.pending`: `{"pending": <id>, "method": …, "done": false}` while it runs, then
`{"pending": <id>, "method": …, "done": true, "reply": {…}}` (its own reply, once), and
`{"pending": null}` when nothing is outstanding. Until it lands, any other request on that
connection is refused at once with `{"ok": false, "busy": true, "error": "busy: …"}` and not
run, so nothing is queued to apply unseen behind it.

Any request's `params` may carry `allow_paths: ["/abs/folder", …]`: every file that request
reads, writes or deletes (command paths such as `file.export`'s `path` or `doc.recovery_*`'s
`dir`, `ui.render`, `ui.screenshot`) must then lie inside one of those folders after `..` and
symlinks are resolved, or the request fails with `… outside the folders this agent may use …`.
The app adds its own recovery folder and, when it lies safely inside the home folder and not in
a hidden folder, the open design's folder (whose hidden files stay out of reach). The bridged
MCP server sends its folders this way on every request ([mcp.md](mcp.md)). Without
`allow_paths` file paths are not limited: a client holding the token can do what the user can.

## Engine

| Method | Params | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `engine.execute` | `command`: command id, `params`: JSON object | the command's result |
| `engine.script` | `commands`: `[{command, params}, …]` | results, stops at the first error |
| `engine.batch` | `commands`: `[{command, params}, …]` (at most 10 000), `rollback?`: bool (default true), `timings?`, `profile?`: bool (default false) | `{completed, results, undone}`, plus `failed: {index, command, error}` when a step fails, and with `timings` `timings: [{index, command, ms}]` (the failing step included) and `total_ms`; `profile` adds each step's `profile: {boolean_ms, tessellate_ms, other_ms}`. Runs the steps in one request, so within one frame, each as `engine.execute` runs it. The first failure stops the batch, and with `rollback` the design goes back to how it was before it (`undone`: the steps taken back). Refused before anything runs, with an error starting `engine.batch unavailable`, while the agent cursor is shown or when a step loads a file (`doc.open`, `file.insert_step`, `file.insert_mesh`). Send such steps one by one. Answered when done, for up to 3600 s |
| `engine.commands` | — | every command: id, label, tab, panel, icon, shortcut, params doc, enabled |
| `document.inspect` | `measure?`: bool | parameters, timeline (errors, timings), bodies, sketches, selection |

Commands never open dialogs when run this way. `solidcraft-cli commands` prints the same registry.

Product images use `render.preflight/start/status/cancel/export` through `engine.execute`.
Keep the returned session-scoped job ID for subsequent calls; status does not block or
render. See [render jobs](render-jobs.md) for capture, cancellation and export semantics.

While an interactive native file picker is open, `ui.inspect` reports `file_picker_busy: true`.
Engine commands, `ui.file` and `ui.home` requests wait for its answer; window resizing,
inspection and screenshots remain available.

Every `sketch.*` command that changes a sketch adds `created: {points, curves, constraints,
dimensions}` to its result (and `wires` for 3D curves): the ids of what it added, in creation
order, next to whatever else the command returns (`curves`, `sides`, `corners`…). Sketch ids are
stable and never reused, even after a delete (`l1`, `l2`, then `l3` once `l2` is gone; only undo
rolls the numbering back with the design), so they can go straight into later commands:

```text
{"id":7,"method":"engine.execute","params":{"command":"sketch.line","params":{"points":[[0,0],[40,0]]}}}
→ {"curves":["l1"],"created":{"points":["l1.start","l1.end"],"curves":["l1"],"constraints":["k1"],"dimensions":[]},…}
{"id":8,"method":"engine.execute","params":{"command":"sketch.dimension","params":{"entities":["l1"],"value":50}}}
```

A bare numeric `value` given to `sketch.dimension` (from the control channel, scripts or MCP) is
read in the design's units, exactly as if it were typed into the dimension box: in an inch design
`"value": 2` makes the line 2 in (50.8 mm) long. Point coordinates stay in millimetres. To pin a
unit regardless of the design, pass an expression with one: `"value": "50 mm"` or
`"value": "0.5 in"`. Angles are degrees unless the expression says otherwise.

The viewport also shows an X/Y/Z-aligned dimension chain between the endpoints of the
currently shown distance (centre, minimum or maximum), with each world-axis distance
labelled separately as an absolute value (including zero).
It uses the design's units and length precision, independently of the view or sketch plane.
Preferences → Graphics → **Show X/Y/Z distances** controls these extra lines and
labels (default on, saved between runs). Set `ui.prefs {"measure_axis_distances": false}`
to hide them while keeping the total distance and the dialog's ΔX/ΔY/ΔZ values. These
overlays remain visible until Measure closes.
Overlay handles `measure:label:x`, `measure:label:y` and `measure:label:z` identify the extra
labels; `prefs:measure_axis_distances` identifies the checkbox.

### Continuous camera motion

Continuous camera motion is also available through `engine.execute` with command
`view.navigate`: pass `camera` (from `ui.inspect`) and `motion: "pan" | "orbit" | "zoom"`.
Pan and orbit take `delta: [dx,dy]` in screen points (each within ±10000); pan also requires
`viewport: [width,height]` (each 1..1000000). Orbit accepts a world-space `pivot` with the
viewport size. Zoom takes `factor` (0.05..20, below 1 zooms in) and an optional world-space
`anchor`. The returned `camera` is applied immediately by the UI, without animation,
document edits, undo steps or a success-log entry per movement.
