# Contributing to SolidCraft

SolidCraft is an open-source parametric 3D CAD app written in pure Rust.
You sketch on a plane, constrain the sketch, turn profiles into solids, and
change a parameter to watch the timeline rebuild. It runs as a desktop app (Windows, Linux), in
the browser (wasm + WebGPU/WebGL2), headless from a CLI, and as an MCP server that AI agents can
model with.

Help is welcome, whether that's a one-line fix or owning a whole area. This page covers how to
build it, how the code is laid out, the few rules that aren't negotiable, and where help is
needed most.

Before choosing a task, check the [command inventory](docs/features.md) and
[roadmap](ROADMAP.md) for implemented capabilities and current priorities.

Questions, ideas or want to say what you're working on? Join the [Discord](https://discord.gg/FtU4NQNVDH).

## Get it running (about 10 minutes on a fast machine)

You need stable Rust 1.95 or newer (required by egui/eframe 0.36). For the web
build you also need `rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown` and [`trunk`](https://github.com/trunk-rs/trunk)
([documentation](https://trunk-rs.github.io/trunk/)).

```sh
git clone https://github.com/tangency-labs/solidcraft && cd solidcraft
cargo run --release -p solidcraft -- --sample      # desktop app with a sample part
cargo xtask test                                   # unit, engine and UI-scenario tests
cargo xtask ci                                     # everything a PR must pass (see below)
```

SolidCraft is the product, repository, Cargo package and executable name.
Build the desktop app with `cargo build --release -p solidcraft`, or the CLI with
`cargo build --release -p solidcraft-cli`. Run the CLI with
`cargo run --release -p solidcraft-cli -- commands` (or `target/release/solidcraft-cli commands`
after building). The old name appears only in the compatibility shims listed in
[docs/compatibility.md](docs/compatibility.md); don't add new uses of it.

Web: `cd apps/solidcraft-web && trunk serve --release`, then open the printed URL (`?sample`
opens the sample part, `?webgl` forces WebGL2). Saving and opening files in the browser needs
HTTPS or localhost, because it uses the Origin Private File System.

Windows from Linux: `cargo xwin build --release --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc -p solidcraft`.

### NixOS: `nix develop`

NixOS has no `/usr/lib`, so nothing is on `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` and a plain `cargo run` finds none of
the libraries the app loads at run time: the Wayland ones winit opens the window through, the EGL
loader wgpu renders through, and libdbus-1, which rfd's file dialogs reach xdg-desktop-portal
through (a dialog then never appears and the pick returns no path):

```
ERROR solidcraft: winit EventLoopError: ... The wayland library could not be loaded
ERROR eframe::native::run: Exiting because of error: WGPU error: Failed to create surface for any enabled backend: {}
ERROR rfd::backend::xdg_desktop_portal::portal::libdbus: Can't connect to a portal: libdbus-1.so not found
```

`nix develop` (the [`flake.nix`](flake.nix) in the repository root) supplies Wayland,
X11, EGL, Vulkan-loader and D-Bus runtime libraries. It also exposes the NixOS
driver manifests in `/run/opengl-driver/share`, so Vulkan can discover the system
drivers. Enable `hardware.graphics.enable` on NixOS; other Linux distributions
may need a matching [nixGL wrapper](https://github.com/nix-community/nixGL).
The default development shell retains the Rust/C toolchain already on `PATH`;
`nix develop .#rust` supplies the pinned toolchain and builds in `target/nix`.

To launch, use `nix run .#solidcraft -- --sample`. To install the app's terminal
commands, desktop entry and generated icons, use `nix profile install .#solidcraft`.
`nix build` alone creates a build result; it does not install a launcher in your
desktop menu. The installed `solidcraft` command runs the wrapped app; `solidcraft-cli` is included as
well. See
[Nix installation and troubleshooting](docs/nix.md) for remote-flake commands,
desktop integration and how to distinguish an old executable on `PATH`.

## How the code is laid out

The [architecture page](docs/architecture.md) has the layer table. The short version:

- `crates/geom`: vectors, planes, meshes, measures.
- `crates/sketch`: our own constraint solver, plus profile finding.
- `crates/kernel`: the B-rep kernel boundary. It wraps [truck](https://github.com/ricosjp/truck),
  and it's the only crate allowed to touch truck. Fillets, chamfers, shell/offset, Delete Face,
  Split Face, STEP/IGES read and write, and face provenance are our own code here. Patched
  copies of three truck crates live in `vendor/` and are excluded from our fmt/clippy rules.
- `crates/doc`: the document. It holds parameters and expressions, the feature timeline and its
  incremental rebuild, components and occurrences, joints, appearances, and persistent naming.
- `crates/io`: design files and mesh formats (3MF, STL, OBJ).
- `crates/engine`: the session and the command registry. **Everything the user can do is a
  command**, and the toolbar, dialogs, scripts, CLI, control channel and MCP all run the same
  commands.
- `crates/ui-egui`: the desktop/web front end (egui + wgpu). It's swappable; nothing below it
  depends on egui.
- `crates/mcp`, `apps/solidcraft`, `apps/solidcraft-cli`, `apps/solidcraft-web`.

`cargo xtask layers` fails the build if a lower layer depends on a higher one.

## Rules that aren't negotiable

1. **Independent.** SolidCraft is independent. Behaviour is designed from public
   documentation, general CAD conventions and user feedback. Reference tests use analytic values
   and open-source tools. We don't drive, script, automate or extract data from commercial CAD
   products, and we never copy another product's code, icons, artwork, help text, tooltips,
   templates or materials. Command ids are our own (`solid.fillet`).
2. **No GPL/LGPL/AGPL code, not even reading it.** That rules out OpenCASCADE, FreeCAD
   (including planegcs), SolveSpace, CadQuery/OCP, LibreCAD and QCAD. SolidCraft is
   MIT OR Apache-2.0, and its solver and blends are written from the maths. (Running an
   open-source application to get reference values for a test is fine; reading its source is
   not.) Permissive
   dependencies are fine. Note which one you're adding and why in the PR. THIRD-PARTY-LICENSES.txt
   lists it once the change lands: the Generated files workflow rewrites it on `main`.
   Nightly/manual CI also scans advisories, bans and sources with cargo-deny; see
   [the local command and coverage limits](docs/book/src/dev/testing.md#dependency-advisories).
3. **Every asset is original or openly licensed and has a row in
   [ATTRIBUTION.md](ATTRIBUTION.md).** Icons are drawn in code (`crates/ui-egui/src/icons.rs`).
   `cargo xtask assets` enforces this.
4. **Never crash.** People trust a CAD app with their work.
   - Non-test code never uses `unwrap`, `expect`, `panic!` or indexing on input-derived data.
     There's no `unsafe` outside `apps/solidcraft/src/open_documents.rs` (macOS file-open events),
     `apps/solidcraft/src/native_crash.rs` (Windows native crash capture) and
     `crates/threedx-client/src/macos.rs` (the 3Dconnexion driver's client API on macOS), and the
     compiler denies it.
   - An unsupported case returns an error ("not supported yet: …"); it never panics.
   - Every call into truck goes through `solidcraft_kernel::guard`.
   - Every crash fix comes with a regression test.
5. **Everything is a command, with a test.** A new feature means a `CommandSpec` in
   `crates/engine/src/cmd/`, engine tests that measure the result (volume, area,
   face/edge/vertex counts against a value you can derive), and for UI work a scenario (below).
6. **One set of camera controls.** Every page or canvas that shows a view (the modelling
   viewport, the Render preview, and any new page such as a flat pattern or drawing) calls
   `navigation::handle` (`crates/ui-egui/src/navigation.rs`) for its camera input, with
   `NavCaps` saying whether it can orbit (off for flat 2D pages) and pick. New canvases must use
   `navigation::handle`; never read drags, the wheel or pinch to move the camera yourself. The
   `hand_rolled_camera_input_is_rejected` test fails if a page does.

Labels, parameter docs, messages and docs use the terms in the
[glossary](https://docs.solidcraft.io/reference/glossary.html): one term for each idea. A change that adds a new
idea adds its term there.

[AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) has the long form of these rules. It's written for AI agents, but it's
the most complete description of the house style.

## Tests

| What | Where | Run |
|---|---|---|
| Unit and engine tests | next to the code, or `*_tests.rs` files | `cargo xtask test` (or `cargo test --workspace --profile ci`) |
| UI scenarios | `crates/ui-egui/tests/scenarios/*.json` | part of `cargo test` |
| Reference tests | `cargo xtask oracle` | `tests/oracle/` (see below) |

A geometry change that changes the robustness goldens re-records them in the same pull request:
`ROBUSTNESS_GOLDENS_BLESS="why it changed" cargo test --profile ci -p solidcraft-engine --lib robustness_goldens::`
(see [docs/robustness.md](docs/robustness.md)); CI runs every seed on pull requests that touch geometry.
[docs/mutation-testing.md](docs/mutation-testing.md) shows how to find kernel behaviour these
black-box suites miss.

**UI scenarios** drive the real app headless: start a tool, click a plane or a sketch point,
press keys, then assert on the result.

```json
[
  {"start": "sketch.create"},
  {"click": {"plane": "XY"}},
  {"start": "sketch.rectangle.two_point"},
  {"click": {"sketch": [0, 0]}},
  {"click": {"sketch": [40, 30]}},
  {"expect": {"errors": 0}}
]
```

A new `.json` file in that folder is picked up automatically. To record a bug before it's fixed,
put `{"pending": "why"}` in the scenario, and remove it in the PR that fixes the bug.

**A failing test without its fix can't merge as-is:** it would turn `main`'s CI red for everyone.
Either include the fix in the same PR, or mark the test `#[ignore = "fails until #123 is fixed"]`
(it can then merge right away), and remove that line in the PR that fixes the bug.

**Use the `ci` profile.** CI runs the tests with `--profile ci`: light optimisation, line tables,
no LTO, and debug assertions off (truck has debug-only assertions that reject valid geometry). It
builds several times faster than `--release`. If a test fails only in a plain debug build, say so
in the PR. `cargo xtask test` builds the tests with it and then runs every test binary at once
(`cargo test` runs them one after another); arguments after `--` go to each binary, e.g.
`cargo xtask test -- shell`. Tests run beside each other on a busy machine, so a test must not
depend on wall-clock timing.

**Ready pull requests test what they touch.** CI maps changed files to workspace packages and
runs Clippy, the test build and tests for those and their dependents. The
[package selector](scripts/ci/affected.py) and [CI workflow](.github/workflows/ci.yml) define
which changes require native checks; documentation, packaging, other-workflow and bot-script-only
changes run the repository checks only, on pull requests and on `main`. Workspace-wide changes,
merge-queue groups, nightly runs and Run workflow select the full workspace. A push to `main`
reuses a successful merge-queue run for the same commit, and runs only the repository checks
when no code changed since the last push to `main` that passed; otherwise it runs the full
suite. Doc tests, reference tests and the Windows jobs run on `main` and nightly only.

**CI shards the tests.** One job builds them into a cargo-nextest archive; two shards run on
pull requests and four during full validation. Every test runs in its own process: don't rely
on state left by another test.
Pull requests skip a few heavy tests (one to twelve minutes each), which run in full validation
(the merge queue, nightly, manual runs and pushes to `main` not already tested by the queue).
Check that validation after merging. They are listed in
`.config/nextest.toml` and the [testing page](docs/book/src/dev/testing.md):

- `solidcraft-engine`: `tests::hostile_params_never_panic`, everything in `tests::robustness` and
  the seeds of `tests::robustness_goldens` (`seed_00` … `seed_95`; pull requests matching the workflow's geometry paths run all but the slowest, `SLOW_SEEDS` in `ci.yml`),
  `pattern_suppress_tests::enclosure_arc_extinction_keeps_a_real_sharp_inner_lip_after_resize_and_reopen`,
  `pattern_suppress_tests::enclosure_datums_follow_wall_height_and_board_depth_with_material_proofs`,
  `cmd::plastic::tests::enclosure_snap_fit_follows_resized_front_wall`, the `atomic_commands` contract tests
- `solidcraft-kernel`: `tests::boolean_identity_on_tangent_primitives`, `tspline::tests::hostile_tsplines_never_panic`, and the `boolean_props` property tests
  (these run only in the nightly "Property tests" job: their inputs are random, so main skips them too)
- `solidcraft-ui-egui` scenarios: `acceptance_sensor_enclosure`

**The action matrix** tries every ordinary action on every face, edge, vertex and body of a
corpus of designs against a checked-in ratchet ([docs/action-matrix.md](docs/action-matrix.md)).
A pull request that makes an action pass should record it with `cargo xtask action-matrix --bless`;
one that makes a passing action fail fails the sample every CI run checks.

**The reference tests** live in [`tests/oracle/`](tests/oracle/), each a `recipe.json`
in our own format with an `expected.json` beside it. SolidCraft rebuilds the recipe and compares
body count, volume, area, centre of mass and bounding box (and, where there is a `reference.stl`,
the surface itself). Expected values are either worked out in closed form
(`tools/oracle-analytic/`) or computed by building the same recipe in FreeCAD, run as a separate
program (`tools/freecad-oracle/`); each file says which. The generated
[reference test report](docs/oracle.md) has the current case count and results. The reference-test
CI job runs `cargo xtask oracle` during full validation; pull-request runs skip it. A case that
fails because of a known bug names its issue in `expected.json` (`"known_failure": "#123"`);
never change an expected value to match SolidCraft's output.

## Changing the design file format

A design file says which format it is in (`"format": "solidcraft/N"`). If your change saves
something new in a design (a field, a feature type, a new kind of name), or makes older designs
mean something else, it needs a format change. **Add one file, and edit nothing shared:**

1. Create `crates/doc/src/format/pending/<what-it-is>.rs` (lowercase, dashes). Start it with a
   `//!` note: what is saved, what older designs get without it, and that the last release asks
   for an update instead of meeting it.
2. If older designs must be rewritten as they open, put `pub fn step(v: &mut Value) ->
   crate::Result<()>` in the same file. Pending steps run in file-name order, after the older
   formats' steps.
3. Don't touch `FORMAT`, `JSON_STEPS`, the history in `crates/doc/src/format.rs`, another
   change's file, or any `v<N>/` folder: those are fixed once released.

That's all. The build counts the files: while any are pending it writes the next format number,
which no release reads, so a release refuses a design that has your change instead of losing it.
A file also lists the pending changes it has (`format_pending`), so a later development build
runs only the steps that file is missing. Two pull requests that each add a change merge without
a conflict. `crates/doc/src/format/pending/README.md` has an example.

**At release time** the maintainer runs `scripts/fold-format-pending.sh`, which moves the pending
files into `crates/doc/src/format/v<N>/` and fixes that number for good (see
[docs/releasing.md](docs/releasing.md)). Never add a file to a `v<N>/` folder afterwards.

## Lists many changes add to

Some files gain an item in many pull requests at once. They are kept so that two changes that
each add an item only meet when their items are neighbours, which spares everyone a conflict
and a fresh CI run:

- **Message catalogs** (`assets/locales/*.json`): one message per line, sorted by id. Add your
  message anywhere and run `cargo xtask lists --fix`; `cargo xtask lists` (in `cargo xtask ci`
  and the Lists workflow) fails on an unsorted catalog or an id that appears twice.
- **`mod` lines**: one per line, in the sorted group they belong to (`cargo fmt` keeps each group
  sorted). Add a new module into the existing group, not as a new group at the end.
- **Languages** (`crates/ui-egui/src/i18n.rs`): one per line, English first, then by id (a test
  checks it).
- **Generated files**: `THIRD-PARTY-LICENSES.txt` and `docs/features.md` are rewritten on `main`
  after each merge by the Generated files workflow (`cargo xtask licences`, `cargo xtask
  features`). Don't regenerate or edit them in a pull request.
- **Design format**: one file per change, never an edit to a shared number (above).

## Sending a change

1. Work is tracked in [GitHub issues](https://github.com/tangency-labs/solidcraft/issues), labelled
   by area (`area:kernel`, `area:sketch`, `area:doc`, `area:ui`, `area:infra`). For anything
   bigger than a bug fix that has no issue yet, open one first. **Claim the issue with a draft
   PR** before you start, so two people don't build the same thing:
   - Check nobody has it: `gh pr list -R tangency-labs/solidcraft --state open --search "#N"`.
   - Branch from the latest `main`, commit `git commit --allow-empty -m "claim: #N"`, push, and
     open a **draft** PR titled `<summary> (#N)`, e.g. `Fillet: variable radius along a chain (#123)`.
   - **The lowest-numbered open PR for an issue wins.** If yours lost, close it (or offer to help
     on the other one).
   - The bot records the claim when the PR is opened: it assigns you, adds `in progress` and
     says so on the issue. It reads `#N` in the PR title and `Fixes #N` in the body. If someone
     already holds the issue, or an older open PR references it, it says so on your PR instead.
   - Want to stake a claim before you have a branch? Comment `/claim` on the issue (below).
   - Push work in progress at least daily. A draft with no pushes for 72 hours may be taken over:
     comment on it first, then open your own claim.
   - Mark the PR ready for review when it is done.
2. Branch from `main` and keep the PR to one topic.
3. Run `cargo xtask ci` before pushing. It runs fmt, the asset, licence and layer checks,
   clippy (`-D warnings`), then the tests with the wasm build check alongside. A PR has to pass it.
   Heavy CI runs after review: a pull request gets the formatting and repository checks and a
   quick compile (`cargo check`) when you push. Once a maintainer has reviewed it they add the
   `approved-for-ci` label when the PR is ready to merge, which runs the full CI (build, tests,
   goldens, Clippy); every push after that runs the full set again. Maintainers merge approved
   PRs in groups by area, so PRs that touch the same code meet a conflict at most once.
4. Reference the issue (`Fixes #12`). In the PR, say what you tested and how. For geometry work, include the measured numbers (and
   the expected ones).

Commenting `/claim` assigns you, adds the `in progress` label, and replies with its automatic cleanup
deadline. It frees a claim with no linked PR after 72 hours, or a claim with a PR after 14 days
without pushes. These automatic cleanup deadlines are separate from the daily progress and
72-hour takeover policy above. A draft PR that references the issue claims it the same way.
`/unclaim` releases the bot claim early (only you or a maintainer can). Issues a maintainer has
taken are never freed automatically.

Help reviewers see what the words mean. For observable CAD, UI or model behavior, please
include actual descriptive screenshots or a short recording in the issue or PR. This evidence
is required for changes or bugs that can be demonstrated in the app, including kernel,
geometry, assembly and backend work. Coding agents should run a small reproduction and
capture the evidence themselves; please don't ask a human for evidence the agent can produce.
Show the actual failure or result, preferably before and after, with brief steps and
expected/actual behavior. An arrow or annotation can help identify the detail that matters.

Flowcharts and Mermaid diagrams cannot replace evidence of visible behavior. Diagrams are
useful for architectural reasoning when actual screenshots cannot illustrate the point.
Changes with no useful observable behavior do not need screenshot or video evidence. Use a
small example without private designs or sensitive details; attach the media or link to an
accessible recording rather than committing generated review artifacts.

Keep an eye on your PR's status, but don't push to it only to catch up with `main` (no merge of
`main`, no Update branch button, no rebase for that alone): every push restarts the whole CI
run for everyone waiting behind it, and `main`'s own run catches what lands in between. When you
push a change anyway, or GitHub reports a conflict, rebase onto the latest `main` (push your
branch with `--force-with-lease`) or merge `main` in once, and resolve conflicts without losing
others' changes. Don't re-run CI on an unchanged commit either: a real failure fails again.
Re-run only a job that runner trouble cancelled, with "Re-run failed jobs". While a task remains
active, follow an open PR through its status changes; at handoff, clearly identify anything
still awaiting merge.

Much of SolidCraft so far was written by AI coding agents (Claude) working in parallel, each
owning one area, with a human setting direction and reporting bugs. Their working notes are in
[AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md). Human contributors are just as welcome. Use whatever tools you like, as
long as the change meets the rules above.

## Labels and triage

The triage bot labels every new issue and PR (`.github/workflows/triage.yml`). It only adds labels;
correct them freely and it won't put them back.

- **PRs** get `area:*` from the paths they change (`crates/kernel` and `crates/geom` →
  `area:kernel`, `crates/ui-egui` and the apps → `area:ui`, `.github/`, `scripts/`, `docs/` →
  `area:infra`, and so on).
- **Issues** get `bug` (in-app reports and the bug template), `enhancement` (feature requests),
  `priority:P1` for crashes, and an `area:*` from the title or the reported command. Until it has
  a priority, an issue carries `needs-triage`; setting a priority removes it.
- **Maintainers** comment `/triage area:kernel P1` (any existing label; `P0`–`P3` for a
  priority, which replaces the old one; `-label` removes one) to sort an issue or PR.
- **Short bug reports without steps to reproduce** get `needs-info` and one comment asking for
  the steps (and the version, when it's missing). An app report that arrived empty is asked to
  paste the report the app copied to the clipboard. The reporter's reply, or an edit that adds the
  steps, removes the label; an issue that stays in `needs-info` for 14 days is closed, and can be
  reopened any time. Feature requests, app reports with their details, and maintainers' issues
  are never asked.
- `needs-triage` is the queue: [open issues with it](https://github.com/tangency-labs/solidcraft/issues?q=is%3Aopen+label%3Aneeds-triage).

## Where help is wanted most

**Kernel speed (slow fillets, booleans, STEP):** please don't rewrite the current kernel code for speed; it is being replaced by [solidcore](https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcore) ([progress](https://tangency-labs.github.io/solidcore/)). Report slow cases with a file under the `kernel-perf` label, and put kernel effort into solidcore instead. See [#1597](https://github.com/tangency-labs/solidcraft/issues/1597).

See the [`help wanted`](https://github.com/tangency-labs/solidcraft/labels/help%20wanted) and
[`good first issue`](https://github.com/tangency-labs/solidcraft/labels/good%20first%20issue) labels.
In order of how much they'd help users:

1. **Fillet and blend robustness.** Fillets are our own code (truck has no fillet operation).
   Constant, variable-radius and chord fillets work, and so do corners where fillets of
   different radii meet, including three rounds meeting at a vertex. Next are setback corners, fillets along curved edges between curved
   faces, and fillets that consume neighbouring faces.
2. **Boolean robustness.** A random-design fuzzer currently gets about half of its designs
   through without a kernel error. Each failing seed is a reproducible bug.
3. **Drawings, CAM and mesh tools.** These are out of scope for now (see
   [ROADMAP.md](ROADMAP.md)), but anyone who wants to own one is welcome.

## Updating the generated feature list

After adding or renaming commands, run `cargo xtask features`. The registry is the
source of truth for `docs/features.md`; do not hand-edit the generated rows.
The generator sorts commands by ID and omits global and per-section counters,
so additions to unrelated areas no longer rewrite shared summary lines.

If two branches still conflict in this file (for example, adjacent additions in
the same area), first resolve the command registry and source conflicts, then run
`cargo xtask features` again and stage the regenerated file. Do not use Git's
`union` merge driver: it can silently retain stale or duplicate command rows.
The generator tests cover stable ordering and additions that leave existing lines
unchanged. The initial switch to sorted rows is a one-time larger diff.

## Licence

By contributing you agree that your contribution is licensed as MIT OR Apache-2.0, like the rest
of SolidCraft. SolidCraft isn't affiliated with any CAD vendor; product names are trademarks of their owners (see NOTICE).

# Updates and privacy

SolidCraft tells you when a newer release is out. It never updates itself without asking, and
the check sends nothing about you or your designs.

## What you see

When a newer stable release exists, a small accent-coloured pill reading **Update to 0.14.0**
(the new version) appears in the title bar next to **Report a bug**. Nothing pops up by itself:
clicking the pill opens a small window with the new version, its release notes and three
choices. In a narrower window the pill shortens to **Update** so the document tabs keep their
room, then to its icon alone.

- **Download** opens the file that fits your installation (see the table below) in your
  browser, or the release page when there isn't one.
- **Skip this version** hides the pill until an even newer release comes out.
- **Remind me later** hides it for three days.

SolidCraft checks every time it starts, so a release that came out since you last opened it shows
up straight away, and again once a day while it stays open.

**Preferences ▸ General ▸ Updates** has **Check for updates automatically** (on by default) and
**Check now**, which checks right away and shows the window even for a version you skipped.

## Updating in one click

Where SolidCraft can replace itself safely, the window also has **Update now**:

| Installed as | Update now does |
|---|---|
| AppImage | Downloads the new AppImage next to the old one, verifies it, renames it over the old file and offers **Restart now** |
| Windows installer (`.msi`) | **Install (closes SolidCraft)**: downloads and verifies the `.msi`, closes SolidCraft (asking about unsaved designs first) and starts the installer |
| Windows portable `.zip` or `.exe` | Downloads and verifies the package, swaps in the new `solidcraft.exe` (and `solidcraft-cli.exe`) and offers **Restart now**; the old file is removed at the next start |
| macOS | **Download and open**: downloads and verifies the `.dmg` and opens it; drag SolidCraft to Applications to replace the old copy |
| Flatpak, Snap, `.deb`, `.rpm`, `.tar.gz` | Nothing: your package manager updates these (the window shows the command), or you unpack the new archive |

Every download is verified before anything changes: its SHA-256 must match the release's
`SHA256SUMS.txt`, fetched over HTTPS from the same release, and, once the project signs its
releases, that list must carry a valid signature by SolidCraft's release key that names the
release (see [releasing](https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft/blob/main/docs/releasing.md#update-signing)).
A download that doesn't verify is deleted and the installed copy is left as it was; **Download**
still gets the package for a manual install. On macOS SolidCraft opens the disk image rather than
replacing the app itself, because the app is ad-hoc signed and not notarized: replacing it in the
background would install code macOS can't vouch for without you seeing it.

Update now needs write access to the installed file: an AppImage in a folder you can't write to
fails with a message, and **Download** is the way to update it.

## Updating from 0.11 to 0.14

SolidCraft 0.11.0 to 0.14.0 only accept packages from the project's old GitHub address. Since
the repository moved to `github.com/tangency-labs/solidcraft`, every release names the new address,
so these versions see that a newer release is out but find no package in it: **Update now** can't
install it, and **Download** opens the release page.

Download 0.15.0 or later once yourself, from the release page or the
[download links](https://github.com/tangency-labs/solidcraft#download), and install it over the old
version as you first installed it. From 0.15.0 on, SolidCraft accepts either address, and
**Update now** works again. Package managers (Flatpak, Snap, WinGet, `.deb`, `.rpm`) aren't
affected.

## What is sent

One HTTPS request each time SolidCraft starts, and once a day while it stays open:

```text
GET https://api.github.com/repos/bherbruck/solidcraft/releases/latest
User-Agent: SolidCraft-update-check
Accept: application/vnd.github+json
X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2022-11-28
```

**Update now** then downloads `SHA256SUMS.txt` (and its signature) and the one package from the
release's own `github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft/releases/download/…` links, with the same
User-Agent. That's all: no version number, no machine or user identifier, no usage data, no cookies. GitHub
sees the request like any other visit to the API (your IP address, the time); see
[GitHub's privacy statement](https://docs.github.com/site-policy/privacy-policies/github-general-privacy-statement).
SolidCraft compares the answer with its own version on your computer.

- Offline, or GitHub doesn't answer within 15 seconds: nothing is shown, and the check is tried
  again an hour later (or at the next start, whichever comes first).
- GitHub's rate limit for anonymous requests (60 an hour per address) is respected: when GitHub
  says to wait, SolidCraft waits that long, Check now and the check at start included.
- Turning off **Check for updates automatically** stops the checks; only **Check now** asks.
- Setting the environment variable `SOLIDCRAFT_UPDATE_CHECK=0` turns all checks off, for
  example on managed machines.

Builds you compile yourself, the Flatpak and the browser app (which updates itself) never check.

## Which file Download gets

Releases attach the main packages under fixed names (see [releasing](https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft/blob/main/docs/releasing.md)),
and SolidCraft picks the one matching how it was installed:

| Installed as | Detected by | Download | How to update |
|---|---|---|---|
| AppImage | `APPIMAGE` is set | `solidcraft-linux-<arch>.AppImage` | Replace the old AppImage with the new one |
| Flatpak | `FLATPAK_ID` is set | doesn't check (see below) | `flatpak update ai.storyteller.solidcraft` |
| Snap from the Snap Store | `SNAP` is set | release page | `sudo snap refresh solidcraft` (snapd also refreshes by itself) |
| Snap from a downloaded file | `SNAP_REVISION` starts with `x` | `solidcraft-linux-<arch>.snap` | `sudo snap install --dangerous ./solidcraft-linux-<arch>.snap` |
| `.deb` | under `/usr`, dpkg knows `solidcraft` | `solidcraft-linux-<arch>.deb` | `sudo apt install ./solidcraft-linux-<arch>.deb` |
| `.rpm` | under `/usr`, an rpm database exists | `solidcraft-linux-<arch>.rpm` | `sudo dnf install ./solidcraft-linux-<arch>.rpm` |
| `.tar.gz` | anywhere else on Linux | `solidcraft-<version>-linux-<arch>.tar.gz` | Unpack over the old copy |
| Windows installer | under Program Files, or in the folder the installer recorded | `solidcraft-windows-<arch>.msi` | Run the installer |
| Windows portable | `solidcraft-cli.exe` beside it | `solidcraft-windows-<arch>-portable.zip` | Unzip over the old copy |
| Windows `.exe` | anywhere else on Windows | `SolidCraft-<version>-windows-x64.exe` | Replace the old `.exe` |
| macOS | inside `SolidCraft.app` | `solidcraft-macos-universal.dmg` | Drag the new app to Applications |

The window shows the command for Snap, `.deb` and `.rpm` installations, with a Copy button. The
Flatpak has no network permission and Flatpak itself (or your software center) offers its
updates, so it never checks. Release builds compare versions as [semver](https://semver.org): a nightly build counts
as the release it was built after, so it's offered only a newer stable release, and release
candidates are offered their final release.

# Keyboard shortcuts

Command shortcuts can be changed in File › Keyboard Shortcuts; these are the defaults.

| Key | Command | Key | Command |
|---|---|---|---|
| L | Line | E | Extrude |
| R | Two-Point Rectangle | Q | Press Pull |
| C | Center Diameter Circle | F | Fillet |
| D | Sketch Dimension | H | Hole |
| X | Construction | M | Move/Copy |
| O | Offset | J | Joint |
| T | Trim | I | Measure |
| P | Project | A | Appearance |
| Ctrl+Z | Undo | Ctrl+Y | Redo |
| Ctrl+N | New Design | Ctrl+O | Open |
| Ctrl+S | Save | Delete | Delete the selection |

Keys handled by the window itself:

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| S | the S box: search every command at the cursor |
| V | show or hide the selected bodies, sketches and planes |
| F2 | rename the selected browser or timeline item |
| F6 | fit the view to the model |
| ← → ↑ ↓ | turn the view 15° (with Shift, a quarter turn) |
| Ctrl+← → ↑ ↓ | pan the view |
| Ctrl+8 | look straight at the selected face, plane or sketch |
| Esc | cancel the running command, or clear the selection |

While a value box has the keyboard (a dimension being added, a dialog field), keys type into
it and single-letter shortcuts don't fire. With Sketch Dimension (D), the box opens as soon as
you click a line, circle or arc (or the second point or line), so D, click, type the value,
Enter.

Mouse and touch:

| Action | Result |
|---|---|
| Click | select (Shift or Ctrl adds) |
| Click again on the same spot | select the next thing under the cursor (click cycling) |
| Hold the left button still (long-press on touch), or right-click › Select Other… | list everything under the cursor to pick from |
| Double-click a sketch curve or edge | select its chain or tangent loop |
| Double-click the middle button | go Home: the home view, framing everything shown (Preferences › Navigation › Middle double-click: Home, Fit or Off) |

Help › Keyboard Shortcuts in the app lists the current bindings, including any you changed.

With the **Touchpad** navigation preset, hold **Shift** while moving the pointer to pan, or
**Alt/Option** to orbit, without pressing a mouse button. Vertical scrolling zooms. These
viewport gestures are separate from rebindable command shortcuts; mouse-button selection
and editing keep their existing modifiers.

### Sketch modifiers

While drawing or dragging a sketch point:

| Keys | Action |
|---|---|
| Ctrl/Cmd or Alt/Option (default) | suppress auto-snap for that gesture |
| Shift | prefer a line midpoint when targeting |

Change the snap-suppress chord in Preferences › Sketch. Selection still uses Shift and
Ctrl/Cmd to add or toggle (Preferences › Selection can make Shift add-only).

# The command engine

Every user-visible action is a **command**: a `CommandSpec` registered in
`crates/engine/src/cmd/`, with a dotted, lower-case id (`solid.extrude`, `sketch.create`,
`timeline.rollback`). The toolbar, dialogs, marking menu, S box, scripts, the CLI, the control
channel and MCP all run commands through `Session::execute(id, params)`. Commands take JSON
parameters and never open dialogs; a dialog is a front-end form that builds the parameters.

```rust
CommandSpec::new("solid.fillet", "Fillet", fillet)
    .at("SOLID", "MODIFY")      // toolbar tab and panel ("" = not on the toolbar)
    .icon("fillet")             // drawn in code, assets/icons/ui/source/icons.rs
    .key("F")                   // default shortcut
    .params("edges: [[x,y,z] | {body, index}]; radius: expr; …"),
```

`run` is `fn(&mut Session, &Value) -> Result<Value>`, and `enabled` is
`fn(&Session) -> Result<(), String>`; the error string is the disabled-button tooltip. The
`params` string is the one-line documentation shown by `solidcraft-cli commands`, MCP's
`list_commands` and the [command reference](../reference/commands.md).

A command that changes the design is undoable by default: the session snapshots the document
before it runs, and a failing command leaves the document unchanged. Feature commands add a
feature to the timeline and let the document evaluate it; they validate their inputs first
(units, ranges, references) and return `BadParams` instead of building a broken feature.

Only the registry's own dotted ids name commands (matched ignoring case); any other id fails
with `unknown command`, which names up to three close ids: a typo's (`solid.extrud`), or one
ending in the same word (`file.open`: did you mean `doc.open`?).

## Adding a command

1. Add a `CommandSpec` to the right file in `crates/engine/src/cmd/` and implement `run`.
2. Write engine tests that measure the result: volume, area, and face/edge/vertex counts
   against values you can derive by hand.
3. The hostile-input test (`hostile_params_never_panic` in `crates/engine/src/tests.rs`) runs
   your command automatically with every documented parameter set to junk. It must return
   errors, never panic.
4. For UI work, add a scenario (see [Test harnesses](testing.md)).

# The kernel boundary and truck

`crates/kernel` is SolidCraft's B-rep kernel. It wraps
[truck](https://github.com/ricosjp/truck) (Apache-2.0) for topology, NURBS geometry, booleans,
tessellation and STEP parsing, and it is the only crate allowed to use truck. Callers get
SolidCraft types (`Body`, face and edge indices, meshes, measures) and a
`KernelError` instead of truck types and panics.

## `guard`

truck can panic on geometry it doesn't handle. Every call into it goes through
`solidcraft_kernel::guard`, which catches the panic and turns it into
`KernelError::Internal`, leaving the model unchanged:

```rust
pub fn guard<T>(what: &str, f: impl FnOnce() -> Result<T>) -> Result<T>
```

A failing feature shows an error on the timeline; it never takes the app down.

## What is our own

truck has no fillets, chamfers, shells or face edits, so these are SolidCraft code in the
kernel: constant, chord and variable-radius fillets with corner blends, chamfers, shell and
offset, Delete Face, Split Face, Replace Face, sewing, STEP and IGES reading and writing beyond
truck's parser, and face provenance (which input face each output face came from, for
[persistent naming](naming.md)).

## Vendored truck crates

Patched copies of `truck-shapeops`, `truck-stepio` and `truck-meshalgo` live in `vendor/`,
wired in with `[patch.crates-io]`. The patches fix robustness bugs found by our tests and the
STEP corpus. `vendor/` is excluded from our fmt and clippy rules, and each patch should go
upstream when it can.

Equal cylinders crossing each other (`tangent_cylinders.rs`) touch at two points, which truck's
mesh-based intersection cannot trace through. When a boolean of such a pair fails, the kernel
splits both cylinder faces along the line through the touching points and takes the boolean of
the split bodies; the shapeops patch that picks the corner of a face at a vertex several curves
end on makes the arms of the crossing connect.

Some truck assertions only run in debug builds and can fail on valid geometry, so tests and CI
run with `--release`.

# Getting started

The desktop executable is `solidcraft`, the CLI is `solidcraft-cli`, and designs are saved as
`.solidcraft`. Designs, settings and setups from builds released under the previous product name keep
working (see the [compatibility notes](https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft/blob/main/docs/compatibility.md)).

## Desktop

Download the installer for your system from the
[Download section of the README](https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft#download) or the
[releases page](https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft/releases), or build it yourself with
stable Rust (1.95 or newer):

```sh
git clone https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft && cd solidcraft
cargo run --release -p solidcraft -- --sample   # opens with a sample part
```

`solidcraft part.step` opens a STEP, IGES, 3MF, STL or OBJ file as a new design, and
`solidcraft design.solidcraft` opens a saved design. Windows builds cross-compile from Linux with
`cargo xwin build --release --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc -p solidcraft`.

### macOS

Open the release `.dmg` and drag `SolidCraft.app` onto Applications.

When updating from a build released under the previous product name, follow the
[macOS upgrade notes](https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft/blob/main/docs/compatibility.md#macos) so you replace it rather than install a second copy.

### Linux AppImage

The first time you open the AppImage it adds a menu entry and icons under `~/.local/share`
(`applications/ai.storyteller.solidcraft.desktop`, `icons/hicolor`), so the desktop shows the
right name and icon. It adds nothing if [appimaged](https://github.com/probonopd/go-appimage)
already made an entry for the file, or if a launcher such as Gear Lever or AppImageLauncher
started it (and removes the entry SolidCraft added before). To
turn it off for good, create an empty file `~/.local/share/solidcraft/no-desktop-integration`, or
start the AppImage with `SOLIDCRAFT_NO_DESKTOP_INTEGRATION=1`.

### Linux Flatpak

Install Flatpak using your distribution's package manager. For an installation that receives
updates, add Flathub for the required Freedesktop runtime and the SolidCraft application feed
to the same user installation:

```sh
flatpak remote-add --user --if-not-exists flathub https://dl.flathub.org/repo/flathub.flatpakrepo
flatpak remote-add --user --if-not-exists solidcraft https://docs.solidcraft.io/flatpak/solidcraft.flatpakrepo
flatpak install --user solidcraft ai.storyteller.solidcraft
flatpak run ai.storyteller.solidcraft
```

A SolidCraft remote added before the project moved to `docs.solidcraft.io` (from
`bherbruck.github.io`) no longer finds updates. Point it at the new address, then update:
`flatpak remote-modify --user --url=https://docs.solidcraft.io/flatpak/repo/ solidcraft` and
`flatpak update --user`.

Releases up to 0.7 used the application ID `ai.storyteller.solvecraft`. If you installed one
of those from the SolidCraft remote, `flatpak update --user` reports it as end-of-life and offers
to replace it with `ai.storyteller.solidcraft`; accept, and your settings and autosaves move with
it. If you installed a `.flatpak` bundle, install the new bundle, launch it once (it copies your
settings), then run `flatpak uninstall --user ai.storyteller.solvecraft` (see the
[compatibility notes](https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft/blob/main/docs/compatibility.md#linux-app-id)).

Alternatively, download the release's `.flatpak` file for your architecture and run
`flatpak install --user ./solidcraft-VERSION-linux-ARCH.flatpak`. The bundle supplies the
Flathub runtime repository address; installation still needs internet access to fetch any
missing runtime. Launch with `flatpak run ai.storyteller.solidcraft`, rather than looking for
a host `solidcraft` binary. Files chosen through Open/Save use the desktop file-chooser portal;
command-line paths outside Documents may need a specific additional filesystem permission.

### Linux Snap

On Ubuntu and other distributions with snapd:

```sh
sudo snap install solidcraft
solidcraft                # or open SolidCraft from the app menu
solidcraft.cli --version  # the CLI, for scripts and `solidcraft.cli mcp`
```

The snap can open designs in your home folder (not hidden folders) and, through the file
chooser, anywhere else. For USB drives and other mounted disks, run
`sudo snap connect solidcraft:removable-media` once. A release's `.snap` file installs without
the store with `sudo snap install --dangerous ./solidcraft-VERSION-linux-ARCH.snap`; it then
doesn't update automatically.

## Web

The same app runs in the browser: [open SolidCraft on the web](../app/) (`?sample` opens the sample
part, `?webgl` forces WebGL2 where WebGPU is missing or misbehaves; the browser remembers it until
`?webgpu`, and an app installed from Chrome or Edge starts with it too). Designs are saved in the
browser's private file storage, which needs HTTPS or localhost.
Planned worker and tiered-storage integration is
described in [web-runtime.md](https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft/blob/main/docs/web-runtime.md)
(design; not yet wired in the shipped wasm build).

After the first visit the web app works offline: the browser keeps a copy of it. Online, each
launch gets the latest published build (the browser downloads it once when it changes); offline,
when the network doesn't answer within a few seconds, or when a new build can't be downloaded
whole, the kept copy starts (and the download carries on for the next launch).

Browsers that can install web apps add **Install app…** to the File menu: it installs SolidCraft
as an app with its own window and launcher icon, working offline like the page. In Chrome, Edge
and other Chromium browsers it shows the browser's install prompt, and once SolidCraft is
installed the item is gone. Safari has no such prompt, so the item shows its steps instead:
Share › Add to Home Screen on iPhone and iPad, File › Add to Dock on a Mac (Safari 17 or later).

To build it yourself:

```sh
rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown
cd apps/solidcraft-web && trunk serve --release --no-autoreload
```

Offline use needs `--no-autoreload`: Trunk's live reload changes the page as it serves it, so it
no longer matches the build the browser would keep. Debug builds (`trunk serve`) never keep a copy.

### Self-hosting with Docker

The web app is also a container image, `ghcr.io/tangency-labs/solidcraft-web`, for Linux on x86_64
and ARM64: `latest` is the latest release, `0.14.0` or `0.14` a release, `edge` the newest `main`.
It serves the app with nginx on port 8080 and keeps nothing on the server: designs stay in each
visitor's browser.

```sh
docker run -d --name solidcraft -p 8080:8080 --restart unless-stopped ghcr.io/tangency-labs/solidcraft-web:latest
```

Or with Docker Compose, using
[`packaging/docker/compose.yaml`](https://github.com/tangency-labs/solidcraft/blob/main/packaging/docker/compose.yaml)
(`SOLIDCRAFT_PORT` picks another port):

```sh
docker compose -f packaging/docker/compose.yaml up -d      # start
docker compose -f packaging/docker/compose.yaml pull && docker compose -f packaging/docker/compose.yaml up -d   # update
docker compose -f packaging/docker/compose.yaml up -d --build   # build the image from your checkout instead
```

Then open `http://localhost:8080/`. On another machine the browser only saves designs over HTTPS,
so put a reverse proxy with a certificate in front (Caddy, Traefik, nginx); the app works under
any URL path, such as `https://example.com/cad/`. To build the image without Compose, from the
repository root: `docker build -f packaging/docker/Dockerfile -t solidcraft-web .`

### 3D mouse in the browser

The web app reads a 3Dconnexion SpaceMouse or SpaceNavigator through the browser's Gamepad API,
with the same switch and speed in Preferences › Navigation as the desktop app. Edge and Chrome
read the device as it is. A browser shows a gamepad to a page only once it has been moved there,
so if nothing happens at first, push the cap firmly once. 3DxWare also turns the cap into
mouse-wheel zoom in browsers; while the cap moves, the web app ignores the wheel and reads the
cap itself. Before the browser shows the cap to the page, that zoom still gets through, so the
first push after opening the page may zoom a little.

Firefox doesn't list 3D mice ([Mozilla bug 1226575](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1226575)).
On Windows it does list 3DxWare's virtual joystick, which can carry the cap instead. Save this
as `%APPDATA%\3Dconnexion\3DxWare\Cfg\Firefox.xml`, then restart Firefox (and 3DxWare, if the cap
still only zooms). It changes Firefox only: there 3DxWare sends the cap's six axes to the
joystick instead of the mouse wheel. Delete the file to undo it.

  </AppInfo>
  <CfgProperties>
    <ID>ID_STR_FIREFOX</ID>

  </CfgProperties>

        <Name>STR_DEFAULT_BANK</Name>

## CLI

`solidcraft-cli` runs the same commands without a window:

```sh
cargo run --release -p solidcraft-cli -- commands                       # every command, as JSON
cargo run --release -p solidcraft-cli -- run examples/bracket.json --out bracket.step
cargo run --release -p solidcraft-cli -- eval examples/bracket.json     # volume, area, faces…
cargo run --release -p solidcraft-cli -- snapshot examples/bracket.json --out bracket.png
cargo run --release -p solidcraft-cli -- exec solid.box '{"length": 20, "width": 10, "height": 5}'
cargo run --release -p solidcraft-cli -- run mechanism.json --in arm.solidcraft  # with a motion.export_animation step: a GIF
```

A script is a list of commands:

```json
{"commands": [
  {"command": "sketch.create", "params": {"plane": "XY"}},
  {"command": "sketch.rectangle.two_point", "params": {"p0": [0, 0], "p1": [40, 30]}},
  {"command": "sketch.finish", "params": {}},
  {"command": "solid.extrude", "params": {"distance": 20}},
  {"command": "solid.fillet", "params": {"edges": [[0, 0, 10]], "radius": 3}}
]}
```

![The bracket example, rendered by solidcraft-cli snapshot](../generated/bracket.png)

`snapshot` looks at the model from the iso view. `--view NAME` takes another standard view (`front`, `back`, `top`, `bottom`, `left`, `right`) or the name of a view saved in the design with `view.save`. `--camera JSON` takes any camera, as the MCP `screenshot` tool does (its conventions are in [the MCP page](mcp.md#camera-and-close-up-recipe)). A script that applies a view itself with `view.apply` sets the camera too. The ground grid lies on Z 0, so it cuts through a part that straddles it: `--no-grid` leaves it out of the picture, and `--no-axes` the origin's axes. The picture is drawn on the GPU with the viewport's own pipelines, so it shows what the window would (a surface analysis such as `inspect.zebra` included); a machine without a GPU uses a software one (Mesa's lavapipe on Linux, WARP on Windows), and with neither (a Mac without usable Metal, a Linux box without Mesa's Vulkan) the CPU rasterizer draws it, without surface analysis colours, and the reply's `renderer` says `cpu` with a warning. `SOLIDCRAFT_GPU=auto|hardware|software|cpu` chooses (`hardware` and `software` fail rather than fall to the CPU), and `solidcraft-cli gpu` lists the adapters and the tier a snapshot would use.

```sh
solidcraft-cli snapshot part.solidcraft --out photo.png --view Photo
solidcraft-cli snapshot part.solidcraft --out close-up.png --no-grid --no-axes --camera '{"target": [30, -20, 0], "yaw": 0.6, "pitch": 0.25, "distance": 60}'
```

### Seeing what a cut or a join is about to do

A picture answers in a glance what a volume cannot: does the tool body reach through the
material, and is it where you meant it to be? `--body NAME:opacity=0.3` draws that body
see-through, so whatever is inside it shows; `--body NAME:color=#cc3333` gives it a colour.
Either key on its own keeps what the design says about the other, and the option is a shortcut
for `appearance.assign`, the command the Appearance dialog runs — the picture is the one the
window would show with the same appearance assigned.

`--tool NAME` is the common case in one option: that body solid in the tool colour, every
other body see-through around it. `--section z=27` cuts the model at a plane so the inside
shows, as `inspect.section` does: an axis and the world coordinate to cut at, `,flip` to keep
the other side, `XY`, `XZ` or `YZ` for a plane through the origin, or the command's own JSON.

![A pin inside a translucent plate, cut by a section plane](../generated/tool-preview.png)

```sh
# The pin the cut would remove, inside the plate it stops 6 mm short of.
solidcraft-cli snapshot plate.solidcraft --out preview.png --tool Pin
solidcraft-cli snapshot plate.solidcraft --out cut.png --tool Pin --section z=12
solidcraft-cli snapshot plate.solidcraft --out glass.png --body "Plate:opacity=0.25" --body "Pin:color=#1a7f4b"
```

A body drawn see-through is drawn see-through everywhere a picture is drawn, not only here:
an appearance with an opacity below 1 (`Glass - Clear` in the library, or any `opacity` you
assign) now reads as glass in `snapshot`, in MCP screenshots and in a design's thumbnail, as it
always has in the window. A face painted with a see-through look of its own still draws at its
body's opacity.

Windows PowerShell 5.1 drops the double quotes inside an argument it passes to a program: write them as `\"` there.

A command that fails stops the script. A feature can also fail later, when a parameter change
rebuilds it; `run` then exits with status 1, lists the failing features and writes none of
its `--out` and `--save` files, because the bodies lack what those features should have made.
`--allow-errors` writes them anyway.

`run` prints each command's result with `--results` (otherwise the measurement), and `eval`
prints the measurement, as JSON on stdout. `--json-out FILE` writes that JSON to a file
instead. The file is plain UTF-8, which is not what a redirect gives you everywhere: Windows
PowerShell's `>` re-encodes a program's output, as UTF-16 or as UTF-8 with a byte-order mark
depending on its settings, and strict JSON readers such as Python's `json.load` then refuse it.

```sh
cargo run --release -p solidcraft-cli -- run examples/bracket.json --results --json-out results.json
cargo run --release -p solidcraft-cli -- eval examples/bracket.json --json-out measures.json
```

To find the slow steps of a script, `--timings` prints how long each command took instead of
the measurement: `{"timings": [{"index", "command", "ms"}], "total_ms"}`, with `index` counted
from 0. `--profile` adds each command's `profile: {"boolean_ms", "tessellate_ms", "other_ms"}`,
its wall time in the kernel's booleans, in tessellation and in everything else. With
`--results` as well, the results go in the same object as `results`; `--results` alone still
prints a plain array.

```sh
cargo run --release -p solidcraft-cli -- run examples/bracket.json --profile
```

A design's history turns into a script that rebuilds it, which makes a bug that only shows
on one design a one-file reproduction:

```sh
cargo run --release -p solidcraft-cli -- script part.solidcraft --out repro.json
cargo run --release -p solidcraft-cli -- eval repro.json               # the same part
```

The script starts with the user parameters (`parameters.add`) and the design's units, sheet
metal and plastic rules and materials, then adds each timeline feature with `timeline.add`,
exactly as the design file holds it: same ids, names and parameter names, so later steps
still find the sketches and bodies they use, and a feature that failed in the design fails
the same way. Edit a step's values to try a change, or delete the steps after a feature to
see the design as it was there. Appearances, folders, named views and configurations are
left out (the CLI notes which), and designs with components or joints are not supported
yet. In the app and over MCP the same script comes from `timeline.export_script`.

Units are millimetres and degrees unless an expression says otherwise (`"1 in"`, `"30 deg"`),
and Z is up.

## Name and compatibility

SolidCraft was renamed from an earlier working name. Since 0.5.0 everything uses the new
name: the `solidcraft` and `solidcraft-cli` programs, `.solidcraft` designs, `SOLIDCRAFT_*`
environment variables, settings folders and the `solidcraft` MCP server. Upgrading keeps
working: designs, settings, recovery files, environment variables and CLI/MCP setups from
earlier builds carry over. Every compatibility shim is listed in the
[compatibility notes](https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft/blob/main/docs/compatibility.md).

Use the SolidCraft documentation and web-app URLs. GitHub redirects links to the renamed
repository; old-name Pages and Flatpak URLs are not maintained as permanent aliases.

# SolidCraft and AI agents (MCP)

SolidCraft speaks the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) over stdio
(JSON-RPC 2.0, one message per line; protocol revisions 2025-06-18, 2025-03-26 and 2024-11-05).
An agent models exactly like a person does: every tool runs engine commands, the same ones the
toolbar, palette, scripts and control channel use, and never opens a dialog.

Persistent headless and bridged sessions expose asynchronous product images through the
ordinary `execute` tool: `render.preflight`, `render.start`, `render.status`,
`render.cancel` and `render.export`. Keep the complete returned job ID; image bytes remain
in the session until explicit PNG export. See [render jobs](render-jobs.md).

For how the same command surface should work in the browser (workers, tiered storage, in-tab
agents), see [web-runtime.md](web-runtime.md). For sandboxed plugins and parametric timeline
features that also use `run(command, args)`, see [plugins.md](plugins.md). Desktop MCP in this
document remains the reference implementation today.

## Start it

```sh
# Headless: an in-process design session, no window (screenshots are drawn on the GPU).
solidcraft-cli mcp

# Headless, starting from a design file or a command script.
solidcraft-cli mcp --in part.solidcraft

# Bridged to the running app, so you can watch the agent model:
solidcraft --control 7878 &
solidcraft-cli mcp --connect 127.0.0.1:7878
```

Bridged, the server finds the app's control token in the token file the app wrote for that port
([control-protocol.md](control-protocol.md#token)); `--token T` or `SOLIDCRAFT_CONTROL_TOKEN` give
it explicitly when the app runs in a sandbox whose data folder the server can't see (prefer the
variable: command-line arguments are visible to other users in the process list).

A bridged server starts even when no app listens on that port yet, so an MCP client that
launches it before the app (or after the app was closed) keeps its tools. The server's
instructions then say the app was not running, and every tool call answers with an error that
starts `no SolidCraft app is listening at HOST:PORT` and says how to start it
(`solidcraft --control PORT`). The first call after the app starts connects to it, reading that
launch's token. When the app quits or crashes mid-session, the next call says the same; a call
that was running when it went away says the app did not answer and may have quit or crashed,
after running the call or not, so inspect the design before sending a change again.
A `batch` that could not be sent says the app is not running, so it is safe to send again.

stdout carries only protocol messages; errors go to stderr. Bridged screenshots are written to a
temporary file by the app and read back by the server, so both must run on the same machine.

### Parameter checking

Commands with a typed parameter contract (`solid.box`, `solid.extrude` and `engine.describe`
so far; `describe_command` shows a command's schemas) can be checked as they are called.
`--param-check off|warn|strict` sets the level for a headless session, including a script or
recipe given with `--in`; the default is `off`, which changes nothing. `warn` runs the call and
adds `param_warnings` to its result, such as ``unknown key `operaton`; did you mean
`operation`?`` (a starting script's warnings go to stderr). `strict` refuses the call, and the
design is left as it was. Calls bridged to the app are not checked yet.

### Which files the agent can reach

Tool calls read, write and delete files only inside the server's folders:

- the folder of the open design (the `--in` design, or whatever the agent last opened or saved),
  but only when it lies strictly inside your home folder (or the temporary folder) and not in a
  hidden folder. Home itself, a folder above it (`/`, `/home`, `/Users`, a drive's root),
  hidden folders such as `~/.config` and folders elsewhere don't count. Hidden files and folders
  inside the design's folder (`.env`, `.git`) are out of reach too;
- SolidCraft's own recovery folder, so `doc.recovery_list`, `doc.recover` and
  `doc.recovery_discard` work out of the box (discarding deletes only real recovery entries);
- the server's own scratch folder (a new private `solidcraft-mcp-*` folder in the temporary
  folder), where `screenshot` without a `path` goes;
- every `--allow-path DIR` (repeat it for more). A folder named here is reached in full,
  hidden files included.

The working folder the server was started in does not count by itself, so `~/.ssh`, `~/.aws`,
`~/.bashrc` and other dotfiles are never in reach by default. stderr lists the folders at
start-up and says when the `--in` design's folder was left out; `--allow-path` adds it back.

Paths are resolved before they are compared, so `..` and symlinks that lead out are refused
(saving through a link writes the file it points to, so the link's target is what counts), and
a new file must go into a folder that exists (a missing folder inside an allowed one is reported as missing; it is not created and does not call for a wider `--allow-path`). On Windows a path must be on a local drive
(`C:\…` or `\\?\C:\…`): UNC, device and NT paths in any spelling (`\\server\share`,
`//server/share`, `\\?\UNC\…`, `\??\…`, `\\.\…`), drive-relative paths (`C:file`), a `:` in a
file name (alternate data streams), reserved device names with any extension (`NUL`, `CON`,
`COM1.txt`, …) and short 8.3 names (`PROGRA~1`) are refused before any file system call, and the
resolved path is checked again, so a link or junction that leads to a share is refused too. This
includes a `sketch.text` font given as a file path and the font file a design's text names when
the design is opened; installed fonts named by family still work.
The server spells its own folders (scratch, recovery) with long names, so they work when the
temporary folder's path has a short name (`…\NAME~1.XYZ\AppData\Local\Temp`, as Windows often
gives when the user folder's name is long).
A refused path is a tool error saying why.

A hard link inside an allowed folder can't be told apart from an ordinary file, so a hard link
to a file elsewhere is reachable through it; don't keep such links in a folder you allow.

```sh
solidcraft-cli mcp --allow-path ~/designs --allow-path ~/exports
solidcraft-cli mcp --allow-any-path   # no limit (the behaviour before this option existed)
```

Bridged, the server sends its folders with every request (`allow_paths`, see
[control-protocol.md](control-protocol.md)) and the app adds its own recovery folder and the
folder of the design open in it, under the same rules, so give absolute paths: a relative one
resolves against the app's working folder, not the server's. The app's own
file dialogs are never limited.

### Tool annotations

Each tool says what it may do, for clients that ask before running tools (or auto-approve on
these hints). `list_commands`, `describe_command`, `inspect_design`, `measure`, `body_topology`
and `crash_reports` are read-only. `set_parameter`, `undo` and `redo` change the design undoably.
`new_design` replaces it (destructive). `execute`, `batch`, `open`, `save`, `export` and
`screenshot` (whose `path` writes a file) can read, write, overwrite or delete files: they are
not read-only, `destructiveHint` and `openWorldHint` are true.

### Client configuration

Claude Code (project `.mcp.json`, or `claude mcp add solidcraft -- solidcraft-cli mcp`; a setup
added under the previous name keeps working, see the [compatibility notes](https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft/blob/main/docs/compatibility.md#mcp)):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "solidcraft": { "command": "solidcraft-cli", "args": ["mcp"] }
  }
}
```

Claude Desktop (`claude_desktop_config.json`), bridged to a running app:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "solidcraft": { "command": "/path/to/solidcraft-cli", "args": ["mcp", "--connect", "127.0.0.1:7878"] }
  }
}
```

### Agent skills

[`skills/`](https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft/tree/main/skills) holds four [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io) for agents that model through this server:
- `solidcraft-modeling` covers building a new part.
- `solidcraft-editing` covers changing an existing design.
- `solidcraft-checking` adds checks for errors SolidCraft does not report, regression tests and porting, next to the other two.
- `solidcraft-mechanisms` covers assemblies: joints placed by world coordinates, motion links, closed loops such as actuators, contact sets and motion studies, checked against analytic values.

They cover the workflow, the command shapes, how to verify with `measure`, and the known traps. With them an agent builds a part in a few `batch` calls and reads far less output. To install them for Claude Code, copy the folders into `~/.claude/skills/`; [skills/README.md](https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft/blob/main/skills/README.md) has the details.

## Tools

| Tool | Arguments | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `list_commands` | `filter?` | The command catalog: id, label, tab/panel, shortcut, parameter docs, enabled now. `filter` matches id, label, tab and panel. |
| `describe_command` | `id` | One command's parameter docs (`params`) and, for commands with a typed contract (`solid.box`, `solid.extrude` and `engine.describe` so far), the JSON Schemas (2020-12) of its parameters (`input`) and of a successful result (`output`); `null` for the others. The same as `execute` `engine.describe {command}`. |
| `execute` | `command`, `params?`, `verbose?` (default true) | Run any command with JSON parameters (`list_commands` shows them). Failures leave the design unchanged. A feature command replies with the feature (`feature`, `name`), every body (`bodies`) and the bodies it created, changed and removed (`created_bodies`, `changed_bodies`, `removed_bodies`). `verbose: false` uses the same compact reply as `batch`. |
| `batch` | `commands: [{command, params}]`, `rollback?` (default true), `verbose?` (default true), `timings?`, `profile?` (default false) | Run steps in order, stop at the first error and undo the completed steps. The reply names the failing step (`failed.index`, `failed.command`, `failed.error`) and every result before it. `verbose: false` keeps the reply small in large designs: feature steps leave out the full body list (`created_bodies`, `changed_bodies`, `removed_bodies` stay) and sketch steps the ids they repeat outside `created`. Bridged to an app that has `engine.batch`, the whole batch is one control request (one frame of the app). Older apps, and apps showing the agent cursor, get the steps one by one. `timings: true` adds `timings: [{index, command, ms}]` for every step run, the failing one included, and `total_ms`. `profile: true` also adds each step's `profile: {boolean_ms, tessellate_ms, other_ms}`, its time in kernel booleans, in tessellation and the rest. | `inspect_design` | `measure?` (default true), `sketches?` (default true) | Design properties (`metadata`: project, author… and other tools' keys; set them with `execute` `document.metadata.set`), parameters, timeline (type, suppressed, rolled back, error, warning, timing), bodies (volume, area, centre of mass, bbox, face/edge/vertex counts, visible; `removed_later: true` while a sketch is being edited on a rolled-back timeline and a later feature deletes the body, which is then not shown), sketches (curves, points, constraints, profiles, DOF, solve status, visible), selection, undo depth. Hide helper sketches, bodies or construction planes with `execute` `browser.visibility` (`{items, visible}` or `{folder, visible}`), and joint glyphs with `{joints: [id or name], visible}` or `{folder: "joints", visible}` (a hidden joint still constrains and drives; `joint.list` reports each joint's `visible`). |
| `measure` | `body?` or `items?` | Volume (mm³), area (mm²), centre of mass, bbox and topology counts per body, with totals. With `items` (one or two selections as `execute` takes them: `face`, `edge`, `vertex`, `sketch_curve`, `profile`), the picked geometry instead: see below. |

A face's `point` lies on it and picks it (its centroid may not: that of a face with a hole is in the hole); a face's `name` picks it for the commands that take faces (`face.delete`, `solid.shell`, `solid.draft`, `solid.offset_face`, `solid.split_face`, `solid.replace_face`, and `face` of `sheet.convert`). |

`measure` with `items` reports each item under `items` (`length_mm`, `area_mm2` or `position`).
A circle, arc, hole or other cylindrical face also gives `diameter`, `radius`, `center` and
`axis`, with `circumference` when it goes all the way round, or `arc_length` and `angle_deg`
for an arc; `round` says which (`circle`, `arc`, `cylinder`). A slot (a sketch profile of two
half circles and two lines, or one half-cylinder end of a slot in a solid) gives `slot`:
`width`, `center_distance` and `overall_length`. With one item these fields are repeated at
the top level. With two items:

- `min` (also `distance_mm`, with `from`, `to` and `delta`): the closest distance;
- `max` (with `max_from`, `max_to`): the farthest distance;
- `center_distance` (with `center_from`, `center_to`): when an item is round, from its centre
  or axis: axis to axis for parallel axes, the closest distance between the axes otherwise,
  and axis to plane, line or point;
- `measure`: the distance the Measure panel shows first (`center` where there is one, else `min`);
- `angle_deg` between two planar faces or straight edges.

Earlier fields are unchanged, so older scripts keep working.

To change a feature after it is made, read its definition with `execute` `timeline.inspect`
(`{feature}`: id or name) and change fields with `timeline.edit` (`{feature, set}`; e.g.
`{"extent": {"distance": "30"}}`). The fields per feature type are listed in the book's
*Solid features* chapter.

Resources: `solidcraft://design` (inspect JSON with measurements) and `solidcraft://commands`
(the catalog).

Errors: an unknown tool or arguments that don't match the tool's schema are JSON-RPC
`-32602` errors; an engine failure (bad command parameters, a feature that fails) is a tool
result with `isError: true` and the engine's message, which the model can read and correct.

`batch` rollback goes back to an engine checkpoint (`edit.checkpoint`) taken before the first
step: the design, the active sketch and the undo history are restored exactly as they were,
however long the history is. Batches that call `file.new` or `doc.open` get the design back,
not its file path. (An older app without checkpoints falls back to undoing as many steps as
the batch added to the undo history.)

## Camera and close-up recipe

The `camera` of `screenshot` (the object `view.apply`, `view.save` and `solidcraft-cli snapshot --camera` take too) is an orbit camera, `{target, yaw, pitch, distance, fov?}`, in millimetres and **radians**. Unlike the `angle` of `solid.move`, a bare number is not degrees here. The eye is at `target + distance * (-sin(yaw) * cos(pitch), -cos(yaw) * cos(pitch), sin(pitch))`, looking at `target` with Z up on the screen. So `yaw: 0, pitch: 0` is the front view: the eye at -Y, looking along +Y, with +X to the right. A yaw of π/2 looks from -X, π from +Y and -π/2 from +X. The pitch is the elevation angle up from the XY plane, and π/2 looks straight down with +X to the right and +Y up. `fov` is the vertical field of view in radians. `0`, or no `fov`, is an orthographic view whose visible half-height is 0.4 × `distance`; with a perspective `fov` the half-height at the target is `distance * tan(fov / 2)`. `inspect.section` removes what lies on the side its normal points to: it keeps the points `p` with `n · p < d`, where `d = n · origin` (`flip: true` keeps the other side). To look into the cut, put the eye on the removed side.

To look closely at one part of a large model, such as a STEP assembly, work in a headless session. These steps change only the open design in memory:

1. Open the model with `solidcraft-cli mcp --in assembly.step` (or the `open` tool, which also takes `up` and `names`, see step 4 and [STEP import](step-import.md)). `inspect_design` lists the bodies with their names and bounding boxes.
2. Remove what is in the way with `solid.remove`, e.g. `{"bodies": ["Cover"]}`.
3. Cut the region out of the rest with `solid.box`, e.g. `{"corner": [40, 0, -45], "length": 20, "width": 50, "height": 45, "operation": "intersect", "targets": ["Housing", "Plate"]}`. Each listed body is trimmed to the box, and one that lies wholly outside the box is removed. The box itself is not kept.
4. If the model lies on its back (many STEP files have +Y up), open it with `up: "y"` (the `open` tool, `doc.open`, `file.insert_step`), which turns the file's bodies a quarter turn about X (Y becomes Z). One already open is stood Z up with `solid.move`, listing every body you keep, e.g. `{"bodies": ["Housing", "Plate"], "axis": [1, 0, 0], "angle": 90}`. It turns the bodies about the world origin, and a bare angle is in degrees. A turn of +90° about X takes +Y to +Z.
5. Colour the parts that matter with `appearance.assign`, e.g. `{"bodies": ["Housing"], "color": "#3a7bd5"}`, and hide helper bodies or sketches with `browser.visibility`, e.g. `{"items": ["Plate"], "visible": false}`.
6. Cut a section with `inspect.section`, e.g. `{"plane": {"origin": [50, 30, 0], "normal": [0, 1, 0]}}` or `{"plane": "XY", "at": 5}`.
7. Take the picture with `screenshot`: a `camera` whose `target` is the centre of the region and whose eye is on the cut side, `source: "model"`, `grid: false` if the region straddles Z 0 (the ground grid would cut through it), and `path`, `width` and `height` as needed. An orthographic picture is 0.8 × `distance` high, so a `distance` of about 1.5 times the region's size frames it. Look at the image, adjust `yaw`, `pitch` and `distance`, and shoot again. Headless, the picture is always a render of the model; bridged to the app, `source: "model"` asks for that render instead of the app's window.

## Compact replies

`execute` and `batch` default to `verbose: true`, preserving the full command results.
For long modelling sessions, set `verbose: false` at the tool-argument level:

```json
{"name": "execute", "arguments": {"command": "solid.box", "params": {"length": 10, "width": 10, "height": 10}, "verbose": false}}
```

Feature replies omit the full `bodies` list while keeping `feature`, `name`,
`created_bodies`, `changed_bodies` and `removed_bodies`. A cut can therefore report a
changed body even when no body name was added or removed. Sketch replies keep new
IDs under `created` and omit only identical top-level `points`, `curves`,
`constraints` and `dimensions` lists. Other fields and errors are unchanged;
inspection commands still return their complete results. Compaction uses the
engine's reply directly, without an additional design-inspection request.

## Demo: an enclosure built over MCP

`examples/demo/enclosure_mcp.py` is a small MCP client. It drives a running app (`solidcraft
--control PORT`) through `solidcraft-cli mcp --connect` and builds an electronics enclosure one
`execute` call at a time (`enclosure_steps.json`): a rounded box, shelled open at the top, a
USB port cut through a side wall, four screw bosses, and then a change of the `width`
parameter that the timeline rebuilds. `examples/demo/record.sh` records the run with ffmpeg,
with each step's caption burnt in.

`examples/demo/enclosure_ui_mcp.py` (v2) builds the same part the way a person would: the
modelling goes through the app's UI over its control channel. The pointer glides to toolbar
buttons and faces and clicks them, the real dialogs open, the sketches go on the model's faces,
and the camera follows. The parameters, the sketch dimensions bound to them and two extrudes go
over MCP. With `--story v3` (the default) one standoff is patterned 2 × 2 in the Rectangular
Pattern dialog with spacings from the parameters, and width and wall are then changed in the
Parameters dialog. `record_ui.sh` records it and draws the pointer and the captions.
