# Import and export

| Format | Read | Write |
|---|---|---|
| `.solidcraft` (versioned container or JSON design) | yes | yes |
| `.json` (self-contained plain JSON design) | yes | yes |
| STEP (AP203, AP214, AP242) | solids, assemblies, units, names, colours | AP242 with names, colours and the component tree |
| IGES 5.3 | manifold solids, or trimmed surfaces sewn into solids | manifold solids with names and colours |
| FreeCAD `.FCStd`, Rhino `.3dm` | solids, through cadmpeg (desktop app only) | |
| 3MF, STL, OBJ | mesh bodies | yes |
| glTF 2.0 (`.glb`, `.gltf` with its `.bin` files) | mesh bodies in the node tree's components, materials as appearances | |
| 3MF with face tags | as 3MF | each triangle tagged with its B-rep face, exact coordinates |
| URDF | | the assembly as a robot: links with meshes, mass and inertia, joints from the assembly's joints |
| DXF, SVG | into a sketch | sketches and flat patterns as DXF |
| PNG, JPEG | canvases and decals | |

Opening a STEP, IGES, FreeCAD or Rhino file creates a design with the file's bodies as a base feature, and
inserting one adds them to the current design. Later features build on them. Mesh bodies render,
measure, move and export, but solid features need B-rep bodies.

Every imported file (STEP, IGES, 3MF, STL, OBJ or glTF) comes in as a new component named after the
file, so its bodies never mix with yours. A STEP assembly keeps its structure: its parts and
sub-assemblies become nested components, and a part used several times is one component with an
occurrence for each place. The imported assembly is rigid: moving its component moves everything,
and its parts don't move on their own. Right-click the component and choose **Unlock Contents** to
joint the parts one by one. Undo removes a whole import in one step.

A glTF file (`.glb`, or `.gltf` with the `.bin` files it names in the same folder) comes in the
same way: its nodes become nested components, a mesh placed several times is one component with
an occurrence for each place, and the whole import is rigid until you unlock it. glTF is in metres
with Y up, so the import is scaled to millimetres and turned to stand Z up (`up: "z"` keeps the
file's axes). Each material's base colour, metal and roughness become the body's appearance, so
the model looks right in Render; textures, skins and animations are not imported. Scaled or
mirrored nodes are baked into their meshes. Compressed meshes (Draco, meshopt) are refused with a
message: save the file uncompressed first.

A 3MF project saved by a slicer comes in too, also when it keeps its objects in model parts of
their own inside the file (the 3MF Production extension): each object on the build plate becomes
a mesh body, with its parts where the slicer placed them.

**File → Save as mesh…** (also on the Mesh tab under Modify, and in the right-click menu of a
body) saves the selected bodies as STL, 3MF or 3MF with face tags (below). With **Send to slicer** ticked, it writes the file to
a temporary folder and opens it in the chosen slicer instead of asking for a file name. The slicer
list shows the slicers found on the computer with their icons; **Custom…** adds any other program
to the top of the list (kept between runs; hover an entry you added and press Delete to remove it).

Closed mechanical meshes with a constant cross-section can be rebuilt as solids with the
`mesh.convert` command (command palette, scripts and the control channel).

**File → Save as mesh…** with the format **3MF with face tags** (`file.export` or `file.save_mesh` with `format: "3mf-tagged"`) writes an
ordinary 3MF in which every triangle also names the B-rep face it lies on and every coordinate
is the tessellation's own double-precision value. Meshing and analysis tools can use the tags to
keep a model's faces (for loads, boundary conditions or feature edges); other 3MF readers ignore
them. The format is specified in [`docs/formats/3mf-face-tags.md`](https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft/blob/main/docs/formats/3mf-face-tags.md).

**File → Export URDF…** (`file.export` with a `.urdf` path) writes the assembly for robot
simulators and ROS: a link per component placement with its mesh, mass and inertia, and the
assembly's joints, so the parts move in the simulator as they do in SolidCraft. The meshes are
written as STL files next to the `.urdf`. See [`docs/urdf.md`](https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft/blob/main/docs/urdf.md).

Saves are atomic: a crash at any moment leaves either the old file or the new one, and the
replaced version is kept as `<file>.bak`. A save keeps the file's permissions, and a design
opened through a symbolic link (a synced folder linked into a project) is saved into the file the
link points to, so the link stays. Unsaved changes are autosaved to a recovery folder,
and the next launch offers to recover them. Older design files are upgraded on open, and files
from a newer version are refused with a message.

**Save** writes a container by default; files named `.json` keep JSON on subsequent saves.
**Save As** offers a container or plain JSON on
desktop; **Save As JSON** is also available in the File menu on desktop and web. Choose
the `.json` extension for plain JSON. **Export Design as JSON** writes an independent,
self-contained copy without changing the current file. Scripts can explicitly pass
`"format": "json"` to `file.save` or `file.save_as` even with a `.solidcraft` name.
Opening detects the format from the contents, so existing JSON designs keep working.
Containers favor fast reading and saving by default. Scripts can request
`"compression": "compact"` when file size matters more than CPU time.

Containers deduplicate identical STEP, mesh and image payloads. Mesh coordinates retain
their original double precision; this is not a conversion to STL. Geometry still rebuilds
from the timeline when opening. When a saved display preview is available, desktop Open
shows it while checking geometry; editing starts after the complete rebuild. Cancelling
keeps the current design. Previews cannot be edited or measured. Scripts can opt in to a disposable geometry
cache with `cache: true` on warm saves; saving never rebuilds cold geometry just to
create one. Ordinary saves and browser downloads default to `cache: false`. An additional display-mesh cache remains opt-in
with `preview: true`. Unsupported or mismatched caches are ignored. Browser opening
still rebuilds synchronously.
Warm saves with explicit `cache: true` can also include a small PNG thumbnail. It travels with the file, so
Home can show the recent design without reconstructing it when no local picture
is available. Missing or incompatible pictures use the usual thumbnail generation.
The default `cache: false` omits the portable thumbnail too.
The repository's `docs/design-container.md` describes limits and encoding details.

Designs are saved in the newest format this version of SolidCraft knows (`"format": "solidcraft/N"`
in the file). It opens designs of every older format and upgrades them as they open; a design
from a newer version asks you to update instead of being guessed at. Development (nightly) builds
save a format number no release reads yet.

Sketch patterns retain their live direction-line references and placement settings when saved.
Older patterns keep their fixed vector directions and original placement defaults.

Upgrading keeps what a design meant. Designs keep recorded body transfers, explicit 3D curve coordinate
spaces and certified face bindings, alongside semantic configuration styles, associative
free-form offsets and cylindrical emboss selections. Older ownership maps, geometry and
expressions retain their saved meaning. Legacy 3D curves with retained associations receive
their producer's coordinate-space marker without changing any saved points; detached curves
retain world coordinates. A lost cross-component association refreshed by an older build may
need an explicit relink or refresh when its source returns. Loading never guesses a numerical
correction. Association records, coordinate arrays and placements are bounded and checked.

## Design properties

**File → Design Properties…** (also under **Document Settings** in the Browser, and on the
top component's right-click menu) records who made a design and what it is: project, part
number, revision, author, organization, description and licence. **OK** applies the changes as
one undo step. Scripts and agents use the same commands: `document.metadata` reads them,
`document.metadata.set` (`key` and `value`, or `values: {key: value, …}`) and
`document.metadata.remove` (`key` or `keys`) change them. `document.inspect` and the MCP
`inspect_design` tool include them.

Exports carry them where the format has a place for them:

| Format | Written |
|---|---|
| STEP | `author` and `organization` in `FILE_NAME`, `description` in `FILE_DESCRIPTION` (on one line) |
| IGES | `author` and `organization` in the global section |
| 3MF | `project` as `Title`, `author` as `Designer`, `description` as `Description`, `license` as `LicenseTerms` |

The part number and revision have no standard place in these formats and stay in the design.

In the file they are one optional top-level `metadata` object; a design without properties has
none, and is saved exactly as before:

```json
"metadata": {
  "project": "ACME enclosures",
  "part_number": "ACME-1042",
  "revision": "B",
  "author": "Jane Doe",
  "organization": "ACME",
  "description": "Vented case for Raspberry Pi 4",
  "license": "CC-BY-4.0",
  "com.acme.description": { "shop_id": 88123 },
  "org.printfarm": { "slicer_profile": "PETG-0.2", "internal_id": 4 }
}
```

- **SolidCraft's keys are unprefixed** and hold text. Every other unprefixed key is reserved for
  later SolidCraft versions.
- **Other tools keep their data under one reverse-DNS key** of their own (`com.example.tool`:
  two or more dot-separated labels of letters, digits, `-` and `_`), holding an object. A tool
  writes only under its own key and leaves the others alone.
- **SolidCraft keeps every key as it is** through open, edit and save, in both the container
  and plain JSON, and never checks what another tool wrote: a well-known key holding something
  other than text (`"author": 42`) is kept, reads as absent, and never stops the design from
  opening. Typing over it in Design Properties replaces it.
- **Other tools' keys are never exported**; Design Properties lists them read-only.
- **Keep values small**: `document.metadata.set` refuses text over 4 KiB, an object over 64 KiB
  or nested more than 32 levels deep, and more than 256 keys or 256 KiB in all. Binary data
  belongs in a file next to the design.

Design properties are first saved in format 21. Inserting or linking another design doesn't
copy its properties; Save As keeps them. A command script of the design
(`timeline.export_script`) sets them in one step.

## Saving in the web app

In the web app, **Save** and **Save As** keep designs in this browser's private storage;
they do not open a dialog for choosing a folder on your computer. Clearing the site's data
can remove those designs. Download a copy to keep it outside the browser or move it to
another device.

1. Open the File menu and choose **Open** to show **Files in this browser**.
2. Choose **Download open design** for the current design, including its unsaved changes,
   or **Download** beside a stored file for its last saved contents.
3. Find the `.solidcraft` file in your browser's downloads. Whether a folder chooser appears
   depends on your browser's download settings.

Use **Open from computer…** in the same panel to reopen a downloaded design. The web app
works on a browser-stored copy; later saves do not update the original downloaded file.
Use **Rename** beside a stored file to change its name. Exports such as STEP and STL are
also downloaded.

# Components and joints

A design is a tree of **components**. **New Component** (`component.create`) adds one, and
**Create Components from Bodies** (`component.from_bodies`) turns bodies into components. Each
component has its own origin, bodies, sketches and timeline entries. The **active component**
(the radio button in the browser) receives new sketches and features; the others are drawn
faded.

A component is placed by its **occurrences**. Paste creates another instance of the same
component, and **Paste New** creates an independent copy. Move an occurrence with the move
triad, then **Capture Position** to keep it or **Revert** to put it back. SolidCraft asks before
the next command if a move wasn't captured. **Ground** fixes an occurrence in place.

Paste New copies nested component definitions, sketches, feature histories and generated
dimension parameters. Repeated child instances remain shared within the new copy. Materials,
appearances and wholly internal joints/motion records receive copied references. Design-wide
user parameters remain shared; retained external links and omitted cross-boundary motion
records are reported. Unsupported destructive links refuse the entire copy. See
[individual-instance and copy details](https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft/blob/main/docs/occurrence-workflows.md).

**Joints** (`joint.create`, J) connect two components by joint origins that snap to faces, edges,
circles and vertices: rigid, revolute, slider, cylindrical, pin-slot, planar and ball, with
offsets, flip and limits. **As-built Joint** keeps the current position, **Rigid Group** locks
components together, **Drive Joints** moves a joint through its values, and **Motion Link**
couples two joints. Links can be chained (one joint drives a second, which drives a
third), and a value is carried through a chain of up to 64 links in whatever order they were
made. Contact sets stop motion where bodies would pass through each other,
**Motion Study** keys joint values along a timeline, and **Interference** shows overlapping
volumes in red, lists the pairs closer than its **Clearance** and each body's nearest neighbour.

A joint origin on a face or a hole keeps the turn it had when it was picked: when the face tilts
(a bend angle or a rotation changing with a parameter) the part on it tilts with the face but
doesn't spin about it.

A joint origin can also sit on an edge of a flat face (`"edge": [x, y, z]`): at the edge's middle,
pointing out of the face with its y into it, or with `"corner": [x, y, z]` at the corner near that
point, its x and y running along the two edges into the face. The edge, the face and the corner
are found again by name, so a bracket set 40 mm in from a panel's corner (a planar joint with
values `[40, 40, 0]`) stays 40 mm in from that corner when the panel changes size.

A joint's offset, angle and values can be typed as expressions over the design's parameters
(`"offset": "gap + 2"`, `"values": ["travel"]`). The joint keeps them and works them out again
whenever the design changes, so a part seated `gap` above a panel moves with `gap`. Renaming a
parameter carries into the joints that use it, and deleting one they use is refused. If an
expression stops working out (say a parameter becomes an angle), the joint is left out of the
solve and `joint.solve` gives the reason, instead of placing the part from old numbers. Typing a
plain number, or driving the value, drops that expression.

**Relations** are joints that tie only part of a placement, so a part is placed the way a
designer describes it, one relation at a time: `parallel` (z along z, free to move and turn
about it), `perpendicular` and `angle` (z square to z, or at the joint's `angle` from mated),
`point_on_plane` (a point on a face's plane, `offset` off it), `point_on_line` (a point on an
axis) and `line_on_plane` (an axis on a face's plane: a cylinder's radius as `offset` lays it
tangent). A relation is made where the parts are: B moves no further than the relation needs.
Several relations between the same two parts add up; the solver meets them together, each one's
degrees of freedom come off what is left, and one that can't be met is reported, not forced:

```json
{"command": "joint.create", "params": {"type": "parallel", "a": "Panel top", "b": "Bracket bottom"}}
{"command": "joint.create", "params": {"type": "point_on_plane", "a": "Panel top", "b": "Bracket corner"}}
{"command": "joint.create", "params": {"type": "parallel", "a": "Panel front", "b": "Bracket face", "flip": true}}
{"command": "joint.create", "params": {"type": "point_on_plane", "a": "Panel front", "b": "Bracket corner", "offset": -40}}
{"command": "joint.create", "params": {"type": "point_on_plane", "a": "Panel end", "b": "Bracket corner", "offset": -40}}
```

leaves the bracket flat on the panel, square to its front, its corner 40 mm in from the front and
the end, wherever the panel's size takes them. Coincident faces are a `planar` joint, a distance
between faces is `planar` with an `offset`, concentric is `cylindrical` and two points that meet
are `ball`.

The check behind it, `inspect.clearance`, does all of that in one call for any number of bodies,
which suits scripts and agents checking a whole assembly:

```json
{"command": "inspect.clearance", "params": {"clearance": 1, "nearest": 2, "skip_within": "component"}}
```

It returns `overlaps` (pairs sharing at least `min_volume`, 0.01 mm³ by default, with the shared
volume, area, box and centre), `near` (pairs closer than `clearance`, with the distance and the
two nearest points; a contact sharing less than `min_volume` is listed here at 0 with its
`overlap_mm3`), `nearest` (each body's `nearest` closest bodies) and `unchecked` (pairs whose
overlap could not be worked out, with the reason). `against` limits the check to pairs with one
body in `bodies` and the other in `against`, and `skip_within` leaves out pairs inside one
occurrence (`"occurrence"`) or one placed component, its subcomponents included
(`"component"`): the parts of a bought component that touch by design. Distances are measured on
the exact faces and edges; the meshes only rule out pairs that are too far apart, and the pairs
left are checked in parallel. `inspect.interference` remains for the overlaps alone: it clears
pairs whose meshes stay apart without intersecting them, intersects the rest in parallel, and
returns after `budget_s` seconds (default 240) at most, listing the pairs it had no time for as
not checked.

Mesh bodies (STL, 3MF and OBJ imports) are not checked by either command: each is listed in
`unchecked` as `{a: name, b: null, reason: "mesh body: not checked"}`, so `count: 0` or an empty
`overlaps` is not mistaken for "no overlap" when a mesh body was in the design.

**Gear**, **Rack and Pinion** and **Screw** (on the **ASSEMBLE** panel) are motion links whose
ratio comes from the parts rather than a typed number:

- **Gear** (`joint.gear {a, b, ra, rb}`) couples two joints that turn. Joint 2 turns ra/rb as far
  as joint 1, the other way round; **Internal gear** (one of them is a ring gear) turns both the
  same way. Pick the round face of each gear, such as its pitch cylinder, or type the radii. Tooth
  counts work as well as radii, since only their proportion counts. Picking a gear's face also
  chooses the joint that gear turns on.
- **Rack and Pinion** (`joint.rack_pinion {a, b, radius}`) couples a joint that turns with one
  that slides: the rack travels the pinion's pitch radius times its turn in radians (r·θ). Either
  joint may drive the other. In `joint.list` the ratio is given per degree, as for any link between
  an angle and a distance.
- **Screw** (`joint.screw {joint, pitch}`, or `{a, b, pitch}` for a revolute joint and a slider)
  advances `pitch` per turn. A cylindrical joint is a screw on its own: its turn drives its travel.
  The thread is right-handed; **Reverse** makes it left-handed.

A radius or pitch may be an expression of the design's parameters, and a picked face is found
again whenever the design changes. Change the parameter or the gear's diameter, and the ratio
follows. The new link leaves the driven joint where it is, so teeth modelled in mesh stay in mesh.
**Reverse** turns the driven joint the other way, for joints whose axes point opposite ways.
Redefining a link (`link: i`, such as turning it the other way with **Reverse**) also leaves the
driven joint where it is, so the gears stay in mesh at the pose they are in. These
couplings are motion links, so they work in closed loops, with contact sets and in motion studies:
a rack can push the piston of a slider-crank, or a pinion can steer through a rack and its tie
rods. Drive the joint that drives the coupling (joint 1, the pinion, or the screw's turn), not the
driven one. A joint follows one link at most, and a coupling that would drive its own driver is
refused. `joint.list` lists each coupling's definition under `links` with an `error` when it can't
be worked out (the picked face is gone); the link then keeps its last ratio.

**Cam** (`joint.cam {a, b, profile}`, on the **ASSEMBLE** panel) makes a follower ride a cam. The
cam turns on a revolute joint (a); the follower is a slider (b, a translating follower such as a
valve tappet) or a revolute joint (b, an oscillating follower such as a rocker arm). The profile
is the cam's outline in a plane square to its axis: a closed profile of a sketch in the cam's
component, or the cam's edges picked on its body (one click on an edge takes the closed loop it is
on in that plane). The follower is:

- a **Knife edge**: a point on the cam;
- a **Roller** of a radius, typed or taken from the roller's round face (picking that face also
  says where the roller is);
- a **Flat face** square to a slider's line, such as a bucket tappet.

A translating follower's line runs along its slider's axis, through its **Tip** when one is picked
(its knife's point or its roller's centre), so a follower offset from the cam's axis rides the
right flank. An oscillating follower needs its tip, or its roller's face, to know its arm. The
follower rides the cam from the side it is on (**Other side** takes the other one). The follower's
travel over a turn of the cam is worked out from the profile and kept with the link, one value a
degree with a smooth curve between them that never overshoots its samples. It is worked out again
whenever the design changes: change the cam's sketch, a parameter or the roller, and the follower
follows. Like the gears, the new link leaves the follower where it is (model it touching the cam),
and the cam is a motion link: it drives in **Drive Joints**, plays in motion studies, works in
closed loops (a tappet can be the piston of a slider-crank) and stops at contact sets. The profile
may also be on the grounded part, with the follower's guide on a turret that the cam joint turns.
`joint.list` gives a cam's link `lift` (the follower's lowest and highest values and its rise)
instead of a ratio. A profile that is not closed, a line or an arm that misses the cam somewhere,
a follower that would jump, and axes that are not square or parallel are refused.

A joint moves one component against another, so its two picks must be on different components.
A STEP file with several parts often comes in as bodies of one component, and picks on two of
those bodies make no joint. The Joint and As-built Joint dialogs say so under the picks and offer
**Create Components from Bodies**: each picked body gets a component of its own and stays where it
is, the picks are kept, and the joint previews. `joint.create` refuses such origins with the same
advice.

Joints may close a loop, as in a four-bar linkage or a slider-crank. When one joint of the loop
is driven, the other joints in the loop follow so that every joint still meets, and the
mechanism stays in the assembly mode it started in (an open four-bar does not flip to the
crossed one). If the motion would take a loop past the point where it can still close, for
example driving a rocker beyond its swing, the motion stops at the last position where the loop
closes, and the drive reports `stopped_by_loop`. A loop that cannot close at all is listed
under `conflicts` and nothing in it moves. `joint.list` reports how many degrees of freedom each
part still has with its loops closed: the moving parts of a four-bar have one between them, and a
loop locked by a rigid joint has none. A joint a motion link drives adds no freedom of its own:
two meshed gears on a fixed housing have one between them, each turning with the driving gear. The Drive Joints dialog says when a drive stops short and
why. While it previews, a row under the values gives the value the joint reached and the reason
(the loop that can't close further, or the two parts a contact set keeps apart), and after OK the
status line repeats it. The value box keeps what you typed. The dialog opens on the joint
picked in the browser, or on the first joint that moves when none is picked.

**Drag a part that joints place** and it moves as far as its joints allow: the point you
grabbed follows the pointer in the plane through it that faces the view, the joints on the
part's chain take the values that bring it nearest, within their limits, through motion links,
and with closed loops kept closed, and a four-bar's rocker stops at the end of its swing. The
whole drag is one undo step. A grounded part, or one no joint places, is not moved; a drag on
it draws a selection box as before. Each frame runs `joint.reach`, which scripts and agents use
directly to put a part's point somewhere: `joint.reach {occurrence, point}` moves the joints on
its chain from where they are to the nearest pose (the arm keeps its elbow up or down, and a
linkage stays on its branch). `at` picks the part's point (the centre of its bodies by
default), `z` with `axis` also turns one of its axes, and `joints` names the only joints to
move (the other joints of a closed loop they are in follow). The answer says whether it
`reached` the point and how close it got (`error_mm`, `error_deg`), and when it falls short,
the limits it rests on (`stopped_by_limit`) or the loop that stopped it (`stopped_by_loop`).
Contact sets are not checked by a reach; drive the joints for that.

The solver places what it reaches from the root and from grounded components. A chain of joints
that is joined to nothing grounded is never placed, so driving one of its joints moves nothing.
The drive says so: `joint.drive` answers `moved: false` with a `reason` and the `unconnected`
part ("Pedestal:1 is not connected to anything grounded"), the Drive Joints dialog shows the same
row, `motion.play` lists such joints under `unmoved`, and `joint.list` names every such chain under
`floating`. Ground a part of the chain, or join it to a grounded part (a rigid as-built joint keeps
it where it is), and it moves.

`joint.drive` answers the joint's values as `joint.list` gives them, in degrees and millimetres
with their units and limits, and `moved` says whether any part moved. A joint's origins are mated
by default: B's z axis is turned against A's, as two faces meet. `flip: true` lines them up
instead, so two origins given at one point with the same z stay as they are. Without an
`angle`, a new joint (other than a relation, which starts where its parts are) takes no turn or a half turn about its axis, whichever turns B less: two
faces that already meet, a plate under a panel, stay as they are instead of B spinning about
their shared normal. For scripts that drive many steps, `quiet: true` leaves the per-part
degrees of freedom out of joint answers, and
`motion.play` with `quiet: true` gives the poses of only the parts that moved.

**Motion Trace** (`motion.trace`, on the **ASSEMBLE** panel) draws the path a point of a part
takes while a joint is driven or a motion study plays, such as the coupler curve of a four-bar.
Pick the point on the part (a face centre, a circle centre, an edge midpoint or a vertex), then
either a joint with the values to drive it from and to (a turn of the joint from where it is, at
first) or a motion study. The path previews in the viewport as the mechanism would move: closed
loops follow, and the path ends where a loop can no longer close or a contact set stops the
motion, which the dialog says under the values. OK keeps the path as a 3D sketch spline in a new
sketch of the root component (**Motion Trace1**, ...), where no joint moves it, and it can serve
as a sweep or pipe path. It is a fixed curve: it
does not follow later changes to the mechanism. A path that comes back to where it started is
kept as a closed, smooth spline.
`motion.trace {occurrence, point, joint, from, to, index?, samples?}` (or `{occurrence, point,
study, samples?}`) answers the world points without changing the design, and
`motion.trace.keep` with the same parameters (and `name?`) keeps them. A trace takes 2 to 500
samples: 100 by default for a joint, one per step for a study.

**Export Animation…** in the **Motion Study** dialog saves the study as an animated GIF, drawn
from the viewport's camera as the study plays (the keys in the dialog count, even before OK).
`motion.export_animation` does the same for scripts, the CLI and agents, without a window: give a
`study`, or a `joint` with `from` and `to` (and `index?`) to animate a drive, and a `path`. A path
ending in `.gif` gets an animated GIF that loops; any other path is a folder that gets the frames
as `frame-0001.png`, `frame-0002.png`, and so on (made if missing; frames of a longer earlier
export there are removed), for a video tool. The web app writes GIFs only. `samples` is
the number of frames (one per step for a study by default, 100 for a joint), `width` and `height`
their size in pixels (800 × 500 by default, at most 4096 a side), and `fps` the GIF's speed (20
by default); `grid: false` and `axes: false` leave out the ground grid and the origin's axes.
`camera` takes the reply of the control channel's `ui.camera` (or any of its fields;
the rest come from the view `view.apply` chose, or the home view framing the model). The frames
are drawn by the same renderer as `solidcraft-cli snapshot`, on a copy of the design, which is not
changed. A GIF keeps one palette for all its frames, so colours don't flicker, and stores only
what changed from one frame to the next. Frames are capped: at most 1000, and a GIF holds at most
2^26 pixels of frames (about 160 frames of 800 × 500).

**Motion analysis.** The **Motion Study** dialog's **Study** box opens a saved study to edit, and
by its timeline the dialog charts what the study does.
**Plot** picks a moving joint value (a joint picked in the Browser is picked here too), or
**Picked point** once a point is picked in the dialog's **Point** box, and **Quantity** whether to
show its value, velocity or acceleration; the chart runs over the
study's steps with a cursor at the step shown, and a click or a drag on it moves to that step.
Values are in degrees and millimetres; rates are per step, or per second once **Duration** says
how many seconds the whole study takes. A picked point charts its distance from where it
starts, its speed and the size of its acceleration. **Check collisions** plays the study and
lists the pairs of parts that pass through each other, with the steps where they do (a click on
one shows the first of them); those steps are shaded on the chart. It checks the parts picked in
**Components** (against the ones picked in **Against**, when there are any), else every
component, or the pairs of the design's contact sets (a choice beside the button once it has any).

`motion.plot {study, joints?, occurrence?, point?, samples?, duration?}` answers the same
numbers: for each joint value its `value`, `velocity` and `acceleration` per sample (with their
units), and for a point its `position`, `velocity` and `acceleration` vectors, `speed` and
`acceleration_norm`. The study plays as `motion.play` places it (closed loops follow, contact sets
stop it), each sample from the one before, on a copy: the design is not changed. Velocities and
accelerations are finite differences between samples, central inside and one-sided at the ends,
so they are as smooth as the samples are dense (up to 1000, one per step by default). Angles are
unwrapped, so a joint that turns on past half a turn keeps counting.
`motion.interference {study, occurrences?, against?, contact_sets?, samples?}` answers each
colliding pair with its `first_step`, `last_step`, the `steps` ranges where they overlap, how
far into each other (`depth_mm`, the most at `deepest_step`) and their shared `volume_mm3`
there (null when it is not cheap to work out). It plays the study as `motion.play` does, but
contact sets don't stop it, and parts are tested at the samples only: a part that passes right
through another between two samples is missed. Parts are told apart by occurrence, as contact
sets tell them apart: an occurrence inside a sub-assembly placed twice is one part, so its two
copies are not checked against each other. A check takes at most 256 bodies; on a large design,
list the `occurrences` to check (an arm, with `against` the parts it must miss). When the work
runs out it says `truncated` and the step it `checked_to`.
`joint.sweep {joint, from, to, index?, step?, refine?, occurrences?, against?, contact_sets?,
report_gaps?, apply?}` drives one joint value from `from` toward `to` and answers how far it gets
before parts touch: `stopped_at` (the last value clear of contact), `stopped_by` (the two parts
and the point `at` which they touch, or `"loop"` where a closed loop can no longer close, or
`"limit"`), and with `report_gaps` the nearest gap at every sample and the nearest each part came
to another (`min_gap`). The samples are fine enough that no part passes through another between
two (or `step` apart), and the first contact is bisected until no part moves more than `refine`
(0.01 mm by default) across it. Gaps are distances between the parts' tessellations
(`gap_method: "mesh"`): exact for flat faces, within `gap_tolerance_mm` for curved ones. Pairs
already touching at `from`, such as parts joined face to face or a door resting on its frame, are
listed in `touching_at_start` and stop the sweep only once they pass into each other, deeper than
they start. The sweep runs on a copy (closed loops follow, contact sets don't stop it) and
leaves the design as it was unless `apply` is true.

**Insert Design** (`component.insert_design {path, translate?}`, on the **ASSEMBLE** panel and
in the **File** menu) adds a component linked to another saved design, so each part can live in
its own document. A STEP or mesh file picked there is inserted as **Insert STEP** or **Insert
Mesh** would. The part's solid bodies come
in as they sit in that design, and they are kept in the assembly, so it opens even without the
part file. The link is stored relative to the assembly's folder once the assembly is saved.
After the part file changes, **Update Links** (`component.update_links`) reads it again.
**Break Link** (`component.break_link`) keeps the bodies and forgets the file, and
`component.links` lists the links and whether their files are found. A linked component holds
the part's bodies only: its timeline, parameters and sheet-metal data (flat pattern, bend
table) stay in the part's own design.

If a source file moves or is renamed, right-click its linked component or occurrence in the
Browser and choose **Relink Source (All Instances)…**. Choose the saved `.solidcraft` design
to use. Relinking updates that component's stored path and solid bodies for **all its
instances**, keeping their identities and placements. Cancelling or choosing a missing,
invalid, empty or self-referencing design leaves the assembly unchanged. The operation is
one undo step and the new path is saved relative to the assembly when possible.

Scripts use `component.relink {component, path}`. The reply includes `previous_path`, `path`,
`warnings`, `joint_errors` and `joint_conflicts`. Changed geometry can invalidate a joint's
face reference: relinking reports those joints in the reply and UI status/message history;
repair the joint or undo the relink. Relink does not repair or verify the intended meaning of
existing joints.
When linked geometry changes and the component has joints, a reminder to check those joints
is also shown even if the solver reports no error: a successful solve does not prove that a
joint still describes the intended connection.

STEP export writes the component tree as an assembly.

Right-click a component in the Browser and choose **Properties** to inspect
material-aware mass, volume, surface area, centre of mass and world bounds. Descendants and
repeated instances contribute to assembly totals; pending moves are included. A component
uses its first placement; `occurrence.properties` selects a specific instance. Root Properties
measures the complete assembly. Volumes are summed, including overlapping bodies, rather than
measuring their union. The same workflow is available through `component.properties` and
`occurrence.properties`; see
[placement and measurement details](https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft/blob/main/docs/assembly-properties.md).

## Part properties and the bill of materials

A component definition carries its own **part properties**: a part number, a description and a
revision, other tools' data under a reverse-DNS key (the same rules as the design's own
properties), and free text properties such as a material grade or a finish. Every occurrence of
the component shares them, Paste New copies them, and they are saved with the component.
`component.metadata {component}` reads them and
`component.metadata.set {component, part_number?, description?, revision?, values?, properties?}`
changes them in one undo step (an empty value removes a field). The root component is the
design itself: its properties are `document.metadata`'s. Standard parts (`parts.insert`) get a
part number from their standard and size (`ISO 4762 M6x20`, or a bearing's designation) and a
description; **Change Part Size** renumbers them, keeping a field you changed yourself.

**Bill of Materials** (`assembly.bom`, on the **INSPECT** panel) counts the placed components:

- `levels: "flat"` (the default) lists the parts at any depth, each counted through its
  subassemblies: a part placed once in a subassembly that is placed twice counts 2. A
  subassembly is listed through its parts, unless it has bodies of its own.
- `levels: "top"` lists the direct children, a subassembly as one row.
- `group_by: ["part_number"]` (the default) puts definitions with the same part number in one
  row; a definition without a part number gets a row of its own. `["definition"]` gives every
  definition its own row.
- `group_children: true` keeps what is placed inside a part with a part number in that part's
  row: a bolt with a washer and a nut placed inside it is one row, the washer and the nut listed
  under it as `children` (items 1.1, 1.2…, with `each` per bolt and `count` in all) instead of
  rows of their own. Bolts with different contents (one with a nut, one without) are different
  rows. `total_occurrences` counts the children too, so it is the same either way.
- `component` lists one subassembly's parts instead of the design's.

Rows are sorted by part number (rows without one come last) and hold `item`, `part_number`,
`description`, `revision`, `count`, `definition` (the component names), `components` (their ids)
and `properties`, with `total_occurrences` beside them. `path` writes them to a `.csv` file
(the columns item, part_number, description, revision, count and definition, every field
quoted; children follow their row) or a `.json` file. The window lists the same rows, switches
between the levels and groupings and shows children under their part, edits a picked row's part
number, description and revision, and exports them. Changing part properties changes no
geometry, so it doesn't evaluate the model or re-seat joints again.

# Extensible libraries: materials, appearances and components

The first [local scalar-library consumer](local-libraries.md) implements only copied
colour/opacity and density/look definitions. Its separate v1 catalog is not the complete
resource-pack/provenance/update system proposed below. Texture/environment descriptors
remain coordinated with the maintainer's renderer work.

Proposal for [#785](https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft/issues/785),
[#786](https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft/issues/786) and
[#787](https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft/issues/787). This page describes planned
contracts and acceptance gates, not an implemented pack format or new commands. It does
not bring the deferred Simulation or Render workspaces into scope.

## Reuse the existing paths

Physical materials already have built-in densities and design-local definitions
(`material.create`, `material.edit`, `material.delete`, `material.list`, `material.assign`).
They drive `component.properties`, survive reopening and participate in configurations.
Appearances have a built-in color/opacity library and body, face and component overrides.
`parts.library`, `parts.insert` and `parts.resize` already generate seven families of
fasteners, pins and bearing envelopes as editable components.

Extend those routes. A shared catalog supplies identity, discovery and provenance;
each entry kind retains its own payload and application rules. A physical material is
not a texture, and a reusable component is not executable plugin code.

## Portable, independently extensible packs

Use one versioned, offline pack envelope for three kinds: physical material, appearance
and component family. Both project contributors and users can author packs without
rebuilding SolidCraft. Start with a directory and JSON manifest, not a new archive format
or an online marketplace. The exact schema belongs in the bounded-loader PR, accompanied
by machine-checked examples; the following are its design requirements:

| Record | Required meaning |
|---|---|
| Pack | Schema version, stable namespaced ID, immutable revision, display name, author, source and license metadata |
| Entry | ID scoped to its pack, immutable revision, kind, label, category/tags, typed payload and per-entry provenance |
| Resource | Relative path, content digest, byte count, media role, author, source, license and included license text where required |
| Dependency | Explicit entry/revision reference; bounded acyclic resolution within explicitly selected packs |
| Selection | Pack ID + entry ID + exact revision; labels and filesystem paths are not identities |

Pack revisions and schema versions are different: the former identifies content, the
latter describes how to read it. Changing content under an existing revision is an error.
Unknown schema versions, entry kinds and required capabilities produce a clear refusal;
they are never silently interpreted as an older format. Optional extensions need an
explicit namespace and preservation rules before being accepted.

Provide three independent scopes:

- **Bundled:** reviewed with SolidCraft and read-only in the library editor.
- **Project:** packs explicitly opened for the current project/team; never discovered
  by silently executing or trusting files beside a design.
- **User:** local packs the user creates, imports, edits or exports. Native file access
  belongs in the app; browser users import/export through the web storage/file workflow.

Discovery order is deterministic. Duplicate labels can coexist, with their source shown.
Duplicate qualified identities/revisions with different contents are errors, not overrides
chosen by scan order. Editing a bundled entry uses **Save a copy** into a user namespace.
Updating a pack is explicit and leaves existing design instances unchanged.

## Designs own their selected definitions

On assignment/insertion, copy the definition, chosen revision, parameters, provenance and
required resource bytes into the design's existing container/resource mechanism. Keep the
source identity for inspection and an eventual explicit Update action. A saved design must
open, rebuild and render the supported appearance without the original pack, network or
another user's home directory. Installing a pack never changes a design or undo history.

Assignment/insertion/update is a normal engine command, atomic and undoable. Preview is
non-mutating. A failed import, unresolved dependency, name collision or unsupported recipe
leaves the document and undo/redo stacks intact. Existing material names and appearance
precedence retain their legacy meaning; introduce stable IDs through a documented migration
rather than reinterpret old name-based assignments. Design-format changes need their own
version/migration and reopen tests, separate from the pack schema version.

## Physical properties (#785)

Keep physical material and appearance selection independent, with an optional default look.
Convert imported density units explicitly to the existing g/cm³ representation; geometry
continues to use millimetres and radians. Never infer units from magnitudes. Properties
need source, edition/date, grade, processing condition and applicable temperature/moisture
when relevant. Unknown properties stay unknown, not zero or guessed values.

Start with density and mass integration through the existing commands. Reserve typed
extensions for elastic constants, yield/ultimate strength, thermal properties and
orthotropic axes, but do not expose these as FEA-ready until their model, units and
validation are implemented. A generic wood density is not an engineering material grade.
User-measured data can be stored with its own provenance and edited without changing the
bundled library.

## Wood and sheet appearances (#786)

Begin with body-local mapping, an explicit physical repeat size and a user-editable grain
frame. Suggest the longest **local** body-bound axis once, with X/Y/Z order for equal
extents; store the chosen frame rather than recompute it on every resize. Manual rotation
and scale survive parameter rebuilds, instance placement, undo and reopening. Shared
component instances transform the same definition-local mapping with their placement.
Non-finite or degenerate frames refuse; automatic choice remains a suggestion.

Visual grain does not rotate the body, its geometric bounding box or a manufacturing
stock frame. Structural grain direction and grain-aware nesting/cut lists are distinct
features, coordinated with [#137](https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft/issues/137).
An anisotropic shading effect also does not imply mechanical anisotropy.

After basic wood mapping, add sheet-specific top/bottom/edge looks: MDF, chipboard,
plywood and compact laminate, then melamine, laminate, linoleum and veneer finishes.
Appearance layers initially describe presentation only. Physical finish thickness or
mass must be explicit modelling/material inputs, never an invisible side effect of paint.
Face/edge assignments require durable identities and must refuse a lost association
rather than paint a nearby replacement face.

Keep texture role, color space, normal-map convention and physical scale explicit.
Coordinate with the [render capability contract](https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft/blob/main/docs/render-backends.md):
the existing color/opacity viewport is not proof of PBR or texture support. A renderer
must report what it supports; unavailable maps use a documented preview fallback with
a visible notice. Export either preserves supported mapping/resources or reports loss.

## Standard and user component families (#787)

Keep the existing fastener insertion/resize path. Add original parameterized BAR, SHS,
RHS and CHS recipes first, with explicit length units, parameter bounds, section frames
and insertion/connection frames. Validate wall thickness against the outer size and
state whether corners are sharp or rounded. Do not label approximate geometry as a
certified standard section. UB/UC need actual flange/web radii and tapers; identifying a
standard does not grant redistribution rights to its published size tables.

A family revision defines a bounded parameter schema, permitted recipe and optional
reviewed size table. A size designation identifies a row, not an arbitrary filename.
Changing size rebuilds the same component identity and preserves supported connections.
Initial recipes must use a small allowlist of ordinary modelling operations. No embedded
native code, shell commands, scripts, arbitrary command IDs or network hooks. Reject
cycles, excessive expansion and unsupported operations before mutating the design.

Custom assemblies follow single components: bounded dependencies, named connection
frames, explicit shared/independent instance semantics and one-step insertion undo.
Store selected parameters and definition snapshots so missing or changed catalogs cannot
silently substitute another part. Geometric envelope models, including existing bearing
envelopes, must remain distinguishable from detailed/manufacturing-ready models.

## Sources and licensing

SolidCraft is MIT OR Apache-2.0. Code and generated recipes must follow the clean-room
rules; never copy commercial CAD materials, templates, geometry, icons or catalogs.
Third-party assets retain their own licenses. Every bundled resource needs its author,
source, license and `ATTRIBUTION.md` row, even if attribution is optional under CC0.
Record hashes and retrieval dates when admitting actual files. A manifest's claimed
license is provenance to review, not automatic evidence of permission.

Sources checked on 2026-10-13; no external assets or datasets are bundled by this proposal:

| Source | Suitable use / admission condition |
|---|---|
| [ambientCG license](https://docs.ambientcg.com/license/) | Downloadable assets and material preview renders are CC0. Candidate wood/sheet texture source; choose and attribute individual files. |
| [Poly Haven license](https://polyhaven.com/license) | Assets are CC0. Site text, logos and other site content have separate rights; API access has separate terms. Do not copy provider implementation code. |
| [Wikidata structured-data license](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:Copyright) | Structured entity/property data are CC0; other page text has different terms. Candidate for individual referenced quantities and identifiers, not unverified engineering-grade defaults. Preserve the underlying measurement references, qualifiers and units. |
| [USDA Wood Handbook, revised 2021](https://research.fs.usda.gov/fpl/wood-handbook) | Reference for moisture, physical and mechanical wood properties. Verify the specific table's rights, species, units and conditions before importing data; no wholesale dataset approval is implied. |
| [NIST data/publication rights](https://www.nist.gov/open/copyright-fair-use-and-licensing-statements-srd-data-software-and-technical-series-publications) and [repository terms](https://materialsdata.nist.gov/terms/) | Candidate property references only. Uploaded data use provider-selected terms; public availability is not a blanket redistribution license. Review each dataset. |
| [Khronos PBR overview](https://www.khronos.org/gltf/pbr) | Public rendering conventions for texture roles and shading properties; a design reference, not a source of CAD material data. |
| Original SolidCraft recipes / user measurements | Preferred initial component recipes and illustrative procedural previews; preserve authorship and label illustrative versus measured values. |

Prefer CC0 resources for the starter texture pack and original recipes for the starter
component pack. Defer uncertain or restrictive data rather than scrape supplier sites,
copy standards publications or assume a downloadable CAD file can be redistributed.

## Phases and acceptance gates

Each implementation PR references these issues without closing them prematurely.

| Phase | Deliverable | Required evidence before calling it complete |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | This proposal, source review and roadmap | Maintainer-reviewable contract; distinguish existing functions from planned ones; no runtime or format changes. |
| 1 | Shared bounded manifest parser, resolver and pack validation/import/export | Project and user manifests use the same schema; deterministic conflicts, invalid versions/IDs, missing resources/dependencies, cycles, path traversal and budget exhaustion fail atomically; native + wasm pass. |
| 2 | Material and appearance catalog integration and browser UI | Create/copy/edit/import/export from the UI; existing commands used; analytic box mass before/after assignment; configurations, undo and offline cold reopening; actual screenshots. |
| 3 | Wood mapping and a small reviewed starter pack | Rotate/scale grain on a public-safe block and placed instance; no flip on resize; reopen without pack; rendering capability/fallback tests and screenshots; attribution for each shipped asset. |
| 4 | Parameterized section families and reviewed standard size data | BAR: area = width × height; sharp RHS/SHS: outer area minus inner area; CHS: π(outer_diameter² − inner_diameter²)/4. Check volume = area × length, hollow membership, insertion frame, resize, connections, undo and offline reopening; screenshots. |
| 5 | Custom assemblies, sheet face/edge layers and expanded catalogs | Bounded nested insertion, shared/independent semantics, durable face associations, explicit updates and loss reporting; measured tests and screenshots for each workflow. |

After phase 1, material/appearance integration and section-family work can advance
independently. Wood mapping depends on actual renderer support, not on section families.
Phase 5 is several separate PRs, each following its relevant earlier workflow, rather
than one change coupling assembly insertion to face painting.

Keep parsing/resource I/O in `io`, durable selected definitions in `doc`, application
and validation commands in `engine`, renderer-specific interpretation in `render`/its
adapters, and discovery/editing UI in `ui-egui`. Lower layers do not depend on the UI
or platform file dialogs. Reuse container resource deduplication; avoid a second blob store.

Before allocating/decoding, enforce manifest byte/entry/string/dependency limits, total
resource bytes, image dimensions/decoded bytes and recipe expansion bounds. Paths must be
relative, normalized and confined to the selected pack, including symlink handling. Phase 1
must publish exact limits and test their boundaries. Do not auto-fetch missing files or
install executable extensions. Explicit import/export is enough for the first delivery.

Run `cargo xtask ci` for each implementation arc and check remote PR results. Geometry
tests use analytic values; UI and observable CAD changes include actual app evidence.
The three issues remain open until their individual workflows pass these gates.

# Troubleshooting: SolidCraft won't start

## 0.10.0 closes a few seconds after it starts (Windows)

SolidCraft 0.10.0 crashes at startup on Windows PCs that draw with Direct3D 12 and the system
shader compiler. That covers older Intel graphics, PCs without a graphics driver (the
"Microsoft Basic Display Adapter"), virtual machines and Remote Desktop sessions. **Install
0.10.1 or later**, which fixes it. Versions before 0.10.0 don't have this problem.

## Start in safe mode

Safe mode starts with default settings (your own settings stay as they are, for the next normal
start), skips the "Recover unsaved design?" offer and draws with the software renderer.

- Windows: run `solidcraft.exe --safe-mode` from a terminal in the install folder, or add
  ` --safe-mode` to the end of a shortcut's *Target*.
- macOS: `open -a SolidCraft --args --safe-mode`
- Linux: `solidcraft --safe-mode` (Flatpak: `flatpak run ai.storyteller.solidcraft --safe-mode`)

Setting `SOLIDCRAFT_SAFE_MODE=1` does the same. From 0.10.2, if two launches in a row stop
before the window opens, the next one starts in safe mode by itself. `SOLIDCRAFT_RENDERER=cpu`
uses only the software renderer and keeps your settings.

## Reset the settings

SolidCraft keeps its settings and its data in the folders below. All installed versions share
them. No version changes anything outside them: no system settings, drivers or registry
entries. Quit SolidCraft, then **rename** (don't delete) the folders. SolidCraft starts with
defaults and makes new ones. Rename them back to restore your settings, or send them to us
with a bug report.

| System | Settings (`app.ron`, `graphics.json`) | Data (`recovery`, `crashes`, `control`, thumbnails) |
|---|---|---|
| Windows | `%APPDATA%\SolidCraft` | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\SolidCraft` |
| macOS | `~/Library/Application Support/SolidCraft` | (the same folder) |
| Linux | `~/.local/share/solidcraft` | (the same folder); thumbnails in `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/SolidCraft` or `/tmp/SolidCraft` |
| Linux (Flatpak) | `~/.var/app/ai.storyteller.solidcraft/data/solidcraft` | (the same folder) |

On Windows, paste `%APPDATA%` or `%LOCALAPPDATA%` into the Explorer address bar to open the
folder. Releases before the rename used `SolveCraft` folders next to these; SolidCraft only
reads them, so you can leave them alone.

- The **`recovery`** folder holds autosaves of designs that were never saved. Rename the data
  folder rather than deleting it, so you can still open those autosaves (`.solidcraft` files)
  with File > Open.
- The **`crashes`** folder holds crash reports. Please attach the newest one to a bug report.

From 0.10.2, SolidCraft also checks the settings files at start. A file it can't read is renamed
to `app.ron.bad-<time>` or `graphics.json.bad-<time>`, and SolidCraft starts with defaults
instead.

## "No graphics adapter" or nothing happens at all

SolidCraft needs Direct3D 12 or Vulkan on Windows, Metal on macOS, and Vulkan or OpenGL on
Linux. Without a graphics driver it falls back to the system's software renderer (WARP on
Windows, llvmpipe or lavapipe on Linux), which is slow but works. From 0.10.2, if no window can
be opened at all, SolidCraft tries the software renderer once and otherwise shows a message
saying what failed (earlier versions closed without a word). Things to try:

- Install the graphics driver from the GPU maker (Intel, AMD, NVIDIA) rather than Windows Update.
- In a virtual machine, turn on 3D acceleration. Over Remote Desktop, try it on the machine itself.
- Run `solidcraft --crash-log` to list recent crash reports, and attach the newest one to an
  issue.

## The desktop stutters or freezes while SolidCraft builds bodies

Some graphics drivers hang on the shader SolidCraft uses to build bodies on the GPU, and the
system then resets the GPU. SolidCraft already builds bodies on the CPU on the AMD FirePro
D300/D500/D700 (Mac Pro 2013). On another GPU that does this, start SolidCraft with
`SOLIDCRAFT_CPU_TESS=1` set to build bodies on the CPU, and open an issue with the GPU's name.

## SolidCraft closes right away on Windows

A graphics driver can crash the app while it starts, before SolidCraft can show anything (an
old Intel Vulkan driver, `igvk64.dll`, did). Windows' Event Viewer names the driver under
*Windows Logs › Application* ("Faulting module name").

From 0.11.1, SolidCraft on Windows starts Direct3D 12 first and loads no other graphics API
when Direct3D 12 has a graphics card; Vulkan and then OpenGL are tried only on a computer
without one. Earlier versions started Vulkan, Direct3D 12 and OpenGL together and preferred
Vulkan. To choose the graphics API yourself, in any version, open a Command Prompt and start
SolidCraft from it:

```
set WGPU_BACKEND=dx12
"C:\Program Files\SolidCraft\solidcraft.exe"
```

`vulkan` and `gl` are the other choices. `setx WGPU_BACKEND dx12` keeps it for apps started
from the Start menu after you sign in again. From 0.11.1 the setting can also live in
`graphics.json` in the settings folder, as `{"msaa": 4, "backend": "dx12"}` (`auto` is the
order above). Safe mode ignores it and always uses the software renderer.

## A design saved by 0.10 won't open in an older version

Designs saved by a newer SolidCraft use a newer file format. Older versions refuse them with
"this design was saved by a newer SolidCraft" and don't change the file. Open them with the
current version.

# Test harnesses

`cargo xtask ci` runs everything a pull request must pass: fmt, `xtask assets`,
`xtask licences --check`, `xtask layers`, clippy with `-D warnings`, the tests with the `ci`
profile and the wasm build check.

| Harness | Where | What it catches |
|---|---|---|
| Unit and engine tests | next to the code, `*_tests.rs` | measured results: volume, area, topology counts against derived values |
| Hostile input | `hostile_params_never_panic`, `crates/engine/src/tests.rs` | every command × every documented parameter × junk values: errors, never panics |
| Sketch fuzz | `crates/engine/src/cmd/sketch_fuzz_tests.rs` | random sketches through the solver and profile finder |
| UI scenarios | `crates/ui-egui/tests/scenarios/*.json` | the real app, headless: clicks, keys, drags, assertions |
| Layout tests | `crates/ui-egui/tests/ui_layout.rs`, `window_widths.rs` | panels and dialogs at every window width |
| Design-file corpus | `apps/solidcraft-cli/tests/corpus` | every saved file version still opens and evaluates the same |
| Kill mid-save | `apps/solidcraft-cli/tests/kill_mid_save.rs` | a save killed at any moment leaves a readable file |
| Reference tests | `cargo xtask oracle` → [docs/oracle.md](oracle.md) | parts rebuilt from `tests/oracle/*/recipe.json`, compared with analytic or FreeCAD expected values |

## Dependency advisories

Scheduled and manually dispatched CI runs have a separate **Dependency advisories** job;
new advisories do not fail unrelated pull requests. To run the same scan locally:

```sh
cargo install cargo-deny --version 0.20.2 --locked
cargo deny --locked check --warn unmaintained advisories bans sources
```

The checked-in `deny.toml` rejects vulnerabilities and unknown registries/git sources.
Unmaintained crates, yanked versions and duplicate versions warn; licences remain covered
by `cargo xtask licences --check`. Review advisory failures and update dependencies rather
than adding broad ignores. The first scan prompted an update to quick-xml 0.41.0 for
[RUSTSEC-2026-0194](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2026-0194) and
[RUSTSEC-2026-0195](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2026-0195).

Coverage excludes the version matching of local path patches: `truck-shapeops`,
`truck-stepio`, `truck-meshalgo`, `matext4cgmath` and `egui-wgpu` in `vendor/`. Their checked-in
code and patches still need comparison with their permissively licensed upstreams; a green
scan does not establish their security or incorporate an upstream fix automatically.

## UI scenarios

A scenario is a JSON list of steps run against the real app with a headless egui context:

```json
[
  {"start": "sketch.create"},
  {"click": {"plane": "XY"}},
  {"start": "sketch.rectangle.two_point"},
  {"click": {"sketch": [0, 0]}},
  {"click": {"sketch": [40, 30]}},
  {"expect": {"errors": 0}}
]
```

A new file in `crates/ui-egui/tests/scenarios/` is picked up automatically. To record a bug
before it's fixed, add a `{"pending": "why"}` step; its test is then ignored with that reason, and
the fix removes the step.

## CI profile

CI runs the tests with `--profile ci`: light optimisation, line tables, no LTO and debug
assertions off. Some truck debug assertions fail on valid geometry; the `ci` profile disables
them while building faster than `--release`. If a test fails only in a plain debug build, say
so in the PR.

Run `cargo xtask test` to build with this profile and run the test binaries concurrently,
with doc tests alongside. Arguments after `--` go to each test binary, for example
`cargo xtask test -- shell`. To run the test binaries sequentially instead, use
`cargo test --workspace --profile ci`.

## CI sharding and heavy tests

On GitHub, one job builds the tests into a [cargo-nextest](https://nexte.st/) archive and four
jobs run a quarter of the tests each (two halves on a pull request; `--partition slice:N/4`,
settings in `.config/nextest.toml`), the slowest tests first; doc tests run in their own job.
Pull requests skip a few heavy tests (each takes one to twelve minutes); they run on every push to
`main`, nightly, and in `cargo xtask test`:

- `solidcraft-engine`: `tests::hostile_params_never_panic`, everything in `tests::robustness` and
  the seeds of `tests::robustness_goldens` (`seed_00` … `seed_95`; pull requests that can change
  them run all but the slowest, `SLOW_SEEDS` in `ci.yml`),
  `pattern_suppress_tests::enclosure_arc_extinction_keeps_a_real_sharp_inner_lip_after_resize_and_reopen`,
  `pattern_suppress_tests::enclosure_datums_follow_wall_height_and_board_depth_with_material_proofs`,
  `cmd::plastic::tests::enclosure_snap_fit_follows_resized_front_wall`, the `atomic_commands` contract tests
- `solidcraft-kernel`: `tests::boolean_identity_on_tangent_primitives`,
  `tspline::tests::hostile_tsplines_never_panic`, and the `boolean_props` property tests
  (these run only in the nightly "Property tests" job: their inputs are random, so main skips them too)
- `solidcraft-ui-egui` scenarios: `acceptance_sensor_enclosure`

The **action matrix** (`apps/solidcraft-cli/tests/action_matrix.rs`) tries every ordinary action
(sketch, offset plane, press pull, hole, draft, shell, fillet, chamfer, construction geometry, move,
mirror, pattern) on every face, edge, vertex and body of a corpus of designs and compares with a
checked-in baseline: an action that passed there and fails now fails the test. Every run checks a
fixed sample; the nightly "Action matrix" job runs it all. After a fix, record what passes now with
`cargo xtask action-matrix --bless`. The results and the causes of the failures are in
[the action matrix page](https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft/blob/main/docs/action-matrix.md).

To run exactly what a pull request runs: `cargo nextest run --cargo-profile ci --profile ci`;
add `--ignore-default-filter` for the full set. A new test that takes over a minute on CI can
join the list (the `default-filter` in `.config/nextest.toml`) if it guards robustness rather
than everyday behaviour.

# Parameters and expressions

Every dimension and feature input is a **model parameter** (`d1`, `d2`, …). **User parameters**
are ones you add yourself, with a unit, an expression and an optional comment. Change them in
**Change Parameters** (`parameters.change`). The timeline rebuilds from the first feature that
uses them.

When creating or editing a sketch dimension, its value editor shows its model parameter
name (`d1`, `d2`, …). Click another driving dimension to use its name: when the value is
just a number (such as `10` or `10 mm`) the name replaces it; otherwise it goes in at the
cursor, replacing selected text and keeping what you typed, so typing `10 + ` and clicking
`d1` gives `10 + d1`. Add arithmetic such as `/ 2` to build a dependent dimension. Press **Enter** to apply
the expression or **Escape** to cancel the edit.
Add and edit user parameters through the existing **Change Parameters** command.

In the SOLID toolbar's CONFIGURE panel, click **Parameters** to open the user and model
parameter editor. The separate **Configurations** button opens the configuration table;
**Configure** remains in the dropdown for configuring columns.

Press **Enter** in the new parameter's name, expression or comment field to add it.
Valid entries return focus to the name field for the next parameter; invalid entries remain
editable. In expression fields, type a parameter or dimension name for autocomplete,
or press **Ctrl+Space** to open suggestions, including in an empty field.
**Up/Down** selects an autocomplete suggestion,
**Enter/Tab** accepts it, and **Escape** dismisses the suggestions. Accepting a suggestion
does not also submit the parameter.

Expressions are unit-aware: `2 * width + 5 mm`, `angle / 2`, `sqrt(area)`, `1 in + 3 mm`, using
`+ - * / ^`, parentheses, `sin cos tan asin acos atan atan2 sqrt abs min max floor ceil round mod
trunc` and unit conversion. A decimal comma works too, outside parentheses: `2,5 mm` is
`2.5 mm` (inside a function's parentheses the comma separates its arguments, so write
`max(2.5, 3)` there). A mixed number is one value, as imperial sizes are written: `2 1/8"` and
`3 7/16 in` are 2.125 in and 3.4375 in (a whole number, a space, then a proper fraction of whole
numbers). A length where an angle is expected (or the other way round) is an
error, not a silent conversion. Cycles are reported with their path (`a → b → a`), renaming a
parameter updates every expression, dimension and feature input that uses it, and a parameter
in use can't be deleted (the error lists its users).

The design's units (Document Settings in the browser: mm, cm, m, in or ft) set how a bare number
typed into a feature is read. In an inch design `2` means 2 in. The Box, Cylinder, Sphere, Torus
and Coil dialogs start with their sizes in the design's units, unit shown (`20 mm`, `20 in`).
Changing the units never moves existing geometry. A size worked out from a bare number keeps
the unit the number was given in: a sphere with a bare diameter of 20 has the radius
`(20 mm) / 2` in a millimetre design. Beside a unit-less expression such as `2 * 5` or a
unit-less parameter, which is read in the design's units, the number stays bare and is read
with it.

Parameters export to and import from CSV or JSON (`parameters.export`, `parameters.import`).
**Configurations** (`config.*`) keep a table of rows, each with its own parameter values and
suppressed features, physical materials and body appearances, switched with `config.activate`.
The table's Library picker selects material or appearance values. Choose **Follow material**
to clear an appearance override. Custom looks retain their colour and opacity across
activation, undo and save/reopen. See
[configuration commands and examples](https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft/blob/main/docs/configurations.md).

# Persistent naming

A fillet stores the edges it rounds, a sketch the face it sits on, a shell the faces it opens.
If those were face and edge *indices*, an upstream edit that adds a face would move the fillet
to another edge. SolidCraft stores **names**, and finds them again every time the timeline
evaluates.

## Why names follow the kernel's history

Names used to be worked out from geometry: sample points of each new face were looked up on the
faces of the feature's input, and the majority won; pieces of a split face were numbered by where
their centres lay. That guess is right most of the time, and wrong exactly when it matters: after
an upstream edit that splits, merges, mirrors or shrinks a face, points can land on a neighbour,
centres can swap order, and a fillet or a sketch quietly re-attaches to a different face. Nothing
tells the user, which is the worst thing a CAD tool can do.

The kernel now reports, for every operation, what each face and edge of its result came from
(`crates/kernel/src/history.rs`: a face's origins and how it changed, an edge's origin edge or
the faces whose meeting made it). Names follow that history, so they are exact and deterministic,
and when a reference can no longer be found exactly the feature says so instead of guessing.

## How a body's faces are named

`crates/doc/src/lineage.rs` composes the histories of the kernel operations a feature runs (a
tool built from a sketch, cut from each target, the cut body split into lumps) into one
**lineage** over operands that can be named:

| Operand | Its faces are named |
|---|---|
| a body of the model before the feature | as they were |
| a moved copy of one (pattern, mirror) | `<name>@F<feature>.<instance>` |
| the cavity side of a shell grown outward | `F<feature>:inner:<name>` |
| a body the feature built | by role: `F<feature>:side:<sketch curve>`, `start`/`top`/`bottom`/`end` caps, `+x`… box sides, `face:<k>` imported faces |
| a copied tool of a patterned feature | `F<feature>:<role>@F<pattern>.<instance>` |

`crates/doc/src/history_names.rs` names each face of the result from its origins: a kept or
trimmed face keeps its origin's name, a fillet or chamfer face is `F<feature>:blend:<edge>` of the
edge it replaces, a shell's inner wall `F<feature>:inner:<face>`. A side's sketch curve is the
curve the profile segment lies on exactly; nothing is sampled.

- **Pieces.** Faces that end up with one name are pieces of one face, and are told apart by the
  faces around them that the others lack: `F2:top#[F2:side:l4,F4:side:l4]` is the piece of the
  block's top bounded by its left wall and the slot's left wall. That survives the slot moving,
  growing or shrinking. Pieces nothing around them tells apart are numbered (`#1`, `#2`): by what
  they came from when that differs (the two halves of a circle's wall), else in kernel order and
  then unverified.
- **Merged faces.** A face made of several (a join flush with the body) takes the name of the face
  they are all pieces of, else the target's; it answers to the others' names too (aliases).
- **Edges** are named by the faces they separate, `<face A>|<face B>`, `~k` when several edges run
  between the same two faces (numbered by where they lie; a reference by such a number is
  reported when only geometry confirms it).
- **Lumps.** When a cut leaves a body in pieces, the whole is named first, so pieces of one face in
  different bodies are told apart, and the bodies (`Bar`, `Bar (1)`) are assigned in the order of
  their least face name, not the kernel's shell order (which an upstream edit can swap; see
  [Older designs](#older-designs)).

Names are worked out lazily, on first request, and shared by a body's clones.

### Where there is no history

A body made by an operation that does not report history yet (some kernel paths return none; see
the kernel's handoff lists, and the doc features that do not compose it yet: sheet metal, plastic
and surface features, emboss, rib, replace face, the faceted thread cut), or a face whose role
is not known exactly (a loft's sides, a coil's or pipe's generated profile, a hole's tool), is
named the old way, from geometry, and its names are marked **unverified** (`model.faces` reports
`exact: false`). A reference that resolves through an unverified name while its stored point no
longer lies on the face says so: `face ... was found by geometry, not exact history; check it`.

## How a reference finds its face again

`crates/doc/src/name_lookup.rs`, in order:

1. the face with that name;
2. the one face answering to it: merged into it (the feature says it was merged), or the named
   piece, which the faces listed in its name still bound;
3. the pieces of it (it was split, or it is on several bodies): the one nearest the reference's
   point, and the feature says it was split;
4. nothing: the feature falls back to the geometry it recorded and says the face no longer exists.

An edge name is found as the edge between the two faces it names, each found as above: when
exactly one edge runs between them it is that edge, even after a split of one of its faces.

A sketch's link to a projected edge (`sketch.project {edge: [x, y, z]}`, and Intersect and
Include 3D Geometry of an edge) keeps the edge's name beside its point. The link is that edge
wherever a change takes it; of an edge that was split it is the piece nearest the link's point,
and the sketch says so. When no edge has the name any more the link is lost and keeps its last
geometry, as it does for a face: it does not take whichever edge is nearest now. A link saved
without a name, by a build that kept only the point, is found by the edge nearest its point, as
it always was, and takes that edge's name when its sketch is next edited.

A command that takes a face as a point can be given a name `model.faces` lists instead
(`face.delete`, `solid.shell`, `solid.draft`, `solid.offset_face`, `solid.split_face`, the `faces`
of `solid.replace_face`, the `face` of `sheet.convert`). It is found with the same lookup
(`naming::locate_one`: the face with that name, or the one face answering to it, on the given
body or any body; a name that finds several faces is refused). The command takes a point on that
face (`naming::named_face_point`: the incentre of the face's roomiest triangle, moved onto the
surface of a plane, cylinder, cone, sphere or torus), which the feature stores like a picked one,
with the name it then gets as before. Nothing new is stored in the design. `model.faces` lists
that point for every face.

### Profiles picked by their curves

A profile picked by a point or an index is stored by the curve ids of its outer loop
(`ProfileSel::Curves`), so it follows dimension and parameter edits exactly. Editing the outline
itself can leave no profile bounded by exactly those curves; the feature then falls back to the
best match and warns, instead of failing and taking its body and everything after it along
(`profile_refs::fallback_loop`):

1. all the stored curves are still there and still close a loop on their own, but another curve
   now cuts the region: the pieces inside that loop that touch it, which together are the region
   that was picked (islands inside stay holes);
2. otherwise the profile whose outer loop shares the most of the stored curves, at least half of
   them (a side deleted and drawn again, a notch trimmed in); a tie goes to the one with the
   fewest curves the loop did not have, and a tie left after that is an error, as is a loop
   that matches nothing.

Loops of offset curves and legacy graph-span multisets keep their exact meaning. Commands still
check a pick with the exact rule, so a curve list that names no profile is refused when given.
A sketch on such an extrude's cap falls back the same way: its certificate names the loop, and
the cap of the same solid extrude at the same end, from the same sketch and on the same body,
that shares the most (at least half) of its curves stands for it, unless the exact cap is still
on another body (`Document::anchored_face_indices`).

A hole placed by a position on a face is the exception to "the point nearest the reference's
point": its position is a place, not a pick. The hole follows its face along its own axis, so it
moves with the face when the face moves, and when the face no longer reaches the position it stays
where it was placed and the feature says so, instead of sliding to the face's edge and drilling
half a hole there. (Holes at sketch points follow their sketch.)

## Older designs

Designs saved before format 14 stored names worked out from geometry, and a few of them name a
face that history names differently (a tube's outer wall was named after the sketch curve nearest
its centre, its inner circle). Migrating such a design marks those names (`?F2:top#2`), and they
are found among the names geometry gives, as the build that saved them found them: an older design
evaluates as it was saved. Picking the face again stores its exact name.

Their features also keep naming the pieces they split a body into in the kernel's shell order
(`Feature::shell_piece_order`, set by the migration): the body names stored after them (fillet and
chamfer bodies, targets, participants, materials, appearances, joints) mean the pieces in that
order. Features added later name their pieces after their faces.

## Not done yet

- Certificates (`FaceSource`, the strict attachment identities behind sketches on faces and
  configured face styles) still travel only where the kernel's planar-source mapping keeps them;
  carrying them through `History::face_sources` would let a certified attachment follow a face a
  later join reshapes, which today is refused on purpose.
- Operations without history, listed above, keep the unverified geometric names.
