# Glossary

This page sets SolidCraft's **ubiquitous language**: one agreed term for each idea, defined once
and used the same way in labels, command ids, parameter keys, the design file, the docs, the MCP
tools and every translation.

Two rules apply:

- **One idea, one term.** When this page names a term for an idea, use that term, not a
  synonym.
- **One term, one idea.** A word that means two things gets two qualified terms (for example
  *construction entity* and *construction plane*), and each meaning gets its own entry in the
  message catalogues.

A pull request that adds a new idea (a command, a parameter, a file key, a panel) adds its term
here. A pull request that renames a label, id or key to match this page keeps the old id or key
working as an alias and lists it in `docs/compatibility.md`.

## How an entry reads

Each entry gives the term and a **definition**: one short sentence in plain technical English
that could replace the term in a sentence. It names no product and doesn't use the term to define
itself, in the way ISO 704 and ISO 10241-1 describe for terminology. A note follows, with the
context:

- **In SolidCraft:** the command ids, parameter keys and design-file keys that use the term.
- **Don't use:** the other words for the same idea.
- **Elsewhere:** general names that people coming from other CAD software may know.
- **For translators:** what the term must not be confused with.

Some of the ids and labels below still use a word this page says not to use. They change in
later pull requests, one topic at a time, each pointing at its entry here.

## Terms

### appearance

How a body, face or component looks on screen and in renders.

An appearance sets colour and surface finish only. It has no effect on mass or strength. Compare
*material*.

- **In SolidCraft:** `appearance.assign`, `appearance.library`, `appearance.list`; the
  `appearances` design-file key.
- **Don't use:** look, colour (for the whole appearance), render material.
- **Elsewhere:** appearance, visual material, colour.
- **For translators:** not the physical material.

### body

One connected solid or surface shape that features create and change.

A design can hold many bodies. A component groups bodies; an occurrence places them.

- **In SolidCraft:** `body.rename`; the `bodies` browser folder; `body_name` parameters.
- **Don't use:** part, solid (for a surface body too), object.
- **Elsewhere:** body, solid body, surface body.
- **For translators:** not a component and not a design.

### browser

The panel that lists the design's components, bodies, sketches, construction planes and joints as
a tree.

- **In SolidCraft:** `browser.group`, `browser.move`, `browser.order`, `browser.visibility`, and the
  other `browser.*` commands.
- **Don't use:** model tree, scene browser, parts browser.
- **Elsewhere:** browser, model tree, feature tree, design tree.
- **For translators:** not the web browser. A language with its own CAD word for the tree may use
  it (in French, *arborescence*), so that "browser" and "web browser" don't share a word. See
  *web browser*.

### component

A named container of bodies, sketches, construction geometry and other components that can be
placed one or more times.

Each placement of a component is an *occurrence*. Editing a component changes every occurrence
of it.

- **In SolidCraft:** `component.create`, `component.activate`, and the other `component.*`
  commands; the `components` design-file key.
- **Don't use:** part, assembly, sub-assembly (for the component itself).
- **Elsewhere:** component, part, sub-assembly.
- **For translators:** not an occurrence.

### constraint

A rule that fixes the relation between sketch entities, such as coincident, parallel or tangent.

A constraint with a value is a *dimension*.

- **In SolidCraft:** `sketch.constraint.coincident`, `sketch.constraint.parallel`, and the other
  `sketch.constraint.*` commands; the `constraint` parameter key; the sketch's `constraints`
  design-file key.
- **Don't use:** relation, condition.
- **Elsewhere:** constraint, geometric constraint, relation.
- **For translators:** a joint between occurrences is not a constraint.

### construction entity

A sketch entity that guides the drawing but isn't part of any profile.

A construction entity can be a line, an arc, a circle or any other curve, and it can carry
constraints and dimensions like any sketch entity.

- **In SolidCraft:** the `construction` parameter of the sketch drawing commands; the
  `construction` field of a sketch curve; the `ui.construction` catalogue entry.
- **Don't use:** "construction" on its own where it could mean a *construction plane*.
- **Elsewhere:** construction line, construction geometry, reference line.
- **For translators:** not a construction plane, axis or point. The browser's Construction folder
  and this line type still share the `Construction` catalogue entry, so German, Korean and Turkish
  show the folder as "construction line".

### construction plane, construction axis, construction point

A plane, axis or point that a feature creates to place other features, and that is not part of
any body.

They are listed together in the browser's *Construction* folder.

- **In SolidCraft:** `construct.plane.offset`, `construct.axis.two_points`,
  `construct.point.vertex`, and the other `construct.*` commands; the CONSTRUCT toolbar panel.
- **Don't use:** "construction" on its own where it could mean a *construction entity*; work plane.
- **Elsewhere:** construction plane, reference plane, datum plane (and axis, point).
- **For translators:** not a sketch's construction entity.

### curve

A sketch entity that is not a point: a line, an arc, a circle, an ellipse, a spline or a conic.

- **In SolidCraft:** the sketch's `curves` design-file key; curve ids in parameters such as `path`.
- **Don't use:** geometry, edge (for a sketch curve).
- **Elsewhere:** curve, sketch curve, segment.
- **For translators:** not an edge of a body.

### design

The model that is open in SolidCraft: its timeline, components, bodies, sketches, parameters and
settings.

A design is saved as a *design file*.

- **In SolidCraft:** `file.new` ("New Design"), `document.units` ("Change Design Units"),
  `document.metadata` ("Design Properties"), `doc.open`, `doc.recover`.
- **Don't use:** document, doc, project, file (for the model itself), part.
- **Elsewhere:** design, document, model, part file, assembly file.
- **For translators:** not the *Project* design property and not the sketch Project command.

### design file

A file in which SolidCraft saves one design, with the `.solidcraft` extension.

- **In SolidCraft:** `file.save`, `file.save_as`, `doc.open`; the `solidcraft/N` format tag.
- **Don't use:** document, project file.
- **Elsewhere:** design file, model file.
- **For translators:** "file" is only for what is on disk: opening, saving, importing and
  exporting.

### dimension

A constraint that sets a size, such as a length, a distance, an angle or a radius, by its value.

A dimension can drive the sketch, or be driven by it and only show the value.

- **In SolidCraft:** `sketch.dimension`, `sketch.dimension_text`, `sketch.toggle_driven`; a
  dimension's id is a constraint id.
- **Don't use:** measurement (for a dimension), size.
- **Elsewhere:** dimension, dimensional constraint, driving dimension.
- **For translators:** not a drawing dimension and not a measured value.

### feature

One step in the timeline that creates or changes geometry, such as an extrude, a fillet or a
construction plane.

- **In SolidCraft:** `timeline.edit`, `timeline.suppress`, `timeline.reorder`, and the other
  `timeline.*` commands; the `features` design-file key.
- **Don't use:** operation, step (in labels); feature (for something SolidCraft can do in
  general: say *tool* or *capability*).
- **Elsewhere:** feature, operation.
- **For translators:** French uses *fonction* for a timeline feature, so "AI features" had to
  become *fonctionnalités IA*. Translate "feature" only in the timeline sense.

### folder

One of the browser's fixed sections of a component: Bodies, Sketches, Construction, Joints.

A folder is part of every component and can't be renamed or removed. A container that someone
makes is a *group*.

- **In SolidCraft:** the `folder` parameter of `browser.group`, `browser.order` and
  `browser.visibility` (`bodies`, `sketches`, `construction`).
- **Don't use:** folder for a group.
- **Elsewhere:** folder, node.
- **For translators:** not a group and not a folder on disk.

### group

A named container that someone makes, in the browser or in the timeline, to keep items together.

A group changes only how items are listed. It has no effect on the geometry or the order in which
features are computed.

- **In SolidCraft:** `browser.group`, `browser.ungroup`, `browser.rename_group`; `timeline.group`,
  `timeline.ungroup`, `timeline.rename_group`, `timeline.move_to_group`; the `group` parameter key;
  the `browser_groups` and `timeline_groups` design-file keys.
- **Don't use:** feature folder, folder (for a group).
- **Elsewhere:** folder, group.
- **For translators:** not a rigid group (a joint) and not a fixed browser *folder*.

### material

The physical substance of a body, which sets its density and mechanical properties.

A material sets mass, centre of gravity and strength values. How the body looks is its
*appearance*.

- **In SolidCraft:** `material.assign` ("Physical Material"), `material.list`, `material.create`,
  and the other `material.*` commands; the `materials` and `user_materials` design-file keys.
- **Don't use:** material for a render or visual material.
- **Elsewhere:** material, physical material.
- **For translators:** not an appearance.

### occurrence

One placed copy of a component inside its parent component.

A component can have several occurrences. Moving an occurrence moves only that copy; editing the
component changes every copy. The browser names occurrences with a number, such as `Bolt M20:3`.

- **In SolidCraft:** `occurrence.copy`, `occurrence.move`, `occurrence.ground`,
  `occurrence.properties`; the `occurrences` design-file key; the `path` of occurrence ids.
- **Don't use:** instance, placement.
- **Elsewhere:** occurrence, instance, component instance.
- **For translators:** not a *pattern instance*.

### part number

A design property that holds the identifier an organisation gives a design.

- **In SolidCraft:** the `part_number` design property, shown in Design Properties and set with
  `document.metadata.set`.
- **Don't use:** part number for a standard part's size.
- **For translators:** see *Words with more than one meaning*, "part".

### pattern instance

One copy that a pattern makes of its features, bodies or sketch entities.

The first instance is the original.

- **In SolidCraft:** `solid.pattern.rectangular`, `solid.pattern.circular`, `solid.pattern.path`,
  `sketch.pattern.rectangular`, `sketch.pattern.circular`; the `count` and `spacing` parameters
  ("between instances").
- **Don't use:** instance for an occurrence; element, item.
- **Elsewhere:** instance, element, occurrence.
- **For translators:** not an occurrence of a component.

### rollback marker

The marker in the timeline after which no feature is computed.

Moving the rollback marker back shows the design as it was at that step. Features after the marker
are kept, not deleted.

- **In SolidCraft:** `timeline.rollback`, `timeline.roll_to`; the `marker` design-file key.
- **Don't use:** timeline marker, history marker, rollback bar.
- **Elsewhere:** rollback bar, rollback marker, end-of-part marker.
- **For translators:** "history" is the undo history, not the timeline. French had three names
  for this marker while English did.

### sketch

A set of points and curves, with their constraints, on one plane, that features use as profiles,
paths and guides.

- **In SolidCraft:** `sketch.create`, `sketch.finish`, and the other `sketch.*` commands; the
  `sketches` browser folder.
- **Don't use:** drawing, profile (for the whole sketch).
- **Elsewhere:** sketch, 2D sketch.
- **For translators:** not a drawing (a sheet with views and dimensions).

### sketch entity

A point or a curve in a sketch.

- **In SolidCraft:** the `entities` parameter of the sketch commands (it takes point and curve
  ids); the sketch's `points` and `curves` design-file keys.
- **Don't use:** geometry (for sketch content), element, object.
- **Elsewhere:** sketch entity, sketch geometry, sketch element.
- **For translators:** "entity" names both points and curves.

### standard part

A ready-made component, such as a screw, nut, washer, pin or bearing, that SolidCraft builds from
a standard size.

- **In SolidCraft:** `parts.library` ("Standard Parts"), `parts.insert`, `parts.fastener`,
  `parts.resize`; the `parts` design-file key.
- **Don't use:** library part, part (on its own), content.
- **Elsewhere:** standard part, library part, fastener, catalogue part.
- **For translators:** see *Words with more than one meaning*, "part".

### timeline

The ordered list of a design's features, which SolidCraft computes from first to last.

- **In SolidCraft:** the `timeline.*` commands; the `features` design-file key, in timeline
  order.
- **Don't use:** feature history, history (for the timeline).
- **Elsewhere:** timeline, history, feature tree.
- **For translators:** not the undo history.

### web browser

A program that shows web pages, such as the one that runs SolidCraft's web build.

- **In SolidCraft:** the web build; the `home.in_this_browser` catalogue entry.
- **Don't use:** browser on its own.
- **For translators:** not the *browser* panel. Where a language uses one word for both, use the
  CAD word for the panel.

## Words with more than one meaning

An English word that means two things can be translated correctly for only one of them while both
share a catalogue entry. Each meaning below gets its own term and, in time, its own entry.

| Word | Meaning | Use | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| Construction | a sketch entity that isn't part of a profile | *construction entity* | sketch drawing commands, `ui.construction` |
| | the browser folder of construction planes, axes and points | *construction plane, axis, point* | the Construction folder, `construct.*` |
| Instance | one copy a pattern makes | *pattern instance* | pattern commands |
| | one placed copy of a component | *occurrence* | "Paste (Instance)" on `occurrence.copy` |
| History | the undo and redo history | history | Undo, Redo |
| | the list of features | *timeline* | "Feature history" (`ui.feature_history`), "Roll History Marker" |
| Part | a standard part | *standard part* | `parts.*` |
| | a body, an occurrence or the design | *body*, *occurrence*, *design* | catalogue texts that say "part" |
| | a design property | *part number* | Design Properties |
| Gap | the space a hem leaves | hem gap | the Hem dialog's Gap row |
| | an open end in the sketch continuity legend | open end | the sketch continuity legend |
| Clearance | the Clearance command | clearance check | `inspect.clearance` |
| | a minimum distance field | clearance | the Interference and plastic rules dialogs |
| Flat | a hole's flat bottom | flat bottom | the Hole dialog's tip |
| | a hem that lies flat on the sheet | flat hem | the Hem dialog's type |
| Round | a round relief or corner shape | round (shape) | relief shapes, plastic rests, ruled surface corners |
| | a fillet | *fillet* | `solid.fillet` |
| Normal | a sketch entity that isn't a construction entity | normal (line type) | the sketch palette's line type |
| | the direction perpendicular to a surface | normal (direction) | the ruled surface's Normal mode |
| | the middle display quality | normal (quality) | `ui.display_quality_normal` |

Some translations show the clash today: Japanese and Chinese show a hole's flat bottom with the
word for "unfold" or "plane", Chinese shows "Round" as "fillet", and Chinese and Russian show the
Normal line type as "normal vector".

## Two commands, one label

A label names one command. Today two pairs share one:

- "Edit Feature": `timeline.redefine` and `timeline.edit`.
- "Break Link": `component.break_link` (an occurrence's link to another design) and
  `sketch.break_link` (a projected sketch entity's link to its source).

Search lists both under the same name, and the label lookup gives both the same translation.

## A feature's type

A feature type has one name: its design-file key, such as `sheet_flange`. The label (Flange) is
its display name. Replies and scripts should use the design-file key; today `timeline.inspect`
reports a different name (`EdgeFlangeFeature`), so a script can't match one against the other.

## Open questions for the maintainer

- **British or American spelling** for labels and docs. Today both are in use (colour and color,
  centre and center, favourite and favorite); ids and keys use American spelling. #2501 proposes
  an English (UK) language option, so either base spelling can be read in the other.

# Sheet metal

The SHEET METAL tab builds parts from a sheet of constant thickness under a **sheet metal rule**
(thickness, bend radius, K-factor), set in **Sheet Metal Rules** (`sheet.manage_rules`).

- **Flange** (`sheet.flange`): a base flange from a sketch profile, a contour flange from an open
  sketch, or an edge flange from a part edge.
- **Hem** (`sheet.hem`) and **Fold** (`sheet.fold`) along a sketch line.
- **Unfold / Refold** (`sheet.unfold`, `sheet.refold`) for working on the flat part.
- **Convert** (`sheet.convert`) turns a plate of constant thickness into sheet metal, or, with
  bend edges, a solid or a shelled body.
- **Create Flat Pattern** (`sheet.flat_pattern`) shows the flat part with its bend lines and a
  bend table, and exports it as DXF or a bend-table CSV through the save picker.

Bends follow the rule's K-factor, so flat lengths match what a press brake will make. Tests
check flat lengths against hand-computed bend allowances.

An edge flange takes its setback off its own edge only. Where that edge ends at an inside
corner of the base (the base runs on past it, like the leg of an L), the rest of the base
stays, and the rule's **bend relief** (`relief_width` and `relief_depth`; Relief Width and
Relief Depth in Sheet Metal Rules) is cut into it beside the bend's end: a slot the relief
width wide, from the relief depth before the bend line to the relief width past the flange's
far edge in the flat pattern. The bend and the flange are then free of the base, folded and
flat. A relief that can't be cut (a width under 0.01 mm, one as wide as the base beside the
bend, or a slot that would cut the base apart) is left out, and the flange feature reports a
warning saying where.

Where a cut-out has taken part of an edge away (a corner cut off the plate, a notch in the
middle of an edge), an edge flange picked on that edge runs along the stretch the cut-outs
leave nearest the pick, and takes its setback off that stretch only. The base on the other
side of a notch keeps its edge, and a pick there, in the same feature or a later one, makes
a flange of its own. Where the base is still left beside the bend's end at such a cut-out, it
gets the bend relief as above. An edge that cut-outs have taken whole is refused.

The setback is cut out of the base's outline as it was drawn: where the bend line crosses an
arc of the outline (a plate with rounded corners, bent inside or in the middle), the arc stays
an arc and ends there, in the flat pattern and the DXF. A free-form curve (an ellipse, a
spline) in an outline that a setback cuts is followed by tangent arcs within 0.001 mm.

Where two bends of one edge flange feature meet at a corner of the base, the rule's **corner
relief shape** (`corner_relief_shape`; Corner Relief Shape in Sheet Metal Rules) says what is
cut there. `notch`, the default, cuts nothing more: the bends end square at the corner, which
leaves a step in the flat pattern between each bend's end and its flange's closed end. `tear`
cuts no relief either, and no step: both bends run to the corner where the two bend lines
meet, and each bend's end is cut straight, in the flat pattern, from that corner to where its
flange's closed end starts. Folded, the two bends touch at the corner and open to the rule's
gap where the flanges start; the bend table lists a torn bend between the middles of its two
ends. A tear whose cuts would cross in the flat pattern, or that would run one bend into the
other folded (flanges at very different angles), is left out with a warning and the corner
keeps its notch. `round`
and `rectangular` cut a relief the size of the rule's **corner relief** across, centred on the corner where
the two bend lines meet: out of the base a round with half that size as its radius, or a square
with half that size as its side, and both bends stop where it begins, cut straight across. The
flange panels keep their ends. The relief is in the folded part, the flat pattern, the bend
table (the bends are shorter) and the DXF (a round relief is an arc). At a corner that isn't
square the round follows the angle of the base and the square becomes a kite, its two cuts
square to the edges. Changing the shape in a rule changes the parts made with that rule. A
relief that doesn't fit (under 0.01 mm across, leaving nothing of a bend, or reaching as far
from its corner as another edge of the base is) is left out, and the flange feature reports a
warning saying where. The reliefs at all the corners are cut together, so a corner's relief
does not depend on the order the corners are cut in; two of them that would overlap are both
left out, each with a warning saying which the other is.

```json
{"command":"sheet.manage_rules","params":{"name":"Sheet 2 mm","thickness":"2 mm","k_factor":0.5,
 "bend_radius":"1 mm","corner_relief_shape":"round","corner_relief":"8 mm","active":true}}
```

The rule's shape and size are the default. An edge flange feature can choose its own for the
corners its flanges make: `corner_relief_shape` (`notch`, `round`, `rectangular` or `tear`) and
`corner_relief` (the size across, a length or an expression) in `sheet.flange`, or Corner Relief
Shape and Corner Relief in the Flange dialog. In the dialog, Rule as the shape and an empty size
take the rule's; either one left out follows the rule while the other is the feature's. Corners are
relieved only between the flanges of one feature, so a feature's choice never meets another's at a
corner, and two edge flange features of one part can have different reliefs under one rule. A
base or contour flange takes its corners from the rule only and refuses both parameters. The
flange gap and the rule's other values stay with the rule for every flange. The feature's choice is
saved with the design (file format 23).

```json
{"command":"sheet.flange","params":{"edges":[[60,0,2],[120,45,2],[60,90,2],[0,45,2]],
 "height":20,"corner_relief_shape":"round","corner_relief":"6 mm"}}
```

Where the edge flanges of one feature meet at a corner of the base, their panels are closed
toward each other at any bend angle: each end is cut square to the sheet, on a line in the flat
chosen so that the edges nearest each other (on the inner faces) run parallel, the rule's
**gap** apart, either side of the plane halfway between the flanges. Flanges at 72° get slanted
ends in the flat; corners that aren't square close the same way, and at 90° it is the corner
the rule always gave. A corner that can't be closed (a gap under 0.01 mm, flanges bending
opposite ways, ends that would overlap in the flat pattern) stays open, and the flange feature
reports a warning saying where. A flange added by a later feature leaves the corner as it was:
the earlier flange keeps its length and the new one ends at its bend.

The flanges of one edge flange feature can each have an angle and a height of their own. An
entry of `edges` is a point `[x, y, z]`, which takes the feature's `height` and `angle`, or an
object `{"point": [x, y, z], "angle": "105 deg", "height": "30 mm"}` whose `angle` and `height`
(either one, or both) replace them for that edge. They are expressions like the feature's own,
so parameters work, and each is a feature input of its own (`Edge angle`, `Edge height`) after
`Height` and `Angle`. The corners between such flanges close like those between equal ones:
the ends run toward each other the rule's gap apart, either side of the plane halfway between
the two flanges, and a taller flange's end keeps that line up to its own tip. This is how to
close a corner between flanges at different angles, because flanges of separate features
don't close toward each other. In the Flange dialog, picking more than one edge shows a row
per edge with an angle and a height box; an empty box takes the value above.

```json
{"command":"sheet.flange","params":{"edges":[[60,0,2],{"point":[120,45,2],"angle":"90 deg"},
 {"point":[60,90,2],"angle":"105 deg","height":"30 mm"},{"point":[0,45,2],"angle":"120 deg","height":"25 mm"}],
 "height":38.6,"angle":"75 deg"}}
```

A flange can also stand on the far edge of another flange: a return, such as a lip turned in
along the top of a tray's walls. It runs along that edge from end to end, so it follows the
closed end of the flange it stands on, slanted or not. Two returns of one feature whose flanges
meet at a corner of the base are closed toward each other as well, with the rule's gap. They
are mitred either side of a plane that runs along the mean of the two panels' normals, bisects
their bend lines and passes where the lines their panels start on cross. Returns that lie in
one plane (level returns on a tray's walls, whatever the walls' angle) then meet on the corner's
bisector, like the sides of a picture frame. Each panel ends on a slanted line in the flat.
Each bend stops square where all of it keeps half the gap from that plane, at the latest at
the end of the flange it stands on, which can leave a short stretch of that flange's edge bare.
Returns turned opposite ways pass each other. A return that meets no other at a corner ends
with the flange it stands on; where the flange beside that one leans in over it, the return is
cut back until it keeps as clear of that flange as the end of the flange it stands on does.
Returns that can't be closed stay open with a warning, as on the base. Returns of separate
features don't close toward each other either: make the returns round a corner in one feature.
A corner relief or a tear changes none of this: it leaves the flanges' closed ends as they
are, so the returns on them close over a relieved or torn corner as over a whole one.

```json
{"command":"sheet.flange","params":{"edges":[[60,2,20],[118,45,20],[60,88,20],[2,45,20]],
 "height":12,"angle":"90 deg"}}
```

(The four returns of a 120 x 90 tray in 2 mm sheet with 90° walls 20 high: each point is the
middle of a wall's far edge on its inner face, so the returns turn in over the base.)

A flange can stand on a straight side edge of an existing flange as well. Select that edge
and the adjoining edge of its supporting panel in one feature to close the new flanges across
the existing bend. The panels are mitred with the rule's gap; `round` and `rectangular` corner
reliefs cut a rounded or rectangular slot across the existing bend zone in the flat material.
The slot's width is `corner_relief`, and it survives unfolding, refolding and DXF export.
`notch` keeps the gap without another cut. A `tear` across an existing bend is not supported
yet and leaves the notch with a warning. A mitre that would overlap the flat pattern stays
open with a warning. Side-edge setbacks on curved panels or on only part of an edge left by
a cut-out are not supported yet. The edge connecting a panel to its existing bend is not a
free edge. See `examples/regressions/sheet-side-flange-corner.json` for a small reproduction.

**Convert** also takes a solid or a shelled body: pick the face that stays fixed and the sharp
edges that become bends (`bends`; Bend Edges in the dialog). The flat faces reached from the
fixed face across those edges become the sheet. A shelled body keeps its walls and their
thickness; any other solid's faces become the outside of the sheet, with the rule's thickness
taken into the body. Each sharp edge stays where the faces of its bend would meet, so the part
keeps its envelope and the flat pattern is the outside lengths less a bend deduction per bend,
2·(R + T)·tan(θ/2) − θ·(R + K·T). A bend can be picked on either skin of a shell; bends turn
either way, follow one another and take any angle (the walls of a tapered tray at 72°). An
edge between two faces of the sheet that is no bend is cut open, each side half the rule's
**gap** from the plane halfway between the two, like the corners of a tray. A bend drawn as a
chamfer (a flat strip between two faces, the chord of the bend's arc, as models without bend
radii draw one) is picked in the middle of the strip: the two faces then meet at their virtual
sharp in one bend of the rule's radius, and the strip is no face of the sheet. A bend modelled
with its radius (a cylinder between two flat faces tangent to it, as sheet metal parts from
other systems come, or a filleted edge) is picked anywhere on its cylinder, on either skin, and
converts the same way: the sheet is bent there with the rule's radius and K-factor, not the
modelled radius, so the flat pattern is the one the rule makes. The result is an
ordinary sheet body: edge flanges, cuts, Unfold, the flat pattern and its exports work on it,
and it follows the solid when a parameter changes (the edges and the fixed face are found by
their names). Without bend edges Convert expects a plate, as before. Either way round walls
(holes, slot ends, rounded corners, notches) stay circles and arcs in the flat pattern and the
DXF, also where a STEP file writes one in pieces, and the holes and slots of every face of the
sheet are its cut-outs, where the bends put them. An engraving in a face of the sheet (a recess
with a flat floor, at most half the thickness deep) becomes a pocket of it, as a plate's does
(below), on either skin of a shell. Not converted yet: curved faces other than bends (rolled
sheet), with bend edges a hole or an engraving that reaches into a bend or a pocket deeper than
half the thickness (cut them after converting), and bends that close a ring.

A plate may carry recesses in one of its faces, such as an engraved label or a counterbore: a
recess with a flat floor and walls square to the plate, at most half the plate's thickness
deep. Each becomes a pocket of the sheet (see the pockets below), so the converted part keeps
it: the sheet is as thick as the plate, the flat pattern is the whole plate with the recess
listed under `pockets` (its outline, side and depth), and the DXF draws its outline on the
pocket layer of its depth, apart from the cut contours, for a laser to mark rather than cut.
The face the recesses are in can be the one picked or the other. A recess deeper than half the
thickness, recesses in both faces, and a plate whose recesses are larger than the face around
them (a thinner plate with raised parts) are refused with the reason. A recess lies in an
opening of the face it is cut into, so the faces of a bent part's legs are none: a bent part is
refused as no plate, and converts with its bend edges. A bend across a pocket is refused as for
any pocket, so fold or flange clear of an engraving.

```json
{"command":"solid.box","params":{"length":100,"width":60,"height":30,"body_name":"Tray"}}
{"command":"solid.shell","params":{"faces":[[50,30,30]],"thickness":2}}
{"command":"sheet.convert","params":{"body":"Tray","face":[50,30,0],
 "bends":[[50,0,0],[100,30,0],[50,60,0],[0,30,0]]}}
```

The `face` can also be the name `model.faces` lists for it (`"face":"F1:+z"`), which saves
computing a point on a face with holes or a curved outline: `model.faces` gives every face a
`point` that lies on it.

For a shop drawing or spreadsheet, `sheet.export_bend_table` returns CSV by default; choose
`format: "json"` for structured data. It includes the sheet rule, thickness, bend angles,
radii, allowances and flat centre-line coordinates. Lengths use millimetres and angles use
degrees. A bend is listed where its centre line has material: one that a cut-out has shortened
gives the length and ends it has left, and one that cut-outs split gives a row for every piece,
all with the bend's number (the flat pattern and the DXF draw the same pieces as bend lines).
Supply `path` to save it, or omit `path` to receive the content through the command
response. `body` defaults to the last sheet body. Exporting does not add a timeline entry or
consume an undo step.

```json
{"command":"sheet.export_bend_table","params":{"format":"csv","path":"bracket-bends.csv"}}
{"command":"sheet.export_dxf","params":{"path":"bracket-flat.dxf"}}
```

The DXF is an AutoCAD 2000 (`AC1015`) drawing in millimetres, made for a laser-cutting shop's
nesting or CAM software: each kind of line is on a layer of its own, with a colour (AutoCAD's
index) and, for the bends, a linetype that the file defines.

| Layer | Colour | Line | Holds |
|---|---|---|---|
| `OUTLINE` | 7 white or black | continuous | the outer contour of each piece of the sheet |
| `CUT` | 4 cyan | continuous | what is cut out inside it: holes, slots, and the loose pieces a cut leaves (the middle of a ring) |
| `TEXT` | 2 yellow | continuous | the letters that text cut through the sheet, with their counters; only with `"text": "cut"`, the default |
| `ETCH` | 6 magenta | continuous | letters as single contours, to be marked and not cut: `"text": "etch"`, and always text machined to a depth |
| `BEND_UP`, `BEND_DOWN` | 1 red, 5 blue | `DASHED` | the bend centre lines, by direction |
| `BEND_NOTES` | 8 grey | continuous | the note beside each bend line, only with `"bend_notes": true` |
| `POCKET_…` | 3 green | continuous | pockets, a layer for each depth (see below) |
| `PERFORATION` | 3 green | continuous | the holes of a perforation field |

`OUTLINE`, `CUT`, `BEND_UP` and `BEND_DOWN` are always in the layer table, the others when the
sheet has something for them. The inner contours (`CUT`, `TEXT`) are written before the outline,
so a program that follows the file's order cuts inside-out.

A round hole is a `CIRCLE`, a circular arc an `ARC`, a whole ellipse one `ELLIPSE` and an arc of
an ellipse an elliptical `ELLIPSE`; the pieces of a spline, the outlines of text and the other
conics are `SPLINE`s of their own degree, so no curve is written as chords. For a machine that
reads only lines and arcs, pass `"curves": "arcs"` to `sheet.export_dxf`: the free-form curves
are then tangent arcs and lines within 0.001 mm.

Letters are told from other cut-outs by where they came from: a cut whose sketch holds text
(Sketch Text) marks the cut-outs it makes as letters, counters included, while the design is
built; nothing more is saved in the design file. A letter that another cut-out overlaps, or
that the sheet's edge clips, has become one shape with it and stays on `CUT`.

```json
{"command":"sheet.export_dxf","params":{"path":"tray-flat.dxf","text":"etch","bend_notes":true}}
```

With `"bend_notes": true` each bend line gets a note on `BEND_NOTES`, `B1 UP 90° R1` (the bend's
number, its direction, its angle and its inner radius; `%%d` is AutoCAD's degree sign). It is 3 mm
high (`"note_height"` changes that), centred half a height beside the middle of the line,
parallel to it and readable from below or from the right. A bend that cut-outs split has a note
for each piece. Notes are off by default, because a program that cuts or marks every layer would
mark them.

A design with several sheet bodies exports one file for each with `"per_body": true`: the files
are `<path>-<body>.dxf` (characters a file name cannot hold become `_`; two bodies that would
share a name get `_2`, `_3`…), and the reply lists them in `files`. Without a `path` it lists
their DXF texts instead.

Base-flange profiles keep their interior holes. Through cuts that cross a sheet edge become
notches in the flat outline; overlapping and repeated cuts remove their combined area once.
The flat preview, DXF and unfolded solid use the same material boundaries. Lines and circular
arcs remain exact. An ellipse, a spline or text stays the curve it was drawn as in the flat
pattern and the unfolded solid; the folded solid follows it with tangent arcs within 0.001 mm,
and the point lists write it as chords within 0.001 mm (the DXF keeps the curve, see above).
Flat-pattern JSON lists each cut-out twice, in the same order: as points (`cutouts`), and
exactly (`cutout_shapes`): a round hole as `{"circle": {"center", "radius"}}`, any other as its
`line`, `arc` (centre, radius, start and sweep in degrees) and `polyline` segments (one
`polyline` for each ellipse quarter, spline or glyph curve).

Cuts can leave separate material pieces, including the centre of a ring cut. These pieces
remain one logical sheet group through Unfold / Refold and export as separate flat outlines.
A cut that parts a piece from the base (a flange cut off along its bend, the part of a ring's
inside on a flange's edge) keeps it too, folded or flat, and its warning says how many pieces
are no longer joined to the base, their area and where they lie in the flat pattern. Islands
inside other material (a ring's centre, a letter's counter) are not counted.
Large profiles that exceed the geometry processing budget report an error instead of
exporting a partial outline.

A Box cut, or a Cylinder cut whose axis is the sheet's normal, machines the sheet like the
extrude of its footprint: through the sheet it is a cut-out (a cylinder a round one), and
part way it is a pocket. A primitive cut at any other angle, or across a folded bend, is refused.

Hole machines the sheet the same way from a flat face of any panel, the base or a flange, on
either side, folded or unfolded: square to that panel, a through hole (plain or tapped) is a
round cut-out of the flat pattern and a `CIRCLE` in the DXF, and a counterbore or a blind
flat-bottomed hole is a round pocket. A hole slanted to its panel or drilled into the edge of
the sheet, a countersink and a drill point are refused.

Parallel, untapered extrude cuts also preserve shallow pockets through Unfold / Refold.
The pocket floor and side walls remain solid geometry; overlapping cuts from opposite sides
become a through hole wherever they remove the whole thickness. Flat-pattern JSON lists
`pockets` with their side, depth and bottom/top thickness coordinates in millimetres.
DXF pocket boundaries use `POCKET_BOTTOM_Z…_TO_…_MM`, `POCKET_TOP_Z…_TO_…_MM`, or
`POCKET_INTERNAL_Z…_TO_…_MM` layers. These are machining operations, so do not treat every
pocket layer as a through-cut contour when importing the drawing into a CAM tool. (Text
machined to a depth is a marking, on `ETCH`.)

Extrude Intersect on a straight base or an unfolded sheet retains the material inside both
the current tool footprint and its depth interval, including interior holes, detached islands
and earlier pockets. A shallow intersection records the removed layers above and below the
retained material as top and bottom pockets. The sheet rule keeps the original stock gauge;
the remaining solid can be thinner. A completely empty intersection removes the sheet and
its metadata together. DXF records pocket depth in its layer names; importing that DXF as
ordinary sketch geometry does not reconstruct the machining depths automatically. Each
positive retained or removed depth layer must meet the kernel's 0.000001 mm extrusion
resolution; smaller layers report an error rather than being rounded away. To Object can
retain a tool that trims to a straight prism, using its actual trimmed footprint. A curved
tool with varying depth is refused before changing sheet geometry. Pocket profiles can move with planar panels when forming,
but a pocket crossing a bend zone cannot yet be refolded. Machining folded bend material,
tapered sheet cuts and other unsupported 3D sheet Cut/Intersect operations report an error before changing
the design; they cannot silently restore removed material during a later sheet rebuild.

Other features that change a sheet body's material without the sheet knowing it (a fillet or
chamfer on a corner, an extrude joined onto it, a Mirror or Combine joined into it) are not in
the flat pattern yet. Such a feature warns, and while the body carries its change the flat
pattern, the DXF and the bend table are refused with an error that names it, rather than writing
a part that does not match the body. A later sheet metal feature rebuilds the body from its sheet
features and says that the change is not kept. Moving the body, splitting its faces and cosmetic
threads leave the flat pattern as it is.

A sketch can be drawn on a flat face of the sheet: the base or a flange, on either side. Pick
the face (or give `sketch.create` the point `plane: {face: [x, y, z]}`) and the sketch attaches
to that panel instead of to a certified source face. It keeps the face's name,
`sheet:<body>:<panel>:<top|bottom>` (the panel is `base` or the flange's feature tag), and finds
the face again whenever the sheet is rebuilt: after a parameter change such as the thickness or
a flange angle, through Unfold / Refold, after the file is reopened and when the body is
renamed. Sketch coordinates are the flat pattern's, so a point drawn on a flange lies where the
flat pattern and its DXF have it, and on the bottom face y runs the other way, as seen from
below. When the face is gone (its flange is suppressed or deleted) the sketch reports a lost
attachment instead of moving to another face; **Redefine Sketch Plane** attaches it to another
face. `fixed: true` still freezes the picked plane in space.

Every face of a folded sheet has a name of that kind, which `model.faces` lists as `sheet_face`:
`<panel>:top` and `<panel>:bottom`, `<panel>:rim.<edge>` for a rim (a base sketch line's id, or a
flange's `far`, `side0`, `side1`; `rim.bend0`/`rim.bend1` for a bend's flat ends and
`rim.ext0`/`rim.ext1` where a flange runs on past its bend toward a neighbour), and
`<flange>:bend.inner` / `<flange>:bend.outer` for a bend's curved faces. A command that takes a
face name takes it too (`sheet:Body1:F3.1:top`), and finds the face from the sheet itself, so the
name stays with that face while the sheet's sizes change and other flanges come and go. Faces the
sheet does not describe (a hole's wall) have none.

# Control protocol

`solidcraft --control PORT` (or `SOLIDCRAFT_CONTROL_PORT=PORT`) listens on `127.0.0.1:PORT` for
JSON lines. Each request is one line `{"id": …, "method": "…", "params": {…}}`; each reply is one
line `{"id": …, "ok": true, "result": …}` or `{"id": …, "ok": false, "error": "…"}`. Requests are
handled on the UI thread between frames; pointer and keyboard input is injected as real egui
events, one pointer event per frame.

### Token

Every connection must authenticate. At start the app makes a random 256-bit token for this
launch and writes it, as one line of hex, to a file only the user can read:

| System | Token file |
|---|---|
| Linux | `$XDG_DATA_HOME/solidcraft/control/PORT.token` (`~/.local/share/solidcraft/control/PORT.token`) |
| macOS | `~/Library/Application Support/SolidCraft/control/PORT.token` |
| Windows | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\SolidCraft\control\PORT.token` |

On Unix the folder is `0700` and the file `0600`; on Windows the file's inherited permissions are
replaced by a single entry for the user. `SOLIDCRAFT_CONTROL_DIR` moves the folder. The file is
removed when the app exits, and the next launch writes a new token. The token file's path is
printed to stderr at start-up.

The first request on a connection must carry the token as a top-level `"token"` member
(`{"id": 1, "method": "ui.inspect", "params": {}, "token": "…"}`); later requests on the same
connection may leave it out. A first line without the right token is answered with
`{"ok": false, "error": "unauthorized: …"}` and the connection is closed, without running
anything. Tokens are compared in constant time.

`solidcraft-cli mcp --connect 127.0.0.1:PORT` reads the token file for that port by itself
(`--token T` or `SOLIDCRAFT_CONTROL_TOKEN` give one explicitly). For a test harness, or a
sandboxed package whose data folder the client can't see, start the app with
`SOLIDCRAFT_CONTROL_TOKEN` set to at least 32 hex characters (for example
`openssl rand -hex 32`) and the app uses that token instead of making one; the file is still
written. A one-line client in Python:

```python
token = (Path.home() / ".local/share/solidcraft/control/7878.token").read_text().strip()
sock.sendall((json.dumps({"id": 1, "method": "ui.inspect", "params": {}, "token": token}) + "\n").encode())
```

### Limits

The channel is untrusted input. A request line may be at most 16 MiB; a longer one is answered
with `{"ok": false, "error": "request too large"}` and the connection is closed, as are
connections that send eight lines that are not JSON. At most 16 connections are served at once
(further ones get `{"ok": false, "error": "too many connections"}`), at most 64 queued requests
run per frame so a flood cannot starve drawing, and a request that the UI thread has not
answered within 60 seconds (3600 seconds for `engine.batch`) is replied to with
`{"ok": false, "running": true, "error": "timeout: … is still running …"}`. The same 16 MiB line
limit applies to the MCP server.

A timed-out request has not failed: it is still running in the app and will still apply (a long
fillet, say), so don't simply send it again. The connection keeps its reply (#1618). Ask for it
with `control.pending`: `{"pending": <id>, "method": …, "done": false}` while it runs, then
`{"pending": <id>, "method": …, "done": true, "reply": {…}}` (its own reply, once), and
`{"pending": null}` when nothing is outstanding. Until it lands, any other request on that
connection is refused at once with `{"ok": false, "busy": true, "error": "busy: …"}` and not
run, so nothing is queued to apply unseen behind it.

Any request's `params` may carry `allow_paths: ["/abs/folder", …]`: every file that request
reads, writes or deletes (command paths such as `file.export`'s `path` or `doc.recovery_*`'s
`dir`, `ui.render`, `ui.screenshot`) must then lie inside one of those folders after `..` and
symlinks are resolved, or the request fails with `… outside the folders this agent may use …`.
The app adds its own recovery folder and, when it lies safely inside the home folder and not in
a hidden folder, the open design's folder (whose hidden files stay out of reach). The bridged
MCP server sends its folders this way on every request ([mcp.md](mcp.md)). Without
`allow_paths` file paths are not limited: a client holding the token can do what the user can.

## Engine

| Method | Params | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `engine.execute` | `command`: command id, `params`: JSON object | the command's result |
| `engine.script` | `commands`: `[{command, params}, …]` | results, stops at the first error |
| `engine.batch` | `commands`: `[{command, params}, …]` (at most 10 000), `rollback?`: bool (default true), `timings?`, `profile?`: bool (default false) | `{completed, results, undone}`, plus `failed: {index, command, error}` when a step fails, and with `timings` `timings: [{index, command, ms}]` (the failing step included) and `total_ms`; `profile` adds each step's `profile: {boolean_ms, tessellate_ms, other_ms}`. Runs the steps in one request, so within one frame, each as `engine.execute` runs it. The first failure stops the batch, and with `rollback` the design goes back to how it was before it (`undone`: the steps taken back). Refused before anything runs, with an error starting `engine.batch unavailable`, while the agent cursor is shown or when a step loads a file (`doc.open`, `file.insert_step`, `file.insert_mesh`). Send such steps one by one. Answered when done, for up to 3600 s |
| `engine.commands` | — | every command: id, label, tab, panel, icon, shortcut, params doc, enabled |
| `document.inspect` | `measure?`: bool | parameters, timeline (errors, timings), bodies, sketches, selection (assembly joints: `engine.execute` `joint.inspect {joint?}`, which reads only: each joint's two origins with the occurrence, the snap as saved, the feature, face, edge or sketch curve its names refer to, and whether it resolves or why not; kind, offset, angle, flip, values, limits, expressions and motion links) |

Commands never open dialogs when run this way. `solidcraft-cli commands` prints the same registry.

Product images use `render.preflight/start/status/cancel/export` through `engine.execute`.
Keep the returned session-scoped job ID for subsequent calls; status does not block or
render. See [render jobs](render-jobs.md) for capture, cancellation and export semantics.

While an interactive native file picker is open, `ui.inspect` reports `file_picker_busy: true`.
Engine commands, `ui.file` and `ui.home` requests wait for its answer; window resizing,
inspection and screenshots remain available.

Every `sketch.*` command that changes a sketch adds `created: {points, curves, constraints,
dimensions}` to its result (and `wires` for 3D curves): the ids of what it added, in creation
order, next to whatever else the command returns (`curves`, `sides`, `corners`…). Sketch ids are
stable and never reused, even after a delete (`l1`, `l2`, then `l3` once `l2` is gone; only undo
rolls the numbering back with the design), so they can go straight into later commands:

```text
{"id":7,"method":"engine.execute","params":{"command":"sketch.line","params":{"points":[[0,0],[40,0]]}}}
→ {"curves":["l1"],"created":{"points":["l1.start","l1.end"],"curves":["l1"],"constraints":["k1"],"dimensions":[]},…}
{"id":8,"method":"engine.execute","params":{"command":"sketch.dimension","params":{"entities":["l1"],"value":50}}}
```

A bare numeric `value` given to `sketch.dimension` (from the control channel, scripts or MCP) is
read in the design's units, exactly as if it were typed into the dimension box: in an inch design
`"value": 2` makes the line 2 in (50.8 mm) long. Point coordinates stay in millimetres. To pin a
unit regardless of the design, pass an expression with one: `"value": "50 mm"` or
`"value": "0.5 in"`. Angles are degrees unless the expression says otherwise.

The viewport also shows an X/Y/Z-aligned dimension chain between the endpoints of the
currently shown distance (centre, minimum or maximum), with each world-axis distance
labelled separately as an absolute value (including zero).
It uses the design's units and length precision, independently of the view or sketch plane.
Preferences → Graphics → **Show X/Y/Z distances** controls these extra lines and
labels (default on, saved between runs). Set `ui.prefs {"measure_axis_distances": false}`
to hide them while keeping the total distance and the dialog's ΔX/ΔY/ΔZ values. These
overlays remain visible until Measure closes.
Overlay handles `measure:label:x`, `measure:label:y` and `measure:label:z` identify the extra
labels; `prefs:measure_axis_distances` identifies the checkbox.

Entering Render requires finishing the current modelling operation; returning restores
the Design camera. See [the integrated Render workspace](render-workspace.md).

### Continuous camera motion

Continuous camera motion is also available through `engine.execute` with command
`view.navigate`: pass `camera` (from `ui.inspect`) and `motion: "pan" | "orbit" | "zoom"`.
Pan and orbit take `delta: [dx,dy]` in screen points (each within ±10000); pan also requires
`viewport: [width,height]` (each 1..1000000). Orbit accepts a world-space `pivot` with the
viewport size. Zoom takes `factor` (0.05..20, below 1 zooms in) and an optional world-space
`anchor`. The returned `camera` is applied immediately by the UI, without animation,
document edits, undo steps or a success-log entry per movement.

## MCP

`solidcraft-cli mcp --connect 127.0.0.1:PORT` bridges an MCP client (an AI agent) to this
channel; see [mcp.md](mcp.md).

## Example

```text
{"id":1,"method":"engine.execute","params":{"command":"sketch.create","params":{"plane":"XY"}}}
{"id":2,"method":"engine.execute","params":{"command":"sketch.rectangle.two_point","params":{"p0":[0,0],"p1":[40,30]}}}
{"id":3,"method":"engine.execute","params":{"command":"solid.extrude","params":{"distance":20}}}
{"id":4,"method":"engine.execute","params":{"command":"solid.fillet","params":{"edges":[[0,0,10]],"radius":3}}}
{"id":5,"method":"ui.screenshot","params":{"path":"/tmp/part.png"}}
```

Preferences → Navigation → View navigator offers **Signed axes** (the original default) and
**Cube**. This choice is saved independently of the mouse preset. The control channel selects it
with `ui.prefs {"navigator_style":"axes"}` or `ui.prefs {"navigator_style":"cube"}`.
Existing settings without this field keep signed axes. Signed-axis tips choose principal views;
clicking an aligned tip again reverses the view.

Hold Shift during an orbit gesture to snap to the nearest standard or diagonal view. This applies to
right-drag, the Orbit navigation tool, and dragging either view navigator. Under the default preset,
Shift+middle also orbits with snapping; middle alone pans. Cube faces choose principal views,
and corners choose isometric views. The middle of each cube edge belongs to its face. Face names
follow the up-axis preference; the small X/Y/Z triad shows world axes. Clicking the same face keeps that view.
The inward-pointing arrows orbit by 90 degrees; the curved arrows at the upper right roll the
view by 90 degrees. The Home button at the upper left returns to isometric and the lower-right circle
fits the model.

The cube is subdued while idle. Hovering its area brightens the cube and navigation bar and
reveals the surrounding controls; the picked face or corner gets a pale blue fill and
blue outline. Moving away restores the subdued state. Navigation-bar controls also brighten
when hovered or when a navigation tool is active.

The cube has six face targets and eight corner targets, with no edge targets. Corner picking
regions lie on the six flat faces, preserving sharp corners with no permanent subdivision
lines. Hovering a corner highlights its parts on the adjacent visible faces together.

The cube widget occupies a compact 112-point square in the viewport corner. A straight-on
cube face is approximately 55 points wide; painting and picking scale together. Face labels
are stretched vertically. View clicks ease through intermediate orientations when Navigation
animated view changes is enabled (the default), at the configured animation speed.

The cube runs `view.navigate` through the command engine. Programmatic callers pass `camera`
and either `direction: [x,y,z]` in the camera's up-axis frame or `action` (`left`, `right`, `up`,
`down`, `clockwise`, `counterclockwise`, `home`, `fit`). The result contains `camera` and `fit`;
UI callers apply the camera with their animation preference, without editing the design.

Shift-orbit snapping includes 45-degree edge views and isometric corner views, with a
lightly damped spring transition and a small boundary margin to prevent flicker.

# Agent chat

Agent chat is a side panel where you talk to a coding agent you already use (Claude Code,
Codex, Google Antigravity, OpenCode, Grok Build and others), or to a model behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint you
choose (Ollama or LM Studio on your computer, OpenAI, any other URL), and have it work on the
design that's open. A coding agent runs on your computer under **your own account** with that
agent: SolidCraft doesn't sell or proxy a model and needs no key for it. An endpoint's key, if
it needs one, goes into your system keychain, never into SolidCraft's settings.

Desktop app only.

## Turning it on and off

Everything about it is on one page: **Preferences → AI**.

- **Show AI features** (on by default) is the master switch. Turned off, SolidCraft shows nothing
  of it: no AI button, no shortcut, no menu entry, no panel, and nothing is looked for or
  started. The page stays, so you can turn it back on.
- **Show button in toolbar** (on by default): the **AI** button at the right end of the toolbar
  row, which stays there however wide the window is. Turn it off to keep only the shortcut and
  the menu entry.

With AI features on, the panel opens from:

- the **AI** button at the right end of the toolbar;
- **Ctrl+Shift+A** (Cmd+Shift+A on a Mac), which also works from the chat's own text box;
- **View settings** (the last button of the navigation bar under the view) → **Agent chat**.

Nothing runs until you need it: SolidCraft looks for installed agents (a quick `--version`
each, in the background) when the panel or the AI page first opens, and starts an agent only
when you send a message or press **Connect**.

## The panel

- **Docking:** drag the panel's header (the dotted grip and the title) to the other half of the
  window and let go. The side it would land on lights up while you drag. You can also pick
  **Left** or **Right** under Preferences → AI → Panel. SolidCraft remembers the side.
- **Width:** drag the panel's inner edge. SolidCraft remembers it.
- **Its own window:** the pop-out button in the header (a window with an arrow) moves the chat
  into a window of its own, named after the design, which you can move anywhere, including
  another screen. The window's own close button closes the chat, which opens there again next
  time; **Dock** (the same place in its header) puts it back in the side panel. You can also
  pick **Own window** under Preferences → AI → Panel. SolidCraft remembers where the window
  was and how big.
- **Minimise** (the line in the header) folds the panel into a thin strip that keeps the chat
  icon, the agent's state, and a count of anything waiting for your answer. Click the icon to
  unfold it. **Close** (×) hides the panel. Neither stops the agent; **Stop** does.
- **The agent switcher** under the title picks the agent for this conversation; switching stops
  the one running. Next to it, when the agent has modes of its own (Claude Code has *Default*,
  *Accept Edits*, *Plan*…), a second drop-down sets the agent's mode. When the agent reports its models (an ACP agent's
  model list, or an endpoint's `/models`), a model drop-down shows the one in use and changes it;
  SolidCraft remembers the last choice for each agent and puts it back on the next session. An
  endpoint's agent also keeps it as its default model. An agent that reports no models shows no
  drop-down.

## Files and pictures

A message can carry up to eight files, to show the agent what you mean: a concept picture, a
sketch, a brief, a part to fit around.

- **+** next to **Send** has **Choose a file…** (a file dialog for the types below) and **Paste a
  picture** (the picture on the clipboard).
- **Drop files on the chat.** Files dropped on the panel (or its folded strip) attach to the
  next message, and the app doesn't open them too. While files are dragged over the chat, it says
  so. The window gives no position while something is dragged, so the drop is the chat's when the
  pointer was last seen over the chat; **+** always works.
- The files show as chips above the text box: a picture's thumbnail, the name, and × to take the
  file off. A picture is read off the window thread, so a large one never stops the window: its
  chip shows a spinner meanwhile, and **Send** waits for it. **Send** sends files with no text.
- **Pictures** (PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP) go to the agent as they are when they are at most 2048 px
  on the long side and 3.75 MB (a picture's base64 then stays under 5 MB, so eight still fit in a
  prompt). Otherwise they are scaled down to 2048 px and re-encoded: as PNG when that fits, as
  JPEG when the picture has no transparency, halved until it fits; a GIF goes as its first frame.
  BMP and TIFF go as PNG. HEIC can't be read: export it as JPEG or PNG first. An agent that takes
  no pictures gets none, and the message says which were left out.
- **Text files** (UTF-8, up to 256 KB: Markdown, plain text, JSON, CSV, YAML, TOML, XML, SVG…)
  go in the message's text, whole as far as the message's 100,000-character cap allows: past it
  a file is cut (and says how much is missing) or named only.
- **CAD files** (STEP, IGES, FreeCAD, Rhino, STL, 3MF, OBJ, glTF) are imported into the design
  at once, as components of their own. A file joins the message once its import is in (its chip
  shows a spinner meanwhile, and **Send** waits), and the message tells the agent it was added; a
  failed import says why and the agent is told nothing of it. Taking a part's chip off the message
  leaves the part in the design (Undo removes it).
- Every file is named in the message. In the conversation the attached pictures show under it as
  thumbnails (hold the pointer over one for a bigger preview, click it to open the viewer, where
  the file's name is shown and ‹ › step through the message's pictures, together with the picture
  of the view); the other files are listed by name. Pictures in any of the formats above are
  decoded in the background, with a spinner until they are in. A file that can't be attached says
  why.

Files stay with their message: one queued while the agent works keeps its files, and one sent
again after a sign-in sends them again. When several queued messages go as one prompt, their
files go with it, at most eight; the rest are named in the chat and not sent. **New chat**
clears the files waiting on the chips too.

## Typing while the agent works

The input stays enabled during a turn. **Enter** queues the message: it shows in the conversation
as a **Queued** bubble that you can **Edit** or remove (×) until it is sent. Several queued
messages go as one prompt, in order, when the turn ends normally.

- **Send now** (on the bubble, or **Ctrl+Enter** / **Cmd+Enter** in the input) stops the current
  step, waits for the agent to say it stopped, then sends the queue as the next prompt, with a
  short note that the agent's previous step was interrupted. What the interrupted message changed
  undoes as one step, like any other message.
- **Stop** (the square next to the input, or **Esc** in the input) stops the agent and keeps
  the queue: the bubbles wait for **Send**.
- **New chat** (the header button, **Ctrl+Shift+L** / **Cmd+Shift+L** with the chat focused)
  stops what runs, clears the conversation, the queue and the files on the chips, and starts a
  fresh session on the same agent, keeping the agent and its mode. It asks first when a message
  is running or queued, or files are waiting. The design's undo history is untouched.

## Agents

Preferences → AI → **Agents** lists every agent the chat can use, each with its kind (a program or
an endpoint), version or model, whether it looks signed in, **Test**, **Default** (the one a new
conversation starts with), its own permission setting, and **Remove** for the ones you added.

### Found by themselves

SolidCraft looks for agents that speak the [Agent Client Protocol](https://agentclientprotocol.com)
on your `PATH` and in the usual install folders a desktop app's `PATH` often misses (npm's
global folder, nvm, Volta, bun, `~/.local/bin`, `~/.grok/bin`, Homebrew, `%APPDATA%\npm`). For each one it
shows its **version** (from `--version`, given three seconds) and whether it looks **signed in**.
Version checks and agent sessions also use those folders on their `PATH`, so adapters can find
runtimes such as Node when SolidCraft is opened from Finder or the Dock. Existing absolute
`PATH` entries keep their order; no shell startup files are run.
SolidCraft only checks whether the agent's own login file (`~/.claude/.credentials.json`,
`~/.codex/auth.json`, `~/.gemini/oauth_creds.json`, …) or one of its key variables exists. It never
reads the file and never starts the agent to find out. On macOS Claude Code keeps its login in
the keychain, so SolidCraft doesn't guess there.

| Agent | What to install |
|---|---|
| Claude Code | `npm install -g @agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp` (the ACP adapter for Claude Code) |
| Codex | `npm install -g @agentclientprotocol/codex-acp` |
| Google Antigravity | Google's ACP server, a separate download from Google's `agy` command (which has no ACP mode): take the zip for your system from the [ACP registry](https://agentclientprotocol.com/registry), unzip it and put `agy_acp_server.par` (`agy_acp_server.exe` on Windows) on your `PATH`. The zip also holds `localharness_external`: leave the two together. It signs in itself (browser). |
| OpenCode | `npm install -g opencode-ai` (`opencode acp`) |
| XAI Grok | [Grok Build installer](https://docs.x.ai/build/overview), then `grok login` (`grok agent stdio` speaks ACP) |
| GitHub Copilot CLI, Qwen Code, goose | listed with their install command when missing |

The panel lists agents that aren't installed with their install command and a **Copy** button.
**Refresh** looks again after you install one. **Test** starts an agent briefly, asks it for a
session and ends it again.

### XAI Grok

Install **Grok Build** and run `grok login` in a terminal to sign in with your Grok account.
In SolidCraft, open **AI → Refresh**, select
**XAI Grok**, then **Connect**. You can make it the default under
**Preferences → AI → Agents**.

SolidCraft reuses Grok Build's sign-in in `~/.grok/auth.json`; it checks only whether that file
exists and does not read or copy its tokens. If sign-in is needed, the panel offers Grok's own
sign-in methods. You can also run `grok login` again and reconnect. Grok controls model access
and usage limits for your account. This connection does not require an API key in SolidCraft.
Grok Build also supports `XAI_API_KEY` for users who choose API authentication.

### Add agent…

- **Installed agent:** your own entry for an installed agent, for example with other arguments.
- **Custom command:** any other program that speaks ACP on stdin and stdout, such as
  `my-agent --acp`. SolidCraft starts it directly, not through a shell.
- **OpenAI-compatible API:** a preset (Ollama `http://localhost:11434/v1`, LM Studio
  `http://localhost:1234/v1`, OpenAI) or a custom URL, the model name, and an optional key.
  The key goes into the system keychain (Keychain on macOS, Credential Manager on Windows, the
  Secret Service on Linux) and is only ever sent over HTTPS or to this computer. **Test** asks the
  endpoint for its models. For these agents SolidCraft runs the conversation itself, with the
  same tools, limits and questions as for a coding agent, and at most 24 model requests per
  message.

## Signing in

If a coding agent isn't signed in, it says so and the panel shows **Sign in to the agent** with
the agent's own ways to sign in:

- **A command for a terminal**, e.g. `claude-agent-acp --cli auth login --claudeai`, with a **Copy**
  button. Run it in a terminal, sign in there, then press **I've signed in: connect again**.
- **A button** for agents that sign in by themselves (Codex's ChatGPT login opens your browser).
- **A variable to set** for agents that take a key from the environment. The panel has no field
  for a coding agent's key, on purpose.

Whatever you typed before signing in is sent once the agent is ready.

## What the agent can do

The agent reaches the open design only through SolidCraft's own tools (the
[MCP server](mcp.md)), which SolidCraft hands it when the chat starts. That server is named
`solidcraft-app`, so an MCP server you set up yourself under the name `solidcraft` (as in
[client configuration](mcp.md#client-configuration)) doesn't take its place:

- **Read the design:** list commands, inspect features, sketches and parameters, measure,
  take pictures of the view.
- **Change the design:** run any modelling command, alone or in a batch. Changes show in the
  window as they happen.
- **One undo per message:** everything the agent changes while answering one message becomes
  a single undo step, named after your message. The conversation shows *N changes, one undo
  step* with **Undo these changes** while nothing else has happened since.
- **Tool cards:** each tool call shows as a card with its state; click it to see what it returned.
- **Formatted text:** the agent's answers show as Markdown: headings, lists, quotes, code blocks
  (with **Copy**), bold, italic, `code` and links (web links only; each link is a button that opens
  it in your browser). What you type, and the agent's thoughts, stay plain text.
- **Attach view:** tick it to send a picture of the current view with your message, for agents
  that take pictures. The picture is taken when the agent starts on the message and then shows as
  a small thumbnail under it. Hold the pointer over the thumbnail for a bigger preview that stays
  while you do; click it to open the viewer (the message's pictures one at a time, with **‹** and
  **›** or the arrow keys, closed with Esc or a click outside). A long message scrolls inside its
  box, so **Send** and the buttons beside it stay in view.

## Permissions

Preferences → AI → **Permissions** decides what the agent may do without asking, for every agent;
each agent can have its own setting in its row.

- **Ask every time:** every change to the design and every file action waits for **Allow**,
  **Always allow** or **Deny** in the panel.
- **Auto-allow model edits** (the default): modelling commands run at once; saving, opening, exporting,
  importing, starting a new design, any command given a file name, and undoing past the start of
  your message still ask.
- **Allow everything:** nothing asks. The page warns you: the agent can then save, overwrite and
  replace your design.

**Always allow** remembers that command for that agent. The page lists what you allowed this way,
per agent, with **Reset**.

These settings cover SolidCraft's tools. A coding agent's own tools (its shell, its file edits)
follow the agent's own mode, which you pick in the panel's header. When an agent asks before
using one of SolidCraft's tools, SolidCraft answers for you, since its own gate checks the call,
and notes it in the chat as *Auto-allowed*. With **Allow everything**, or after **Always allow**,
the agent's other questions are answered the same way and noted too.

What counts as "a command given a file name": a parameter that holds a file or folder (`file`,
`dir`, `output`, …), or `path` and `source` when the value reads like a file name (a separator, `~`,
a leading dot or a known extension), or any value of those in a command that exports, imports,
saves, opens or inserts. A sweep's or pattern's `path` (curve ids) and an occurrence's `path`
(ids) are geometry and run without a question.

## What it can't do

- **Files wait for you** unless you chose **Allow everything**. **Cancel** or **Stop** declines
  everything that's waiting, and a question nobody answers is declined after four minutes. The
  [MCP server's folder limits](mcp.md) still apply after you allow: the design's folder, the
  recovery folder and the server's own scratch folder.
- **A limit per message.** The agent may make 24 changes per message by default; you can set
  the number on the AI page. Reading the design doesn't count. When it reaches the limit, it's
  told to stop and report what's left; send another message to let it carry on.
- **No crash reports,** whatever the permissions. Crash reports can hold other designs and file
  paths.
- **Not the rest of the app.** It can't click the interface, change settings, quit, or drive the
  chat itself.
- **Its own tools stay off where we can turn them off.** SolidCraft declares no file system and
  no terminal to the agent, runs it in an empty working folder of its own, and asks the Claude
  Code adapter to turn off its shell, file and web tools for the session.

When the panel's agent is stopped, another agent is picked, or SolidCraft quits, the agent and
every program it started (the CLI it wraps, its MCP server) are stopped.

## Privacy

Nothing goes anywhere except to the agent you run, or the endpoint you added. SolidCraft starts
a coding agent as a program on your computer and talks to it over its standard input and
output. What the agent sends to its own service, under your account and that service's terms,
is between you and that service, exactly as when you use the agent in a terminal. SolidCraft
never sees, stores or passes on a coding agent's password, token or key. An endpoint's key is
kept in the system keychain and sent only to that endpoint. SolidCraft's own connection to the
agent's tools uses a random per-launch token in a file only you can read, which never passes
through the agent.

## Trying it without an account

A scripted test agent is in the source tree. It makes a block, rounds it and measures it, with
no model behind it:

```sh
cargo build --release -p solidcraft-ui-egui --example acp_test_agent
```

Then add it under Preferences → AI → **Add agent… → Custom command** with the path of
`target/release/examples/acp_test_agent`. Put "save" in your message to see an Allow / Deny card,
or "ask" to see the agent ask its own permission.
